articles.title: Marcos’ critics should be silent after Romualdez’ arrest, says Lacson
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — The arrest of former House Speaker and presidential cousin Rep. Martin Romualdez should hush President Marcos’ critics, Sen. Panfilo Lacson said on Monday evening. “With the…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The arrest of former House Speaker and presidential cousin Rep. Martin Romualdez should hush President Marcos’ critics, Sen. Panfilo Lacson said on Monday evening.

“With the arrest of his cousin, former Speaker Romualdez, the President’s critics who have accused him of weak leadership and a lack of resolve in confronting the flood-control mess should now be silenced by his actions,” Lacson stated in a social media post.
“Let the trial proceed and let the evidence speak. Most importantly, the former Speaker is now given his day in court,” Lacson also said.

In his last State of the Nation Address, Marcos vowed that the cases against his cousin in connection with the flood control mess would still be pursued. This is amid accusations that Marcos is shielding his allies in the corruption scandal, and instead targeting the opposition.

At 7:20 p.m., Romualdez was arrested at Cardinal Santos Medical Center in San Juan City for plunder after supposedly receiving P7.44 billion worth of kickbacks from government projects, including flood control infrastructure from 2022 to 2025.
At around 4 p.m., hours before the news of his arrest, Romualdez was rushed to the hospital after a “cardiovascular event” and a panic attack, according to Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla.

Lacson also commended the Office of the Ombudsman, which filed the plunder case against the congressman earlier today, saying, “The Ombudsman likewise deserves all the praise and support from the Filipino people.”
Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla previously characterized Romualdez as a “central figure” in the flood control mess, noting that it would be difficult to go against plentiful resources.
It was government contractors Curlee and Sarah Discaya in 2025 who first linked the former Speaker to the infrastructure anomalies.
According to the Discayas, Quezon Rep. Marvin Rillo introduced Romualdez to them as his close friend when Rillo demanded kickbacks in exchange for government contracts.

In early 2026, two witnesses linked the Discaya couple to Romualdez, alleging that a broker for a South Forbes Park home had introduced them to Curlee Discaya, who said it was the former House Speaker who bought the property.

Romualdez previously denied having any role in the flood control scheme, with his lawyers pressing that the congressman had been prejudged by the Ombudsman as a mastermind figure in the infrastructure ordeal. /cb

articles.title: Laoag boosts barangay emergency response with new vehicles
articles.summary: SAN ILDEFONSO, Ilocos Sur — The city government of Laoag in Ilocos Norte has begun distributing the first batch of multipurpose vehicles to the city’s 80 barangays to strengthen their capacity to…

blocks.text: SAN ILDEFONSO, Ilocos Sur — The city government of Laoag in Ilocos Norte has begun distributing the first batch of multipurpose vehicles to the city’s 80 barangays to strengthen their capacity to respond to emergencies and other community needs.
The city government announced this on Monday, Sept. 7, noting that the vehicles were funded by the city government through the initiative of Mayor James Bryan Alcid.
Each multipurpose vehicle is equipped with a stretcher, oxygen tank, first-aid kit, blood pressure apparatus, ladder, and chainsaw, among other equipment needed during emergencies.
The vehicles are intended to serve various barangay needs, particularly during medical emergencies, disasters and other situations requiring immediate assistance.

With the additional vehicles, barangay officials are expected to respond more quickly to emergencies and provide assistance to residents, particularly during calamities and other urgent situations. /mcm

articles.title: Search continues for missing Benguet resident
articles.summary: BAGUIO CITY — Search and rescue operations are underway for a man who has been missing since Sept. 3 in Barangay Sagubo, Kapangan, Benguet. The missing man was identified as Raul Aludos Juan, a…

blocks.text: BAGUIO CITY — Search and rescue operations are underway for a man who has been missing since Sept. 3 in Barangay Sagubo, Kapangan, Benguet.
The missing man was identified as Raul Aludos Juan, a resident of the barangay.

His disappearance was reported to the Kapangan Municipal Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Office (MDRRMO) around noon on Sept. 5. Barangay officials and local volunteers immediately conducted an initial search but failed to locate Juan by evening.

The municipal disaster office later activated its search and rescue team and coordinated with barangay officials, police and the Bureau of Fire Protection for operational briefings and continuing field operations.
Authorities appealed to residents to report any information that could help locate Juan.
They may contact the Kapangan MDRRM Office at 0919-533-6001, Kapangan police at 0998-598-7789, BFP at 0950-143-1993, or the Rural Health Unit at 0907-210-0468. /mcm

articles.title: Plans for flagship local government overhaul on hold after legal advice
articles.summary: Angela Rayner to announce review into local government shake-up as decisions on four areas withdrawn and 16 paused

blocks.text: Plans for a major reorganisation of local government have been put on hold after the government received new legal advice that suggested they might not comply with the law.

The Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government (MHCLG) said the review is to ensure the process is robust and aligns with the new government’s aim to “rewire the state”, and follows “updated and privileged legal advice”.

The reorganisation plans, announced in December 2024, proposed the abolition of the current two-tier system of districts and counties in favour of a smaller number of unitary authorities – or so-called “mega councils” – covering large geographical areas.
At least eight councils had launched legal challenges or were considering doing so due to opposition to the government’s choice of boundaries for new councils.
Reform UK-led Kent county council is set to consider a judicial review at a meeting on Tuesday after it did not receive a response from the government to a letter setting out concerns.
Plans for reorganisation in Essex, Hampshire, Norfolk and Suffolk have been withdrawn in the light of new legal advice.

Councils in Essex launched legal action in June after it emerged that its own preferred option to create three unitary councils in the county was backed by senior government officials but rejected by the then communities secretary Steve Reed.

There has been little appetite for the proposals within local government, with many councils regarding the changes as expensive and time-consuming, and offering little in the way of cost savings that would ease local authorities’ dire financial crisis.
Decisions on 14 further areas will be reviewed and paused alongside the cases of Cambridgeshire + Peterborough and West Sussex, which are yet to have a decision confirmed.

The government will also confirm that local elections in May 2027 will go ahead on existing council boundaries, saying it remains committed to effective and sustainable local government and simplifying these structures.

Communities secretary Angela Rayner is expected to tell parliament on Monday: “As we are now more determined than ever to devolve power closer to the people we represent, it’s only right that as a new secretary of state I make sure that everything we do is working towards that plan to change Britain, without delay.
“The prime minister told the House last week he was ‘prepared to look at local government reorganisation’ and he asked me as his communities secretary to ‘do that’.
“In that context, in light of legal advice, I want to satisfy myself firstly that the right process is in place, that it is robust, and of course complies with the law.
“And, secondly, I want to fully test whether our proposals for local government reorganisation meet the priorities of a new administration and a new prime minister, and any additional considerations.
after newsletter promotion
“I do not take this lightly. I recognise the huge amount of work that has already gone into progressing reorganisation in each of these areas and I am very grateful for it.”
MHCLG said reorganisation in Surrey will not be affected by the review and the two new unitary authorities, East and West Surrey, will go live in April 2027.

Cllr Sean Matthews, chair-elect of the County Councils Network, said: “Many of our members will be relieved that the decisions they viewed as damaging to local services and financially unsustainable have been withdrawn or are being reviewed. For our councils that do want to proceed with reorganisation in their area, we will support them in their next steps and we will be seeking further clarity from government in the coming days.

“With the government clearly listening to our concerns, we now stand ready to work with ministers. Where reorganisation is desired, this review must ensure a robust, legally compliant process in line with the original criteria. This should include establishing realistic implementation timescales and ensuring that any further decisions only create sustainable new unitary councils capable of improving local services.”

Jonathan Carr-West, chief executive, Local Government Information Unit (LGIU), said: “What began as the most ambitious change to local government in a generation now looks in danger of becoming a colossal white elephant – a huge drain on time, resources and goodwill. Those councils undergoing local government reorganisation have been trying to implement a massively complex project, under intense pressure and to very challenging timescales. Our overriding concern is that local government leaders, staff and councillors have strained every sinew to meet the deadlines set by MHCLG. Today’s announcement – whatever the reasons behind it – rides roughshod over 1000s of hours of work.
“If the prime minister is serious about his ambitions to rewire the state, then lessons must be learned from this debacle and learned fast.”

articles.title: Russia announces it is closing Germany's consulate in St. Petersburg
articles.summary: The tit-for-tat reaction comes after Germany said it is shuttering Russia's consulate in Bonn and its cultural center in Berlin.

blocks.text: The Russian Foreign Ministry announced on Monday that it is closing Germany's consulate in St. Petersburg.
The German consulate in St. Petersburg must cease its operations by September 18 the latest, according to Russia's Foreign Ministry.

"It was the German authorities who, once again, provoked a new round of escalation in bilateral relations," the Foreign Ministry said, adding Berlin "bears full and complete responsibility" for the consequences.
The move is a direct response to Germany's closure of the Russian consulate in Bonn and Russia's cultural center in Berlin.

Germany recently announced those measures after it said Russia was responsible for an attempted drone attack at Leipzig Airport. Russia has called the idea that it is behind the attack an absurd fabrication.
More to come...

articles.title: U.K. government slams 'thuggish' anti-migrant protesters, after demonstrators block port
articles.summary: The British government on Monday condemned the "intimidating and thuggish behaviour" of anti-immigrant demonstrators who converged on a port in southern England where migrants were brought ashore…

image.caption: Police officers blocked anti-immigration protesters in Portsmouth, England, on Sunday, after activists blocked off a road leading to a busy ferry port. (PA Images/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New

The British government on Monday condemned the "intimidating and thuggish behaviour" of anti-immigrant demonstrators who converged on a port in southern England where migrants were brought ashore after crossing the English Channel.
Coast guard assisted boat carrying 140 people crossing English Channel from France
Hundreds of protesters, many dressed in dark clothing and wearing masks, faced off with police in Portsmouth late Sunday in an attempt to prevent lifeboats from bringing the migrants to land.
They then tried to block buses carrying the new arrivals to a processing facility for asylum seekers.
"The right to peaceful protest is fundamental to our democracy, but it must never cross a line into disorder," the government said in a statement.

The Portsmouth protest came a day after hundreds of masked anti-immigration protesters blocked roads leading to Britain's busiest ferry port of Dover on Saturday, clogging traffic and disrupting travellers as well as cargo vehicles heading for France .
Both groups appeared to be led by Daniel Thomas, an ally of veteran far-right activist Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, better known as Tommy Robinson.
We went on patrol with a migrant aid group on the French coast
Successive U.K. governments have struggled to stop people — more than 40,000 last year — making the dangerous journey across one of the world's busiest shipping lanes.
The issue has been depicted as a crisis by politicians, including Nigel Farage of the hard-right party Reform UK, and has been used as a rallying point by anti-immigration activists.

items: In northern France, beaches turn to border zones as migrants wait months to cross the English Channel

blocks.text: British Prime Minister Andy Burnham's government says stepped-up law enforcement co-operation between Britain and France has helped reduce the number of people making the crossing so far this year by more than 40 per cent compared with 2025.

The boat carrying about 140 people to Portsmouth had left early Sunday from Normandy, far west of the beaches near Calais, France, where most departures have taken place — making it a much longer and riskier journey.
Britain's Maritime and Coastguard Agency spokesperson said lifeboats, a coast guard helicopter and a plane were involved in the operation to bring the migrants to shore.

articles.title: Trump administration attacks UK plans to boost traditional media on social platforms
articles.summary:
US embassy says Downing Street’s plan to give BBC, ITV and other established media more online visibility carries risk of ‘censorship’

The Trump administration has raised “serious concerns”…

blocks.text: The Trump administration has raised “serious concerns” over Downing Street’s plan to force YouTube and other digital platforms to hand more prominence to established broadcasters, warning the move risks “facilitating censorship”.

In a pointed intervention, the US government said the proposals to boost traditional media outlets in social media algorithms could “establish a template that authoritarian regimes could invoke to justify more control over online content”.
It also warned it could undermine “independent journalists” and amount to “extraterritorial censorship of protected speech by Americans online”.

The statement, made via the US embassy in London, raises the stakes in the plans to give the likes of the BBC, ITV and other established media more visibility on increasingly dominant digital platforms.

Ministers, regulators and public service broadcasters have suggested new rules are needed to counter growing misinformation online as people increasingly turn to less regulated online platforms such as X, YouTube and TikTok.

In a consultation this year, the UK government said it would consider legislating should the platforms not act to prioritise trustworthy content. However, Washington claimed such a plan risked effectively removing the content of “independent journalists” over established outlets.

“Preserving a free, open internet and protecting freedom of expression online are top priorities for the Trump administration,” it said. “A framework that empowers governments to influence which sources receive preferential visibility risks becoming a mechanism for viewpoint-based censorship.

“If the UK compels platforms to boost government-preferred media in algorithmic feeds, the effect on a government-disfavoured speaker or media source’s reach is not meaningfully different than outright removal. The US government would likely consider such a measure as facilitating censorship.”

The administration has asked what safeguards will be in place to ensure “any biases and preferences of UK government officials and third-party organisations” do not influence the plan in ways that disadvantage “independent or minority-viewpoint journalism”.

A spokesperson for the Department for Culture, Media and Sport said: “We welcome engagement and responses to our media green paper. We believe strongly in free expression and fair competition, and any action we take will ensure these are protected.”
Insiders say any measures would only affect the UK. The US complaint highlights its readiness to fight for the largely US-based tech companies that run the world’s largest digital platforms.
Donald Trump also has a long record of attacking and bypassing the established media, regularly accusing major outlets of “fake news” and biased coverage. He often tries to reach supporters online.

The US president is still engaged in his lawsuit with the BBC over an episode of Panorama in which it spliced together one of his speeches. The BBC has apologised for the edit, but stated the show did not defame Trump.
Social media companies have previously been sceptical about artificially boosting the prominence of traditional media, arguing that it goes against the principle of creator content.
Online content creators have compared the proposals to state control and fear their content would be pushed down the rankings as a result.
Simon Squibb, a UK YouTube creator, said he was encouraged that his concerns were shared by an “entity that I think politicians will listen to”.
“This is a very dangerous potential direction for the UK to go in,” he said. “I’m happy that the USA has stepped in.”
Supporters of the enforced prominence plans have couched them as a way of dealing with misinformation and preserving culturally British content.

However, the government has also been clear that it wants to help public service broadcasters survive the economic turmoil created by the rise of digital platforms, which all media companies are confronting.

articles.title: Federal investigators search for cause of Amazon cargo jet crash that killed five
articles.summary:
Theories begin to emerge that plane may have landed too fast and too far down the runway to be able to stop in time

Federal investigators got plans under way on Monday for determining what…

blocks.text: Federal investigators got plans under way on Monday for determining what caused an Amazon cargo jet to barrel off a runway at Miami international airport on Sunday afternoon and crash, killing five people and injuring five others.

Video footage showed the jet wobbling a little and coming in fast and far along the runway, with storm clouds clearly visible in the sky behind, as expert theories began to emerge that the Boeing 767 may have landed too fast and too far down the runway to be able to stop in time.

The aircraft overshot the runway around 2pm Sunday after arriving in south Florida from San Juan, Puerto Rico, and plowed across a perimeter road used by warehouse workers and other businesses before coming to rest in a parking lot. With its nose tipped forward, flames then burst out of part of the jet and thick, dark smoke began billowing into the air.
Authorities have not named the five who died or the five people injured, three critically, or released exact details on where the casualties were located.

The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) said chairwoman Jennifer Homendy would hold a news conference later on Monday. US transportation secretary Sean Duffy said on social media that the agency would “assess the scene after an Amazon cargo plane overran the runway”.

The crash trapped the pilot and copilot in the cockpit and some occupants in cars, said Miami-Dade rescue fire chief Ray Jadallah said. The agency said crews also had to extricate a person who was trapped under a vehicle.
Jadallah described the incident as a “very complex situation” where the plane crashed into multiple vehicles as it ran off the tarmac, trapping several people inside their vehicles.

Video of the Amazon Prime Air Boeing 767-33A, operated by contractor 21 Air, posted to social media show it touching down far along the runway. Other footage shows the plane with a left hand wheel on the landing gear still a little above the ground as the jet speeds down the tarmac, apparently abnormally fast, and then overruns the end of the runway, where the right undercarriage collapsed and the wing caught fire.

Typically, the landing zone is within the first 3,000 ft (914 meters) of a runway. Aviation safety expert Steve Arroyo said if it was beyond that area, the plane should normally have aborted the landing and gone around for another attempt.

Mary Schiavo, who is a pilot and former inspector general of the transportation department, said video posted online shows the Amazon plane floating above the runway for an extended period without flaring the nose upward to force the main landing gear onto the ground.
Storm clouds can be seen in the area and strong winds reported. Schiavo said that if the plane had a tail wind, that could have contributed to it floating further down the runway.
“A tail wind would certainly add to your troubles if you’ve already given up a good chunk of the runway by not touching down and landing right away,” Schiavo said.

Miami airport is not equipped with “arresting beds”, systems of lightweight, crushable material that the federal aviation authority (FAA) says have been installed at more than 120 airports nationwide at the end of runways to help safely stop planes that overshoot.
Some 200 emergency personnel responded to the incident, finding the plane with heavy flames and smoke from a complex engine compartment fire, the fire department said.

The flight operators, 21 Air, is a cargo carrier based in North Carolina. The 32-year-old Boeing 767 was originally built to carry passengers and flew for several airlines for more than two decades before being converted to a cargo plane in 2015, according to flight-tracking site Flightradar24.

More than 160 flights were canceled and nearly 325 delayed by late Sunday, according to FlightAware, a website that tracks flight disruptions. Officials from Orlando international airport, more than 200 miles north of Miami, said some flights were diverted there. Flights later resumed, although two runways at the busy airport remained out of service on Monday morning.

Kelly Nantel, an Amazon spokesperson said in a statement on Sunday: “We can confirm that an Amazon Air plane operated by 21 Air experienced an incident while attempting to land at Miami International Airport today. And Amazon said in a further statement that it would cooperate with any investigation.

“We’re heartbroken to learn that five people lost their lives in today’s incident at Miami international airport,” the company said. “Our deepest sympathies go out to the families, loved ones, and all those affected by this devastating loss.”

items: The Associated Press contributed reporting

articles.title: Carbon capture tech exists. Scaling it up is the hard part
articles.summary: Europe just opened a carbon capture and storage plant billed as the continent's largest. But global climate scenarios call for far more capacity than exists anywhere on Earth.

image.caption: CCS targets point sources, like at this coal plant: a single smokestack where CO2 can be captured before it disperses into the atmosphereImage: Florian Gaertner/photothek/IMAGO

blocks.text: For years there has been talk of capturing and storing the carbon dioxide generated by burning fossil fuels as one way to keep the planet from overheating. In fact, the United Nations' climate science body envisions somewhere between 350 to 1,200 gigatons of CO2 storage within the century to avoid the worst effects of climate change.
But is it really happening? Yes and no.

Carbon capture and storage, or CCS, is an effort to trap CO2 at what's called a point source. This might be a smokestack or at an ammonia factory — in other words, a single, concentrated spot where the planet-heating greenhouse gas is emitted.
After being captured, it is compressed and transported, usually using pipelines or trains, before being stored geologically — in aquifers or old oil reservoirs, for example.

CCS is related to, but distinct from, carbon dioxide removal (CDR), which involves pulling CO2 out of the atmosphere after it's already been emitted. That CO2 is often stored similarly to CCS, but uses very different technologies for capturing.

"Given the legacy of emissions in the atmosphere, given where we are in terms of emissions reductions, we're going to need these approaches," said Wil Burns, co-director of the Institute for Carbon Removal Law & Policy at American University.
"We just have to figure out how to use them thoughtfully and still keep our eye on the prize of decarbonizing."
The technology works, but scaling is another matter
The feasibility of CCS and CDR is a subject of much debate among scientists and climate campaigners.
Advocates for scaling up the technology as a key pillar of decarbonization say the main hurdle is getting more plants built, which would require government subsidies and policy intervention.

Without governments putting a price on carbon or offering tax credits, experts say it's hard to imagine investors shelling out for these expensive commercial projects. Renewable energy, by contrast, has become so cheap over time that it's often commercially viable on its own.
"It's ready to go, technologically. We know how to do this process," said Susan Hovorka, a geoscientist at the University of Texas-Austin, researching CCS since 1998.
Carbon capture: Is it feasible?
How CCS began

CCS traces its roots back to the 1960s, when oil companies began piping natural CO2 into oil fields for enhanced oil recovery — that's where captured CO2 is injected into old oil fields to help push more oil out of the ground. It wasn't until 1996 that the first large-scale CCS project designed to reduce emissions went online in Norway.
Progress since then has been slowly ramping up. In 2020, there were 26 operational commercial CCS facilities around the world. As of last summer, the number has nearly tripled.
But others say the technology remains in its infancy, and our real-world capabilities lag far behind our technical knowhow.

"What is not well-established and basically doesn't exist at scale is the commercial experience doing this," said Danny Cullenward, an economist at the University of Pennsylvania's Kleinman Center for Energy Policy. "And proving that it works; that it's easy, that it's cost-effective, that it can be deployed at large scale, that it works in lots of different places."

Researchers from the University of Texas-Austin recently revealedthat though small-scale pilot projects have been successful in injecting CO2 into the ground, many of the world's large-scale CCS initiatives are pumping far less into storage sites than promised.

And they are not unlimited. While previous estimates put the Earth's CO2 storage capacity somewhere between 10,000 and 40,000 gigatons, a new study foundthe number is just about 1,460 gigatons, meaning most CCS-reliant climate scenarios would breach the planetary limit for storage over the next 250 years.

blocks.caption: Visitors walk through the Northern Lights facility in Norway, where captured CO2 is compressed and prepared for injection thousands of meters beneath the seabedImage: Benoit Doppagne/BELGA/picture alliance

blocks.text: Climate models bet heavy on new technology

Starting this week, the European fertilizer giant Yara will open what it calls Europe's largest carbon capture project. It will harvest excess CO2 at its factory in Sluiskil Netherlands, liquefy it, and ship it to Norway's Atlantic coast to be stored in an underground rock formation, some 2,600 meters below the seabed.

That plant will only be able to capture 800,000 metric tons of CO2 annually. To meet that 350 gigaton threshold — the lower end of the UN's climate scenarios used to inform climate policy — would require about 5,800 more Yara-size plants to open tomorrow.

The International Energy Agency, another intergovernmental body that models climate data, projected7.6 gigatons of carbon will be captured every year by 2050, with almost all of it stored. Right now, the world's 77 operating plants are capable of capturing 64 million tons annually. That output would need to be multiplied by 119 over the next quarter-century to reach the IEA number.
"The scale of what's being called for in those scenarios is astronomically beyond any real activity that exists today," Cullenward said.
He says climate models tend to underestimate renewables and lean too hard on "gee-whiz" technologies.

That's because models basically have three ways to hit an ambitious climate target: add more renewables, use less energy, or bet on some new technology that solves the problem without forcing society to change much.
"If you tell a model to solve an impossible problem, it's like pouring water down a flight of stairs — it's going to find the fastest way to get to the bottom," Cullenward said.

blocks.caption: CO2 tanks at the Northern Lights storage facility where captured carbon — including from Yara's Sluiskil plant — is liquefied before being injected into a rock formation deep beneath the seabedImage: Alessandro Della Valle/KEYSTONE/picture alliance

blocks.text: A license to keep drilling?

One of the most contentious arguments about CCS is whether it represents a legitimate decarbonization solution or is a tactic from oil and gas companies to justify and prolong more fossil fuel extraction.

In 2023, about 80% of the world's CCS capacity was used for enhanced oil recovery, according to research and advocacy group, Oil Change International — ultimately increasing emissions and defeating CCS's climate benefit.
Some researchers also argue that CCS poses a moral hazard, or a situation where having a form of protection allows for more risk-taking.
On the other hand, advocates for the technology often talk of reserving CCS for what's called "hard-to-abate" industries, like cement.

"I don't think we're going to get to five or 10 or 20 gigatons a year of carbon removal," Cullenward said. "But we may need to get as much as we can and to me that's a reason to be more engaged rather than less engaged."
Why carbon capture needs a reality check

articles.title: 2027 budget: P197.3-B rail infra budget eyed
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Malacañang on Monday said the administration is pushing a P197.3-billion budget for rail infrastructure under the 2027 National Expenditure Program (NEP). The move is intended…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Malacañang on Monday said the administration is pushing a P197.3-billion budget for rail infrastructure under the 2027 National Expenditure Program (NEP).
The move is intended to accelerate the progress of the North-South Commuter Railway System, which is expected to ease commuters’ travel and stimulate the country’s economy.

“Under the Fiscal Year 2027 National Expenditure Program, P123.84 billion will be allocated to the project, which will connect Metro Manila, Bulacan, Pampanga, and Laguna,” Palace Press Officer Claire Castro said at a briefing.
“The said budget also includes P67.44 billion for Phase 1 of the Metro Manila Subway Project, which is expected to help ease traffic congestion in Metro Manila,” she added.

The budget also includes P1.17 billion for the LRT Line 1 Cavite Extension Project, P1.94 billion for the MRT Line 3 Rehabilitation Project, and P603 million for the LRT Line 1 South Extension Project.
The proposed P197.30-billion allocation is P73.18 billion, or 58.96 percent, higher than the P124.12 billion proposed for rail transport under the 2026 NEP. /mcm

articles.title: Sightings of Meghan at star-studded retreat fuel Cotswolds rumours
articles.summary:
Reports of Soho Farmhouse visit add to speculation Duke and Duchess of Sussex could be settling in the area

When the Duke and Duchess of Sussex landed back in England earlier this summer,…

blocks.text: When the Duke and Duchess of Sussex landed back in England earlier this summer, six years after they moved to California and quit as working royals, speculation was rife about where they would call home.

Now, members of the luxury countryside retreat Soho Farmhouse have said they spotted Meghan arriving for an early morning coffee, sparking speculation that the couple were settling down in the exclusive countryside enclave of north Oxfordshire. Correspondent for the Royalist Tom Sykes said the duchess was seen arriving at the Comfy Farm lounge before 9am, where she was introduced to senior staff members by name.
The Cotswolds club, set in 40 hectares (100 acres) of countryside and featuring a luxury spa, 40 discreet guest cabins, and an indoor-outdoor pool, is a hotspot for celebrities.

If it is true that the Sussex family are staying in a property near the club, their neighbours will include the Beckhams, who live within walking distance of Soho Farmhouse and are often seen enjoying dinners and strolls in the grounds.

Paul McCartney also visits with his fashion designer daughter, Stella, who has a house nearby. Meghan and Harry previously rented a house in picturesque Great Tew, a village full of thatched chocolate-box cottages a stone’s throw from the Beckhams.

Another potential neighbour is Geri Halliwell-Horner and her husband, Christian Horner, who live in a £9m former vicarage in nearby Banbury. They share a love of animals with Meghan and boast a menagerie on the estate including miniature donkeys. The Telegraph reported that the Sussexes left their rescue chickens back in Montecito but would transport their dogs over.

There have been rumblings of a royal return in the Cotswolds, with the local papers reporting on their move. Their children, Archie and Lilibet, are enrolled at a school for the new term, and parents at a school in the area have reported being sent letters reminding them to maintain the privacy of other children and parents and not to take pictures or share any information about others there.

blocks.caption: The picturesque village of Great Tew, Oxfordshire, where the royal couple previously rented a house. Photograph: Greg Balfour Evans/Alamy

blocks.text: Although the more than 200,000 members have made Soho House feel less exclusive to some, Soho Farmhouse is still a favourite venue for A-list stars including Taylor Swift, Kate Moss, Tom Cruise and Harry Styles. This could be because it costs £325 a month to be a member, which screens out many members of the public, and taking photographs inside any of its venues is strictly forbidden. The chain recently announced it had banned Meta glasses over privacy fears.

There could also be more royal reunions in the offing, as Princesses Beatrice and Eugenie are regulars at Soho Farmhouse. Eugenie was the first member of the royal family to visit the couple when they moved out to the US.

It is a venue that is likely to feel safe to Meghan. In Harry’s memoir, Spare, he wrote that Soho House on Dean Street was “her headquarters whenever she came to London”. He added: “Sometimes she just left her luggage at Soho House for weeks. They stored it without question. The people there were like family.” The couple met there for their first date.

During the same 2016 visit, Meghan was pictured cycling around the grounds of Soho Farmhouse with Made in Chelsea star Millie Mackintosh. She also reportedly hosted her hen party at the Cotswolds retreat in 2018.

blocks.caption: Prince Harry and Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, arriving for an awards show in London, 2020. Photograph: Hannah McKay/Reuters

blocks.text: Meghan is a close friend of Soho House executive Markus Anderson, who is thought to have introduced her to high society in London when she visited in 2016. The two met in 2011 in Anderson’s home country, Canada, as she filmed the TV show Suits.

Harry has several charitable events in the UK planned, including the WellChild awards in London at the end of this month. He will also be getting ready for the Invictus Games, to be held in Birmingham next summer. It has been reported that Meghan may be seeking acting roles, and she recently said she “sometimes” missed her old job and liked being around a crew when filming her Netflix cookery show.

The pair “love” the Oxfordshire countryside and reportedly made the Cotswolds their base when they visited earlier this year to see King Charles. They also rented a place when they were still working royals.
In Spare, Harry wrote: “We thought we could move into Oxfordshire full-time.
“We loved it out there. The air fresh, the verdant grounds plus, no paps.” It seems, perhaps, they have finally achieved this.
Soho House has been approached for comment. A spokesperson for the Sussexes declined to comment.

articles.title: Romualdez seeks continued hospital confinement amid plunder case
articles.summary: Former House Speaker Martin Romualdez on Monday sought the approval of the Sandiganbayan Third Division to grant him "continued hospital confinement" as he faces his plunder case.

blocks.text: Published September 7, 2026 9:59pm
Former House Speaker Martin Romualdez on Monday sought the approval of the Sandiganbayan Third Division to grant him "continued hospital confinement" as he faces his plunder case.

The Office of the Ombudsman earlier filed a ₱7.4-billion plunder charge against Romualdez, former Ako Bicol party-list Rep. Zaldy Co, and their two co-accused over their alleged involvement in a kickback scheme on flood control projects.
A few hours later, the anti-graft court’s Third Division issued arrest warrants against them. Romualdez at that time was already confined at Cardinal Santos Medical Center in San Juan City.
A "24 Oras" report said Romualdez was read the warrant and his rights in the presence of his lawyer.

In a nine-page manifestation addressed to the Sandiganbayan, Romualdez said that he was admitted to the hospital on September 7, 2026, and cited a medical history concerning his cardiovascular health and brain condition.
In the document’s prayer, Romualdez requested the following to the Court:

items: Authorize the serving of any arrest warrant upon him at the Cardinal Santos Medical Center
Allow him to remain under continuous lawful custody at the hospital for as long as inpatient confinement remains necessary, until he is medically cleared for transfer
Approve the custody and security protocol he proposed
Note that his submission to any warrant does not constitute a waiver of his previous objections to the case

blocks.text: Under the former speaker’s suggested custody and security protocols, he proposed that he be permitted to complete his booking and custodial documentation upon the service of the warrant.
Other requests under the proposed protocols include, among others:

items: Continuous medical custody by Dr. Rosalio Torres and other responsible officers of the hospital designated by the Court
Round-the-clock security guards
Visitor restrictions and a visitor log
No departure from or transfer out of the hospital without the court’s approval
Arrangements for his required court appearances consistent with medical advice and court orders

blocks.text: Heart, brain condition
In his manifestation for hospital arrest, Romualdez cited his medical history, including the angioplasty surgery he underwent in October 2024 due to his coronary artery disease.
The document stated that since then, he has required continuing cardiac monitoring and treatment.

“He is currently confined due to the following: Hypertensive Atherosclerotic Cardiovascular Disease, Unstable Angina, Coronary Artery Disease, S/P PCI (post percutaneous coronary intervention), Cerebrovascular Ischemic Disease, Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus, Hypertension, Dyslipidemia, and Primary Hypothyroidism,” the motion read.
“... Accused previously underwent Angioplasty Surgery on 05 October 2024 due to Coronary Artery Disease, and has since required continuing cardiac monitoring and treatment,” it added.

The document noted that Romualdez’s current status, as reflected in his medical certificates, justifies the necessity of continuous inpatient care, warning of risks should his treatment be interrupted or if he be transferred.

His attending physician, Dr. Torres, pledged to immediately inform the court if Romualdez’s health changes significantly or if he becomes healthy enough to be cleared for transfer out of the hospital.
Shortly after police secured the former Speaker at the Cardinal Santos Medical Center, he was placed under arrest and underwent the booking process in his hospital room.—LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Nathan Fielder teases Elizabeth Holmes documentary with eyebrow-raising trailer
articles.summary: Fielder's new film about Holmes, You Can See Everything, was made with documentarian and filmmaker Lance Oppenheim and centres on the weeks leading up to Holmes's incarceration in 2023.

image.caption: Nathan Fielder, creator and executive producer of the television series The Rehearsal, arrives at the 86th annual Peabody Awards on Sunday, May 31, 2026, at the Beverly Wilshire in Beverly Hills, Calif. (Chris Pizzello/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: Entertainment·New
Fielder's new film about Holmes, You Can See Everything, was made with documentarian and filmmaker Lance Oppenheim and centres on the weeks leading up to Holmes's incarceration in 2023.
Documentary centres on weeks leading up to Holmes's incarceration following 2022 Theranos fraud conviction
If you were wondering what possible antics Nathan Fielder has been up to after watching the latest season of The Rehearsal, we have your answer.

The Vancouver-born comedian, writer and director released a teaser late Sunday for his next project, a documentary about Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes who was famously convicted of fraud in 2022 after her company claimed to have created a type of blood testing that could screen for hundreds of diseases with small amounts of blood.
Fielder's film, titled You Can See Everything, was made with documentarian and filmmaker Lance Oppenheim and centres on the weeks leading up to Holmes's incarceration in 2023.
Oppenheim's previous works include Spermworld (2024), an FX-produced doc about sperm donors and Some Kind of Heaven (2020) about a Florida retirement community.

items: Theranos's Elizabeth Holmes sentenced to more than 11 years in federal prison

blocks.text: Fielder grew to fame with Nathan For You, a series on Comedy Central in which he gives horrible business advice to entrepreneurs. Previously he won (and baffled) Canadian hearts and minds with his appearances on CBC's This Hour Has 22 Minutes, in field segments titled "Nathan On Your Side" in 2008 and 2009.
You Can See Everything is being distributed by Gen Z favourite A24. The trailer features the company's signature high-saturation colour grading and overall eeriness.

It includes a roughly-one minute close-up conversation between Holmes and Fielder. The two intensely gaze at each other, as Holmes says, "Why would I deceive you? There's no — there's no reason for me to do that."
A long-ish silence follows and Fielder — with an incredulous expression on his face — says, "You're being real right now?"

The trailer was released in conjunction with a surprise screening Sunday at the Telluride Film Festival in Colorado. Reviews haven't yet surfaced from the screening, several critics posted their superlative-filled reactions to social media.

Film director Daniel Howat wrote on X after the screening that You Can See Everything "is maybe the most hysterical, shocking, insane documentary I’ve ever seen. Endlessly thought-provoking ... A work of genius."

Los Angeles-based music producer Erik Nordgren called it "easily the best film of the year for me, arguably on my best of the decade list. It turns from an uneasy-as-hell doc into something structurally, stylistically, and formally even more shocking. Like nothing I’ve ever seen."

The exchange harkens back to another uncomfortable, lesser-known interview Fielder conducted on This Hour Has 22 Minutes with former CBC president Hubert T. Lacroix in 2008. The two sit across from each other and Lacroix is put on the spot when he says he's a fan of Fielder's work but struggles to come up with any examples.
You Can See Everything is set to release in theatres next month.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Verity is a reporter for CBC in Montreal. She previously worked for the Globe and Mail, Toronto Star and the New Brunswick Telegraph-Journal.

articles.title: House panel eyes restoring funds to DepEd programs cut from 2027 NEP
articles.summary: The House Committee on Appropriations is considering restoring funding for several DepEd programs that were cut or not included in the proposed 2027 National Expenditure Program (NEP).

blocks.text: The House Committee on Appropriations is considering restoring funding for several Department of Education (DepEd) programs that were cut or not included in the proposed 2027 National Expenditure Program (NEP), with committee chairperson Mikaela Suansing asking the agency to submit a prioritized list of programs for possible augmentation.

Suansing raised the issue during the committee’s deliberations on DepEd’s proposed 2027 budget on Monday, noting that while the department’s overall proposed budget for next year is higher by ₱41.3 billion than this year's budget, much of the increase is set to go to Personnel Services.

“So just extrapolating from there, we see that there was a P16-billion cut. There was a P16-billion cut in the other programs, the other components, and MOOE [Maintenance and Other Operating Expenses], capital outlay," she said.
She added that the affected programs included special needs education, school-based feeding, ARAL and mental health, among others.
Suansing said that Congress had previously augmented several of these programs during the last budget cycle.
“So siguro po titignan natin [perhaps we will look at] which among the programs which comprise the P16-billion decrease in MOOE and capital outlay, we can consider for augmentation.”
House asks: What happens if funding isn’t restored?
Suansing asked Angara to explain the consequences if the funding for the affected programs remained at the levels proposed in the 2027 NEP.
“What would happen if we’re unable to restore the funding for these particular programs?” she asked.
Angara said the impact would be particularly felt in the School-Based Feeding Program.
The 2027 NEP allocation is back at around ₱11 billion, compared with the roughly ₱26 billion Congress provided for the program in the 2026 GAA.
Angara said the lower allocation would mean a shorter feeding cycle.
“So right now you’re looking at 120 days instead of 180 days, which is the whole school year…” he said.
He said children who stop receiving meals before the end of the school year could fall back into the same problem the program seeks to address.
“…pag hindi natin pinakain for the remainder of the school year, babalik din sila. So in a way, parang you go forward, but you go back.”
(…if we don’t feed them for the remainder of the school year, they will return to the same condition. So in a way, you move forward, but then you go back.)
Angara also said the lower allocation would mean DepEd could not provide universal feeding for Grade 1.
“And the second is we won’t have universal feeding for Grade 1. So we’ll have it for Kinder, but not for Grade 1,” he said.
The department would also have less room to expand its central kitchens and provide more hot meals.
DepEd reports 45.8% utilization of 2026 feeding funds

Suansing also asked about DepEd’s ability to absorb the larger ₱26-billion feeding allocation in the 2026 GAA, recalling concerns about whether there would be enough milk suppliers and kitchens to implement the program.
Angara said the program currently had a 45.8% utilization rate, but explained that school-based feeding is tied to the school calendar and some payments carry over to the following year.
He said utilization had reached 90% in 2025 and 81% in 2024, indicating an improvement in the department’s ability to spend the funds.
Suansing said the figures suggested DepEd was on track to utilize the 2026 allocation.
ARAL faces zero funding in 2027 NEP
Suansing also pressed Angara on the ARAL program, recalling that Congress had funded the program during the previous budget cycle.
She asked how many students would be excluded if funding for ARAL were not restored.
“That would be all, but I think we would be forced to reallocate within the current budget," said Angara.
He said DepEd could potentially take money from other existing needs to keep the program running as he described ARAL as a potential “game changer” for learners who are falling behind.

DepEd’s supplemental budget request separately seeks funding for programs not covered or insufficiently funded in the 2027 NEP, including its learning recovery priorities. The department is seeking a total of ₱145.19 billion in supplemental funding.
Suansing said SpEd, along with other inclusive education programs, was among the areas Congress wanted to strengthen.
Angara said the department had also requested additional funding for special needs education, including personnel, facilities, equipment and program support.
The 2027 supplemental request includes ₱541.57 million for SPED, as well as funding for Madrasah, Indigenous Peoples education and multigrade education.
Mental health was likewise among the programs identified by lawmakers for possible augmentation.
The supplemental request includes funding for mental health and guidance services, school counselor associates and other learner support programs.
DepEd asked to re-prioritize ₱145B supplemental request
With DepEd seeking ₱145.19 billion in additional funding, Suansing acknowledged the difficulty of accommodating the entire request given the government’s fiscal space.
She asked Angara to submit a more streamlined and prioritized list of requests.

Suansing also asked DepEd to submit the re-prioritized list by Wednesday noon, citing the House’s upcoming plenary schedule and the chamber’s process of reviewing institutional budget requests through its Budget Amendment Review Subcommittee.
She nevertheless told DepEd that the committee would seek to accommodate its requests.
Earlier, Appropriations Vice Chair Maria Carmen Zamora said the committee had seen broad support from lawmakers for increasing, not cutting, DepEd’s proposed budget.

“Out of the 34 members who asked questions, I have not heard any single member who posed for the cut of the budget, but instead all of these 34, from the minority and majority, have proposed for the increase of the proposed budget," she said.
Zamora said lawmakers highlighted SNED, inclusive resource center construction, school-based feeding, computerization, school building, ARAL and mental health programs, among others.

DepEd’s proposed FY 2027 budget is ₱973.4 billion for the department proper, while its six attached agencies have a combined proposed allocation of about ₱2.56 billion, bringing the total to around ₱975.96 billion.

The department’s Personnel Services allocation is proposed to increase by 8.64% to ₱766.74 billion, while MOOE would decrease by 15.94% to ₱174.32 billion and Capital Outlay by 67.49% to ₱32.34 billion.
DepEd is seeking ₱145.19 billion in supplemental funding to address gaps in learning recovery, personnel, school infrastructure, learner support and inclusive education.
The committee subsequently terminated its deliberations on the proposed FY 2027 DepEd budget under House Bill No. 10858, including its attached agencies. — BM, GMA News

articles.title: Pakistan: Can creating new provinces fix governance?
articles.summary: Pakistanis broadly agree that the country needs more responsive and effective government, but many question whether simply creating more provinces is the solution.

image.caption: Supporters of creating more provinces say Pakistan's four existing provinces have become too large and centralized [FILE: April 2026]Image: Akhtar Soomro/REUTERS

blocks.text: A politically sensitive debate has reignited in Pakistan over whether its four-province system can effectively govern a country of around 260 million people.

Ahsan Iqbal, minister for planning and development, recently called for a national political debate on administrative reform. He proposed creating 12 to 15 new provinces or setting up 160 empowered district governments to improve governance and the delivery of public services.
Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi, who first raised the idea of an administrative "reset" in July, said on Saturday that any new administrative units should be created with public support.
Defense Minister Khawaja Asif, meanwhile, has called for greater decentralization and devolution of power to the grassroots.
Despite the growing calls to create new provinces, no formal decision has been taken.
Even within the ruling coalition, there is disagreement over how and when such reforms should be pursued.
There are also questions about whether creating smaller provinces improves governance, or whether devolving power directly to local governments would be more effective.
Basmati rice: India, Pakistan and the EU dispute
More provinces, better governance?
Pakistanis broadly agree that the country needs more responsive and effective government, but many question whether creating more provinces is the solution.

"Smaller provinces are not a substitute for empowered local governments. Even with smaller provinces, you will still need empowered local governments to make the system effective and improve service delivery to the people," Miftah Ismail, a former finance minister and economist, told DW.
Supporters of creating more provinces argue that Pakistan's four existing provinces — Punjab, Sindh, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, and Balochistan — have become too large and overly centralized.
Iqbal, the planning minister, has argued that the existing system has not delivered adequate improvements in health, education, and other social services.
Interior Minister Naqvi, on the other hand, has called for an administrative structure that is better suited to Pakistan's growing population.
But there is disagreement over the solution.

"Without effective local governments, whether there is one province or 25, decision-making will remain centralized at the provincial level," Abid Qaiyum Suleri, executive director of the Sustainable Development Policy Institute, an Islamabad-based think tank, told DW.

He said any proposal for new provinces or administrative units should be assessed against potential improvements in local tax collection and the costs of creating new provincial institutions, including secretariats, assemblies, and bureaucracies.
Suleri stressed that it should also be examined whether such changes would deliver justice and public services more effectively.
Can Pakistan still help end the US-Iran war?
Altering the political balance

"Pakistan's history suggests that empowering local governments is a better choice in terms of governance and provision of services," Muhammad Shoaib, a political scientist and assistant professor at Quaid-i-Azam University in Islamabad, told DW.
The debate, therefore, is not simply about how many provinces Pakistan should have, but whether creating smaller units would actually make the government more responsive to citizens.
Creating new provinces could also affect the political balance in the country.
New provinces would mean new governments and assemblies, while potentially changing political representation and the distribution of federal resources.
Any attempt to redraw boundaries could also reopen disputes over water, taxation, and natural resources.

The political resistance is already tangible. Sindh's provincial assembly has opposed creating new provinces or administrative units in the province, while political groups have warned against dividing existing territories.
Why Pakistan may be too reliant on EU trade
A risky strategy?
Shoaib said dividing resources would present a major challenge, even if all provinces were reorganized at the same time.
"Even if all provinces are divided simultaneously, the division of resources like finances, water, and jobs, and special privileges for territories within provinces will be a challenge," he said.
"Challenges like these require lengthy negotiations and compromises for political consensus," he added.
The issue is therefore not only about administrative efficiency, as redrawing provincial boundaries could also redistribute political and economic power.
Ismail believes redrawing provincial boundaries would be risky, particularly in Sindh.
He said empowering existing local governments within current provincial boundaries would be a safer option.

"We can learn from the US and the southern states of India, where empowered small administrative units, while competing with each other, are more responsive to citizens and deliver better services," Ismail said.

Shoaib said Pakistan could also learn from other countries, particularly democratic systems that have empowered local governments and taken time to work through the division of large states into smaller units.
"In Pakistan's case, the risk of resistance and perpetual resentment is real. A partially finished division will aggravate existing ethnic tensions," he said.
For Pakistan, the debate is therefore about more than whether the country should have four provinces or 12 or 15.

It is about whether changing the administrative map can actually bring power, resources, and accountability closer to its people, and whether such a transformation can be achieved without creating new political and ethnic tensions.
