September 7, 2026
Zelenskyy says Russian drone targeted SBU chief's office

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Monday that a Russian drone which struck the headquarters of Ukraine's SBU security service in Kyiv on Friday had been aimed directly at the office of the agency's chief.
The revelation adds to the significance of one of the most high-profile Russian strikes on a Ukrainian government building since the start of the full-scale invasion.
SBU chief Oleksandr Poklad was not there at the time and was unharmed.
Zelenskyy said he had instructed the SBU to prepare an "appropriate, tangible response" and suggested Ukraine could retaliate in a similar manner.
Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha called the strike a "major escalation."
Black smoke was seen rising from the SBU building, close to the UNESCO-listed St. Sophia Cathedral.
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said at least 12 people were wounded in the wider attack on the capital, although it was not immediately clear whether any of them were injured at the SBU headquarters.
The strike also damaged nearby buildings and shattered windows in the area.
It was the first time the SBU headquarters had been hit since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022.

The SBU plays a central role in Ukraine's war effort and has carried out long-range and covert operations against Russian military targets. It was behind Operation Spiderweb in 2025, when drones targeted Russian strategic bombers at air bases deep inside Russia, as well as the 2022 bombing of the bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea.

articles.title: Sara Duterte trial recap, Sept. 7: '11th hour' admissions, switching articles
articles.summary: Three key moments and developments from Day 22 of the impeachment trial, September 7.

blocks.text: September 7, 2026 | 4:40pm

MANILA, Philippines — Nearly two-thirds of the confidential fund recipients that the House asked the Philippine Statistics Authority to check have no record of ever being born, married or dying, a statistician of the agency told the impeachment court Monday, September 7.

By the close of the day's proceedings, the defense had confirmed on the record that indeed, the odd and unusual names on those Office of the Vice President acknowledgment receipts are aliases — a disclosure the prosecution questioned for coming at the "11th hour."

PSA Assistant National Statistician Marizza Grande took the stand through direct, cross, redirect and two rounds of senator-judge questioning before being excused in the afternoon; the defense waived recross.

The court today spent its first hour on stipulations covering former DepEd special disbursing officer Edward Fajarda. The prosecution asked to recall his subpoena after a medical certificate showed he needs another 30 days to recover from a stroke.
The prosecution remains on Article I, which covers the alleged misuse of P612.5 million in confidential funds.
Here are the three highlights from today's proceedings.
1. PSA statistician: the 63% being non-existing is unusual
Grande testified that 1,685 of the 2,669 names the House good government committee submitted for verification in 2024 have no birth, marriage or death record.
This includes the now-infamous "Mary Grace Piattos" who's listed as having been paid confidential funds by the OVP.
Of 677 DepEd payees, 398 had no record of any kind; of 1,992 OVP payees, 1,287 had none.
Only 152 names across the full list returned a unique, single match.

The PSA also found 34 people who died before the 2022 disbursements — one, Marlene Sunga, dead since 1965 — and 25 minors, including infants barely a year old when the funds were supposedly released to them, based on the records.
Asked by Sen. Joel Villanueva to describe these findings, Grande confirmed it was unusual for 63% of all names on a list to not show up in their records.
She explained that her office normally sees a negative rate of 7 to 8% on walk-in requests for verification, and about 38% on the largest bulk request it had handled before.

Defense counsel Justin Nicol Gular used his cross to mark the limits of what the PSA can find out about the confidential fund payees. Under cross, Grande confirms PSA runs no field investigations and depends on what local registrars and foreign posts send it.
Registration is also not exactly universal: a tiny 3% of births go unregistered, and death registration sits at about 84 percent.
"We are testifying as to the availability of the record and not as to the existence," she said.
2. Defense belatedly says names are aliases

Sen. Risa Hontiveros asked defense counsel Justin Nicol Gular to clarify their position after observing the defense had been arguing two things at once — that the names on the receipts could be real people who happened to not be in the records, and that aliases would never appear in the records at all.
Gular was careful to say that the defense would be reserving its full position for its presentation of evidence, which will come after the prosecution concludes all four articles.
He added: "That is classified information, but these are in fact aliases, your honor, for the consideration of this court."

Prosecutor Mae Divinagracia then pointed out that the defense had two chances to state the same, in its answer to the impeachment articles and during pre-trial. Because it did not state its position on the authenticity of the names on the receipts, the prosecution built its case without assuming the names were bogus.
"With all due respect, it's already a tad too late for the defense, to be adopting the position that these are aliases," Divinagracia said.

"It's not only the defense who has the right to due process, even the prosecution is entitled to due process. We are entitled to know what we are working on, the theories of their case... We're already at the 11th hour, and there's still none. What is their position?" she added.

Lead defense counsel Sheila Sison replied that the prosecution must first discharge its burden of proof, and until it does, the defense may stay silent. "This is not yet the time for the defense to present its evidence, or whether we will even present evidence if the proper time comes," she said.
3. Prosecution reorders the remaining articles, drops two colonels

Lead prosecutor Gerville Luistro told the court the prosecution will present its evidence on unexplained wealth next, moving it ahead of bribery. Neither article is being dropped, she said. "The only thing that is being changed is the order of presentation."

Sen. Erwin Tulfo pressed her on whether the prosecution intends to present Cols. Raymund Dante Lachica and Dennis Nolasco, who served as security officers for OVP and DepEd's confidential funds, respectively.

Luistro confirmed the prosecution will not call either, saying the allegations of misuse and misappropriation have already been established. Luistro also put on record that the choice of witnesses is the prosecution's to make.

Escudero confirmed that right and noted the defense may still call the two, since both are listed as common witnesses in the pretrial order. Failing that, the court can summon a witness itself after both sides rest, but that witness would answer only senator-judges.
Police Maj. Jovelyn Magay, DepEd Assistant Secretary Sunshine Fajarda and COA's Bresilio Sabaldan are set to testify tomorrow.

articles.title: Weather tracker: Typhoon Saudel causes mass evacuations in south-east China
articles.summary:
Torrential rain causes widespread damage; while north-west South Africa hit by thunderstorms and central-southern US faces oppressive heat

Typhoon Saudel brought days of torrential rain to…

blocks.text: Typhoon Saudel brought days of torrential rain to the Zhejiang, Jiangxi, Fujian and Guangdong provinces in south-east China last week. The city of Putian, in Fujian province, recorded 416.5mm of rain in a 24-hour period between Thursday and Friday, with surrounding villages recording more than 500mm in the same period. In Fujian, authorities estimate that almost 600,000 people were evacuated from high-risk, flood-prone areas. A further 128,000 people in 53 counties were also affected across Jiangxi, with emergency evacuations affecting 9,000 people.

Flooding, landslips and infrastructure damage were reported widely in the region. More than 2,500 teachers and students were trapped in a school compound in the Zhejiang city of Wenzhou on Wednesday after extreme rainfall caused flash floods in low-lying areas. At least 1,260 people reportedly had to be rescued in Putian after a river embankment collapsed on Thursday, flattening 100 homes. On Saturday, a landslip in a village of Suichuan county, in Jiangxi province, killed three people and nine others remaining missing.
This is the seventh typhoon to affect China this year, and Saudel arrived shortly after Typhoon Narra dumped heavy rain on Guangdong, Hainan and Guangxi late last month.

The South African Weather Service implemented several thunderstorm warnings late last week, covering a large swathe of the northern and western provinces. Disruptive rainfall, damaging winds, excessive lightning and hail were all reported, with rainfall totals expected to have reached at least 75-100mm for parts of the Northern Cape and North West provinces over the weekend. In Johannesburg, eight families were evacuated from an apartment building after strong winds tore off a significant part of its roof.

Oppressive heat in the US affected states across the central-southern plains and the Mississippi valley this weekend, with maximum temperatures easily reaching the high 30s (Celsius; high 90s Fahrenheit). However, with high humidities, the heat indices in this region have been closer to 40-43C (105–110F). The unrelenting temperatures will continue across the midwest and southern US this week, with maximum temperatures continuing to reach the high 30s.

articles.title: DICT hopes Roblox-national ID age verification integration can be template for Meta
articles.summary: The DICT hopes success with integrating Roblox's age verification mechanisms with the national ID system can serve as a technical and policy template that Meta can follow

blocks.text: DICT. Department of Information and Communications Technology Secretary Henry Aguda on September 7, 2026.
Screenshot from House of Representatives Livestream
The DICT hopes success with integrating Roblox's age verification mechanisms with the national ID system can serve as a technical and policy template that Meta can follow

items: DICT Secretary Henry Aguda expressed hope that integrating Roblox's age verification and the Philippines' national ID system can serve as a model for Meta's social media age verification.
During a budget hearing, Aguda discussed a meeting with Meta and Roblox, where Roblox proposed using the national ID for age verification, allowing API calls based on digital biometrics.

Meta acknowledged technical challenges in implementing such integration globally and is sending a team to assess feasibility, while also making changes in the US following a settlement regarding teen access to its platforms.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – Department of Information and Communications Technology (DICT) Secretary Henry Aguda said the agency hopes success with integrating Roblox’s age verification mechanisms with the national ID system can serve as a technical and policy template that Meta can follow when it comes to social media age verification.
During the House committee on appropriations’ DICT budget hearing on Monday, September 7, Aguda was asked about the outcome of the meeting with Meta in Singapore as it related to age verification.

He explained that during the meeting — with social media company Meta Platforms and game development platform company Roblox — Roblox themselves broached the topic of using an integration of the Philippines’ national ID with their age verification systems.

According to Aguda, such a proposed system would simply be a qualifier to determine if a user is a certain age that can use specific age tiers of Roblox accounts. He said there is an eVerify solution within the national ID system that may allow for such to happen.

“Kahit na wala pang physical card, basta yung digital biometrics niyo nandoon na sa Philippine Statistics Authority, puwede na sila mag API calls.” (Even wihout a physical card, as long as the digital biometrics are with the Philippine Statistics Authority, they can make API calls.) These API or Application Programming Interface calls would allow Roblox to tell if a user is getting the content appropriate for their account.

blocks.caption: LIST: What Roblox has done to safeguard child users

blocks.text: According to Aguda, Meta cited technical complexities in performing this as it has not done such an integration anywhere in the world, and is worried that it would make around 170 countries it serves follow suit in requesting similar accommodations.
Meta is making some changes to how it operates in the United States in light of a settlement with US states that would add limits to how teens gain access and use its various social media platforms.
Aguda said Meta will send a technical working team to study the feasibility of the plans they’ve discussed with the DICT.

“We are hoping that if Roblox is successful in the integration, it can become a technical and policy template for the other social media platforms to follow,” Aguda said in a mix of English and Filipino.
The DICT is seeking P19.491 billion for its fiscal year 2027 budget. – Rappler.com

articles.title: UK government condemns 'thuggish' anti-migrant protests in Portsmouth
articles.summary: Hundreds gathered in Portsmouth after some refugees arrived by boat from France, a day after masked protesters disrupted traffic at the port of Dover.

image.caption: Hundreds of protesters gathered in Portsmouth following the arrival of about migrants who had crossed the English Channel from FranceImage: PA/PA Images/picture alliance

blocks.text: Britishminister Emma Reynolds on Monday slammed "thuggish" anti-migrant protests that blocked roads in the English coastal city of Portsmouth.
Hundreds of protesters gathered in Portsmouth on Sunday following the arrival of about 140 migrants who had crossed the English Channel from France, UK media reported.
"This is thuggish and intimidating behavior," Reynolds, who is Chief Secretary to the Treasury, told Sky News, adding that the police brought the Portsmouth protest under control.
The demonstration came a day after masked protesters disrupted traffic at Dover terminal, blocking routes to the busy ferry port.
Masked protesters in Dover
On Saturday, hundreds of masked people blocked traffic at England's port of Dover as part of an anti-migrant protest, halting ferry traffic between France and the UK.

Video footage showed demonstrators, reportedly backed by far-right groups, in balaclavas chanting "stop the boats," in a reference to refugees and migrants who attempt the dangerous English Channel crossing in a bid to reach Great Britain.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham's Labour Party government said that "the right to peaceful protest is fundamental to our democracy, but we condemn the behavior in Dover and the travel disruption it has caused."
The Dover demonstration caused a traffic jam of about four miles (6.4 km) and temporarily halted traffic into and out of the port.
Britain has struggled for years to curb small-boat crossings from France, although Reynolds said arrivals were down 43% from last year to about 17,000 so far this year.

articles.title: Minister condemns ‘thuggish’ far-right, anti-migrant protesters in Portsmouth – UK politics live
articles.summary:
Emma Reynolds says demonstrations ‘cross a line’

Good morning. John Healey is giving his first major speech on economic policy since he became chancellor seven weeks ago.…

blocks.text: Minister condemns ‘thuggish’ far-right, anti-migrant protesters in Portsmouth

Good morning. John Healey is giving his first major speech on economic policy since he became chancellor seven weeks ago. It is meant to be the main government news of the morning and, as Pippa Crerar writes in her preview story, Healey will argue the government’s plans to boost growth across the whole country will enable the British economy to “turn a corner”.
Healey’s deputy, Emma Reynolds, the chief secretary to the Treasury, has been giving interviews as part of the build-up.

But, as well as taking questions about growth and tax, Reynolds has also found herself taking questions about the latest far-right protest about immigration, triggered by a large boat carrying migrants arriving for the first time in Portsmouth.
Commenting on the behaviour of the protesters, who blocked roads and some of whom were masked, Reynolds said:

double quotation markThis is thuggish and intimidating behaviour. This is not peaceful protest. Obviously, as a politician, I absolutely support people’s right to peaceful protest. But this crosses a line and I just want to take the opportunity to thank the police and other emergency services who have brought this under control. We do not want to see this kind of behaviour anywhere, frankly.
Here is the agenda for the day.
Around 9.30am: John Healey, the chancellor, gives a speech on economic growth in the West Midlands.
11.30am: Downing Street holds a lobby briefing.
2.30pm: Angela Rayner, the housing secretary, takes questions in the Commons.
After 3.30pm: Emma Reynolds, the chief secretary to the Treasury, is due to make a statement to MPs.
Afternoon: MPs start debating the remaining stages of the health bill.
And Chris Bryant, the Northern Ireland secretary, is today meeting the Northern Ireland political leaders, as MLAs (members of the legislative assembly) return to Stormont after the summer recess.

I’m afraid we are no longer able to have comments open below the line every day on this blog. If you want to contact me, please email politics.live@theguardian.com. You can use this email to flag up corrections, comments for publication, questions or complaints.

blocks.text: Healey says he wants growth story 'written in more places'
John Healey is about to deliver his speech on the economy. Here are extracts that were released overnight by the Treasury.
On the UK turning the corner

double quotation markA new story about Britain. An optimistic story. One of resilience. Pride. Huge latent potential. A country turning a corner. A country whose people, businesses and communities are ready to seize the opportunity of new technologies and new ideas.
On what makes good growth

double quotation markAsk an economist what growth is and you’ll get a number. But ask the country and you’ll get a different answer. A young person getting a new job in a company that’s on the up. A sole trader winning a new contract that pays for a holiday with their kids. A business winning a new export order, giving the community around it a new lease of life.” The prime minister laid out a clear diagnosis of what has gone wrong in the past. The solution is a fundamental shift that starts with putting power in the right places. The next chapter of Britain’s growth story will be written in more places.
On the importance of wealth creation

double quotation markInstead of getting in the way with complexity and red tape, we need a strong, strategic centre wired to enable local leaders and their ambitions. That’s why we created No 10 North, working on a dual mission with the Treasury, removing obstacles so that local leaders and businesses can pull together to drive growth and productivity. I want to see wealth creation in this country. I want to see businesses make a profit. And to create the conditions for that we need an active, accountable state at all levels to remove blockages and create the conditions for more investment.

articles.title: How quiz-show winnings kick-started coach's career - with Old Trafford next
articles.summary: Lithuanian coach Valdas Dambrauskas cut his teeth in English football, and now returns in the Champions League with Sabah.

blocks.text: On Thursday, Valdas Dambrauskas will walk out at Old Trafford as manager of Sabah in the Champions League.
The Lithuanian's career will come full circle, some 20 years since he made his first steps into coaching with Manchester United Soccer Schools.
"This is beyond my imagination," Dambrauskas told BBC Sport. "To go through that tunnel on to that pitch.
"I've been many times to Old Trafford with the kids, and now I'm going to come as a coach."
This only scratches the surface of Dambrauskas' remarkable story.
It begins with an appearance on the Lithuanian version of Who Wants to Be a Millionaire?, Dambrauskas using his modest winnings to move to London and forge a career in football.

It is a tale of casual jobs, a determination to succeed and a nomadic coaching career across Europe - which now brings the 49-year-old back to England in the Champions League with the Azerbaijani club.
As Sabah's players and staff celebrated reaching the Champions League two weeks ago, unbeknownst to Dambrauskas he was becoming a social media star.
It all related to that appearance on Who Wants to Be a Millionaire? in 2002.
Not because he was on the show, but how he spent the money he won.
"This is so long ago," said Dambrauskas with a wry smile. "A back-in-the-year story that really was forgotten.
"And now suddenly everybody is speaking about this."
Dambrauskas walked away with 4,000 litas (about £725). That might not sound like much, but it was six months' wages to the average Lithuanian.
For Dambrauskas, the real story should be his career and not a game show.
"Everybody now takes only this part, you know, about the money," Dambrauskas said. "But yes, it is a true story.
"My idea was somehow I will try to go on these [coaching] courses to gain the coaching badge, maybe go back one day to Lithuania and start to work as a football coach."
What began with Who Wants to Be a Millionaire? would map out his whole career.
'I was doing two, three, sometimes four jobs'
Dambrauskas says he had known since the age of 12 he would not make it as a player, but coaching would keep him close to football.
He arrived in London in August 2002 aged 25 on a student visa with limited English.

What followed would be eight years of hard work where he would coach for community projects, at a semi-professional club, within professional youth programmes - and hold down multiple jobs while raising two children.
In 2004 he enrolled on a course in sports science and coaching at London Metropolitan University, the first real step in his career.
Then he started out coaching by volunteering with the Access to Sports Project for deprived children in Finsbury Park.
He went on to work with London Tigers, a charitable community organisation which runs teams from junior level right through to semi-professional.
Starting out as a volunteer, across five years he progressed to manage the first team in non-league football in the Spartan South Midlands League, FA Cup and FA Vase.
Dambrauskas became the first Lithuanian to achieve a Uefa coaching licence through the London Football Association.
"I went on every possible course, every possible conference, London Football Coaches Association meetings," Dambrauskas said.
"Everywhere I could go just to gain some information, some knowledge, some extra diploma, extra course.
"That was very important for me and I took my chances."
He got his first break at a professional club when Manchester United Soccer Schools took a chance on him in 2004.
Dambrauskas spent five years coaching on residential courses in the UK and in Europe.
"That was the best thing that could happen in my life," Dambrauskas said.
"I went through three or four interviews. I will be forever grateful to [Foundation chief executive] John Shiels, the way he gave me this chance, because I didn't have experience.
"I'd never been in a place with so many great personalities as I got in the Manchester United Soccer Schools."
After a short spell with Fulham, Dambrauskas moved to Brentford. He credits academy director Ose Aibangee as one of the biggest influences on his career, pushing his limits.
All the while he was juggling home life and working multiple jobs to make ends meet.
"I was a gardener, a handyman, doing newspaper rounds at the beginning, also polishing floors in a pub," Dambrauskas said.
"So many jobs. Working in retail, and then as a sports development officer, then a sports development manager, and the central YMCA.
"I was doing two, three, sometimes four jobs."
As well as the trip to Manchester United this week, Sabah will complete their Champions League group games at Arsenal in January.
This also feels like fate for Dambrauskas - one of the buildings at London Metropolitan University on Holloway Road overlooked Emirates Stadium.
When asked about his time in England, Dambrauskas' face lights up.
"When I hear this word 'England', it for me sounds like opportunities," Dambrauskas said.
"It was really amazing. England gave me all this and I'll forever be grateful."
Dambrauskas was working three jobs - at Brentford, London Tigers and as a sports development manager - when the opportunity arose to coach full-time.
It meant leaving England to return to Lithuania, champions Ekranas appointing him assistant first-team and reserve-team coach at the end of 2010.
After four years at Ekranas he was named manager of Zalgiris Vilnius, Lithuania's biggest club, where his career really took off.
Dambrauskas won two league titles, three Lithuanian Cups and two Lithuanian Super Cups across three seasons - including a treble in 2016.
Then came a series of moves in which Dambrauskas took charge of eight teams over nine years in seven countries.
First RFS, with whom he won the Latvian Cup, and then Gorica in Croatia.
A third league title came with Bulgarian side Ludogorets Razgrad, along with another Super Cup and Europa League qualification.
Dambrauskas then returned to Croatia with Hajduk Split, a time which he described as "absolutely amazing" as the club won the Croatian Cup - their first trophy for 10 years.
Next up was a spell in Greece with OFI Crete, then Omonia in Cyprus - who qualified for the Conference League - and Diosgyori in Hungary.
Finally, in the summer of 2025, he arrived at Sabah, the 10th club of his career.
Dambrauskas completed the league and cup double in his first season, as the club won the title for the first time.
It took his trophy tally to 13 across five countries.
Next stop, the Champions League.
Dambrauskas had to navigate four knockout ties to get Sabah to the Champions League, and they are the only club to make it all the way through from the first qualifying round.
Welsh club TNS, Finland's KuPS, Danish side Aarhus and Israel's Hapoel Beer-Sheva were all knocked out.
The final qualifying game was as dramatic as Dambrauskas' own story.
Sabah were going out, then a goal by Tellur Mutallimov in the fourth minute of stoppage time sent the tie into extra time. They went on to win 5-2 on the night and 6-4 on aggregate.
"To go to the Champions League is something beyond imagination," Dambrauskas said.

"We have never qualified for the Conference League, we have never qualified for the Europa League. We have never passed more than two rounds in a row in one competition, and now suddenly we are here."
Sabah are based in the town of Masazir - 30 miles north of the Azerbaijan capital Baku - with a population of just 19,000.
Known as the Owls, Sabah were only formed in 2017 and on Tuesday will celebrate their ninth birthday.

Like many small clubs, their Bank Respublika Arena home, with a capacity of less than 9,000, does not meet Uefa regulations. Instead, the club are expected to play their matches at the Olympic Stadium in Baku.
Sabah will host Borussia Dortmund, Barcelona and Napoli, and face a trip to Villarreal - as well as the visits to England.
"It can be a very hard draw, and it can be a Sabah draw," said Dambrauskas, clearly excited by the prospect.
"You dream for this, to play in this competition, to play against those teams.
"So now is the time to show that you can handle it, to find a way to compete and we will try to do this.
"We have a good team, we have an ambitious team, we have hungry players who are really keen to show themselves."
Sabah president Magsud Adigozalov last week was full of praise for Dambrauskas' impact.
"His influence goes beyond tactics," Adigozalov told Report. "He has instilled a mindset and winning mentality in the team.
"Even in the most difficult moments, the team never abandons its game or fighting spirit, which is the result of the coach's work."
Twenty years ago, Dambrauskas looked out over the pitch at Old Trafford during one of his job interviews, dreaming that one day he would stand in one of the dugouts.
Now his coaching career will return to where it started.
"I lived in England when the battle between Manchester United and Arsenal was the biggest rivalry. Alex Ferguson and Arsene Wenger," Dambrauskas said.
"Now I'm going to come back as a coach in the Champions League and hear that anthem. It's really amazing."

articles.title: Japanese woman goes viral for giving birth to 7th child
articles.summary: A woman in Japan went viral and captured the public’s attention after announcing the birth of her seventh child, amid the country’s falling birth rate. Japanese writer and former political candidate…

blocks.text: A woman in Japan went viral and captured the public’s attention after announcing the birth of her seventh child, amid the country’s falling birth rate.

Japanese writer and former political candidate Kotoe Hashimoto announced on social media platform X on Aug 29 that she had given birth to her seventh child, thanking the medical staff who attended to them.
The post, which includes a photo of Hashimoto cradling her newborn, has been viewed 27 million times on X and received 10,800 likes on Facebook.
In a follow-up post later the same day, she also thanked the public for their congratulatory messages.
“I believe that now is the time for Japanese women to have children,” she said. “The rise and fall of our nation depends on the active role of women.”
Her post struck a chord among the Japanese.

“I think you’re absolutely right. I feel that the key to changing the current state of Japan, which is heading towards (demographic) collapse, is precisely the conscience of Japanese women,” Facebook user Etsugaku Kankou replied to her post.
Another user, Hideto Umegaki, said: “It’s a national treasure to give birth to seven children.”

Hashimoto, who ran as a candidate under the Party of Hope during the 2017 general election, has used her social media accounts to discuss the country’s demographic challenges and advocating for Japanese women to have more children.
She was not elected, and the conservative party, which was founded by Tokyo Governor Yuriko Koike, disbanded in October 2021.
The baby’s birth comes as Japan’s fertility rate fell to a fresh record low in 2025, extending a decade-long slide despite years of government efforts to reverse the trend.

The total fertility rate – the average number of children a woman is expected to have over her childbearing years – slipped to 1.14 from 1.15 a year earlier, according to data by the country’s Welfare Ministry.
The reading was the lowest since comparable records began in 1947.

Japan, one of the world’s oldest societies, faces mounting demographic pressures. A shrinking workforce and rising social security costs are placing strain on public finances at a time when the government is also seeking to fund higher defence spending and other growth initiatives. /dl

articles.title: It's back to school season. Here's why there's a push to get rid of cars at dropoff and pickup
articles.summary: As the school year starts, the non-profit environmental association Green Communities Canada is continuing its efforts to implement pilot projects clearing regular student dropoff zones of cars.

image.caption: Children play in a School Street zone free of cars outside St. Leo Catholic Elementary School in Edmonton in June. (Nicole Roach/Green Communities Canada)

blocks.text: As Lily Dejnicki prepares to get back to the classroom, she hopes to see fewer cars during the morning and afternoon rush hours outside her school.
The 13-year-old would like to see the return of a pilot project to get cars out of the regular dropoff zone at her school, Sts. Peter and Paul Catholic Elementary in Mississauga, Ont.

As part of the School Streets project promoted by a non-profit environmental association, volunteers directed cars away during dropoff and pickup times by using barricades and signs. Kids and parents were encouraged to cycle and walk to and from school, as opposed to driving.
"It was lots of fun," said Lily, who is going into Grade 8.
"Kids … wouldn't rush home," she said. "Instead, they would … take a couple minutes to play and stuff outside."
Anita Dejnicki, Lily’s mom, sits on the school’s parental advisory council and said more parents were talking to each other and more kids were active and playing compared to before.
"Once it ended, it just seemed like it was quiet again."
As the school year starts, environmental association Green Communities Canada is continuing its efforts to implement School Streets across the country.

The pilot at Sts. Peter and Paul Catholic Elementary, which ran for a month, is part of a bigger push led by the organization called the National Active School Streets Initiative. It received $3 million in funding from the Public Health Agency of Canada in 2024.

At least 20 School Streets are planned for the 2026-2027 academic year. Over the past few years, they have been piloted in six provinces: British Columbia, Alberta, Manitoba, Ontario, Quebec and Nova Scotia.
Nicole Roach, sustainable mobility director at Green Communities Canada, said School Streets usually take the form of a temporary barrier installed on both ends of one street next to a school.
The street is typically one that is not on a major thoroughfare or one that is going to cause issues for buses or students with disabilities, she said.
For those who need to drive, one alternative is to drive to a nearby parking area and walk together the rest of the way, Roach said.
Roach points to safety and air pollution from cars as among the reasons to implement School Streets.

"Many schools at pickup and dropoff are just absolute chaos," she said. "We see a lot of dangerous driving behaviour, really unsafe environments for the children walking or wheeling or even just getting to their vehicle for pickup."
Lily, who walks to and from school, said the usual lines of cars at dropoff and pickup can be bothersome.
"It would kind of be not … too safe because it would be really, really crowded," she said.
"Most of my friends … liked [the School Street]. But some people didn't really like it. They would … say that there's no point in doing it."
A bumpy road
Although it's estimated that at least 36 schools across Canada have tested School Streets, implementing them long-term has proven challenging.
Just two permanent, year-round School Streets exist, and at least one pilot ground to a halt after pushback.
Last year, a School Street project at Corliss Public School in Mississauga was cancelled after a parent started a petition, raising concerns about safety and disruption.

"Every day, children and parents are forced to navigate confusing road closures and restricted areas, which not only causes delays but also increases the risk of accidents," the petition, which collected nearly 200 signatures, said.
"The setup leads to congestion in nearby areas, forcing parents to opt for potentially unsafe detours or parking in locations that are less supervised."
Kerstyn Lutz, who studied four School Street pilots in the Greater Toronto Area in 2022, recalls witnessing disruption first-hand.

"At least at the beginning, [it] felt like chaos. You have cars driving up to these barriers, they don't know what to do," said Lutz, a PhD candidate at the University of Toronto at the time of her research. "We have to have vehicle diversion plans…. The reality is not everyone is going to walk."
What do the experts say?

But Raktim Mitra, an urban planning professor at Toronto Metropolitan University who studies sustainable transportation behaviour, said there’s no evidence to suggest School Streets push congestion onto nearby roads or lead to more unsafe driving.
Over the past year, Mitra collected data on travel patterns close to two School Streets pilots in Mississauga.
More cars drove below the designated speed on the street, and a "significantly" higher number of cars were yielding to pedestrians in nearby streets, he said.
As for clogging up nearby streets, Mitra said none of the data suggests that to be a likely problem.
"None of the nearby roads … reached a congested condition."

While children who travel to school by themselves may encounter more people, there's no evidence that more walking as a result of such an initiative would lead to more potentially problematic interactions with strangers, said Lewis Smith, spokesperson for the Canada Safety Council.
"We believe that the bigger concern is teaching children to recognize unsafe situations, to recognize unsafe behaviors and be able to respond to them accordingly."
As for benefits, Mitra and Lutz noted more kids cycled or walked to school.
The absence of cars outside the school also led to a reduction in air pollution in the immediate area, Lutz said.
Canada's 'culture of mobility'
School Streets began in Italy in the 1990s and has spread to other countries.
Mitra said Canada's "culture of mobility" is a factor that can make School Streets face opposition, particularly in suburbs where car travel is the dominant mode of transportation.
He said many parents are used to driving and that "asking them to change that culture … is always difficult."
Bogota goes car-free for a day to combat recent air pollution
Resources to enforce School Streets programs have posed another challenge.
In 2023, a year-round program at Lord Roberts Elementary School in Vancouver ended because there weren’t enough volunteers to supervise the School Street.

The volunteer burden is the reason why many School Streets only run as short pilots, said Lucy Maloney, a Vancouver city councillor who was president of the parental advisory committee at Lord Roberts at the time.
"Trying to run a School Street all year round where parents are required to set it up and dismantle it and supervise it is just too much for people to manage."

items: Groups given $3 million by Vancouver for car-free Granville strip aren't saying how they'll spend it
Car-free stretch of 17th Avenue not happening this summer — but group still hoping for next year

blocks.text: Maloney, who plans to push for more School Streets as a councillor, said there are measures that could reduce reliance on volunteers such as retractable bollards or camera enforcement.
Lutz is skeptical whether School Streets with permanent, physical infrastructure would work for Canada’s suburban streets.
"Is it going to work the same way it works in a country like Italy? Probably not, because they're already better built for walkability than we are."
For urban areas, Mitra sees School Streets as a possibility.
"About half of our children who attend elementary school … live within half a mile [0.8 kilometres] from their schools, which technically is a 10- to 12-minute walking distance," he said.

items: 'People want this': Toronto city council votes in favour of expanding car-free streets
Car-free Corydon: Heart of the village to become pedestrian corridor on Sundays

blocks.text: While he doesn’t foresee every child walking to school, he said the program can help those who live close by convert short car and bus trips.
"I think that would have significant impact in reducing localized congestion and improving the health and well-being and safety of children."
Lily, for one, sees many positives.
"When I come to school … I'm actually looking forward to doing something … rather than just, like, going straight home."

articles.title: Why more than 150 years later, Hamilton's Nine Hour Movement still matters
articles.summary: On May 15, 1872, 1,500 workers marched in Hamilton, demanding the workday be reduced to nine hours, a movement that ultimately failed, but paved the way for laws that protect workers today.

image.caption: National Steel Car workers have been on strike since Aug. 12. The local union president says strikes like this are a continuation of the work the nine-hour pioneers started 150 years ago. (Submitted by Frank Crowder)

blocks.text: Hamilton·New
On May 15, 1872, 1,500 workers marched in Hamilton, demanding the workday be reduced to nine hours, a movement that ultimately failed, but paved the way for laws that protect workers today.
Despite its failure, the movement marked the start of progress in the Canadian labour movement
On May 15, 1872, 1,500 workers marched in Hamilton, demanding the workday be reduced to nine hours. Though the movement ultimately failed, it paved the way for laws that protect workers today.
At the time, Hamilton was coming into its "heyday" as an industrial city, according to Stephanie Ross, a professor in the School of Labour Studies at McMaster University.
The workday the movement was aiming to reduce was typically 10 to 12 hours at the time, six days a week, according to Ross.
"You can imagine, it was exhausting," she said in an interview ahead of Labour Day.

It became a big issue for Canadian workers of the day, who believed that they should have "time for themselves." A relatively normal belief now, but not a concept factory owners — who, Ross said, saw workers as a means of production — supported back then.
Hamilton workers played a big part in the movement, mostly centred around railway yards, where workers in different crafts worked together and shared ideas about the kind of workplace they wanted.

Workers in Toronto's printers union and Montreal's rail yards were also having similar conversations at the time and — realizing all employers would have to reduce work hours in order for the movement to succeed — joined forces.

items: Here's what's closed in Hamilton on Labour Day
Trump tariffs, affordability crisis and striking workers: What you need to know about Labour Day in Hamilton

blocks.text: 'Those fights, 150 years later, still happen'

In addition to the 1,500 workers who marched in Hamilton, Ross said a lot of people lined the street to support the demand. It became, virtually, a general strike in Hamilton, involving all the craftspeople in the city.
"The nine-hour workday was a safety measure … to give people's bodies time to relax and to spend more time with their family," said Frank Crowder, president of United Steelworkers (USW) Local 7135.
"Those fights, 150 years later, still happen."

items: 1,200 National Steel Car workers in Hamilton on strike after rejecting contract offer

blocks.text: Crowder is one of the 1,200 workers on strike at National Steel Car in Hamilton, asking for higher wages and for the union to have a say in a "dangerous" incentive program.
He said workers at National Steel Car want the same thing workers in the Nine Hour Movement wanted at the time: more time to rest and spend with their families.
Workers at the company have an incentive program that allows them to take lower pay and get paid an extra 25 per cent of their wages if they make enough product.
Recently, production levels have been set too high for workers to achieve, Crowder said. The union has no say in the program, as per their collective agreement.

"These workers will not have time for their families if they can't return home to [them] … We don't have time to rest our bodies because we're overexerting ourselves trying to meet a quota that is unattainable," he said.
"So the fight still happens today for at least that connection to the nine-hour workday."
Crowder says the company has not returned to the bargaining table, despite an open invitation from the union.

items: Labour Day parade, King William Comes Alive! and more to do this weekend in Hamilton

blocks.text: A failed movement

The Nine Hour Movement ultimately failed after printers in Toronto were engaged in a fight with The Globe that forced them to go on strike early, said Ross. In April of 1872, 10,000 people protested in defence of the printers union in Toronto.
The Globe's editor, George Brown, who was anti-union, according to Ross, tried to have those workers arrested and charged with criminal misdeeds.
Despite its failure, the movement marked the beginning of other things in the Canadian labour movement, Ross said.

Canada's first prime minister, John A. Macdonald, saw it as an opportunity to gain the working class vote and to "put a spoke in the wheels of George Brown's bicycle," who was his political rival, Ross said.

items: Sir John A. Macdonald was erased from some public spaces. Now there's a movement to bring him back

blocks.text: Macdonald's government passed the Trade Unions Act in June 1892, decriminalizing unions in Canada which, prior to the act, were not legally allowed to organize to set wages in a particular industry, according to Ross.
The act was an important step towards organizing around the shorter working day, she said.
The Nine Hour Movement also led to the creation of the early version of the Hamilton & District Labour Council and started to build cross-union federations such as the Canadian Labour Union.
The movement also helped workers — who, up until that time, had been pitted against each other and strongly identified with their occupations — realize they shared interests across workplaces.
"That's partly why Hamilton should be understood and continues to be understood as a place where workers are on the leading edge of struggles that have a wider impact," said Ross.
Crowder said the history of the movement highlights how unions have been fighting for workers this entire time, even when it was illegal.
"We're still as necessary today as we were back then," he said.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Aura Carreño Rosas is a reporter at CBC Hamilton. She's originally from Venezuela. She has extensive experience in covering stories about immigrants and migrant workers as well as interesting people with diverse journeys. You can contact her at aura.carreno.rosas@cbc.ca

articles.title: Dutch elm disease ravaged Canadian cities. Can we help trees protect themselves?
articles.summary: Scientists in the state of Vermont have spent the summer spreading Dutch elm disease to thousands of trees. It's an experiment to see if a new generation of elms might have resistance to a plague…

image.caption: Foresters and researchers in Vermont have spent the summer injecting young elm trees with thousands of spores that cause Dutch elm disease, the fungal infection that has decimated elm populations in North America. They're hoping to determine if elms bred from trees that survived the lethal disease c

blocks.text: Scientists in the state of Vermont have spent the summer spreading Dutch elm disease to thousands of trees.
You read that correctly.

Researchers with the U.S. Forest Service and the Nature Conservancy want to see if a new generation of elms — bred from survivors of the disease — might have resistance to the fungus spread by bark beetles that has been decimating elm populations in the U.S. and Canada for decades.
The goal is one day repopulating areas where towering elms were once ubiquitous, lining city streets and thriving along river banks.
"The loss of the trees over the years has been devastating," Gus Goodwin, a senior conservation planner for The Nature Conservancy, told The Associated Press.

Time will tell if the Vermont experiment will result in a strain of trees resistant to Dutch elm disease (DED). Researchers working on similar efforts here in Canada hope science will offer solutions at a time when the disease is becoming a threat in new areas.

"We're not losing our elm population," said Alison Morrison, a manager at the University of Guelph arboretum which operates the Elm Recovery Project. "What we've lost is our elms' ability to grow old."
Ottawa's elms are crashing down
The Elm City that lost its elms

Fredericton was once known as the "City of Stately Elms" until the disease spread there and elsewhere in eastern Canada in the 1960s and 70s, leading to the loss of an estimated 10,000 trees. Now there's only about 1,000 mature trees left standing.
University of New Brunswick forest management professor Anthony Taylor has several elms on his property outside Fredericton, ones that survived the first wave of DED.
"But now I see there's another wave of the disease killing some of the trees on my woodlot," he said, "which is sad to see."

When bark beetles carrying the DED spores colonize a hospitable elm, the disease attacks its vascular system and blocks the water-conducting tissue, depriving the foliage and branches of water, preventing photosynthesis and eventually killing the entire tree.
That can happen within one to four years of infection.

items: Alberta municipalities on alert as Dutch elm disease cases increase in province
Saskatoon residents call for more trees as Dutch elm disease continues to spread

blocks.text: The beetles further spread the fungus by laying eggs in an infected tree, creating a new generation of carriers that can then fly to the next healthy tree. The fungus can also spread through roots.
In order to control DED, Taylor says, infected elms are immediately cut down and disposed of.
In decades past, however, other nearby elms would also be removed even if they were healthy.
"It's called sanitization, where we try to eliminate the pest by eliminating the plant that's carrying," explained Morrison.
But that may have "unintentionally" had a detrimental effect when it came to DED-tolerance, she says, by taking trees that could withstand the disease out of the population.
Why experts recommend ‘trap trees’ to combat Dutch elm disease
A nightmare for elm-lined streets
Where cities from Manitoba to the Maritimes watched their elm trees disappear in the 1960s and 70s, the disease has become a threat in new places in recent years.
Edmonton has confirmed 17 infected trees since it was first detected in the city in 2024. Saskatoon recorded 23 cases so far in 2026, 11 years after DED was first found there.
"It is a considerable threat to Saskatoon's urban forest," said Nolan Ramler, a park superintendent. The city has approximately 26,000 elms, he said.

City foresters act fast to remove infected trees, he says, but there's also an onus on local residents to stop the spread — including respecting the annual four-month ban on pruning elm trees, and not storing or burning the wood.
"We have officially transitioned ... to more of an active management strategy because the fungus is now considered unavoidable and it's widespread in the community," he said.
Saskatoon removing infected elm trees
While the disease may be here to stay, the concern is which trees it kills.
Losing the mature trees, says Morrison, means losing their shade canopy and ability to absorb storm water.
She says they are "another tool in our toolbox" when it comes to mitigating and adapting to the effects of human-caused climate change.
"If we can bring elms back into our communities with confidence," she said, "that adds another species ... to build a complex ecosystem. And those are the ones that are the most resilient."
LISTEN | Dutch elm disease strikes beloved tree honouring First World War soldiers:
Saskatoon Morning4:58The City of Saskatoon removes memorial tree stricken by dutch elm disease
A test of time

Scientists and foresters across North America, including at the Elm Recovery Project in Guelph and a city-run project in Fredericton, have been working toward improving resiliency against DED by crossbreeding and cloning trees that did not succumb to the disease.
In Guelph, Morrison says, they have been working toward this goal for almost 30 years.
"We have 109 trees that we have essentially tortured with Dutch elm disease, and multiple strains of it that persist, in a gene bank here," she said.
Those trees, she says, have gotten to the point where they can now produce seed and the next phase will be "seeing what these seedlings are capable of."
That's where the Vermont experiment is at now — the seedlings of resistant trees — and at much larger scale, with some 6,000 trees.
Starting in the spring, the U.S. Forest Service and Nature Conservancy researchers began injecting them with thousands of fungus spores to test which ones survive and which ones ultimately die.

items: One of Toronto's oldest elm trees is on its last legs. Researchers are racing to re-grow copies
Dutch elm disease study in Fredericton shows mixed results

blocks.text: Because this kind of breeding program means generations of trees, it takes time.

“We ... will grow and love those trees for about 15 or so years, at which point they should produce seeds, and that seed can be used for restoration,” Leila Wilson, a research ecologist with the U.S. Forest Service, told The Associated Press.
Taylor says if it works, it could mean elms here could coexist with DED, as elms in Europe have evolved to do, with only minor negative impacts from the disease.
Elms in Canada, he says, could also evolve naturally but it could take centuries considering the disease only arrived in this county just under a hundred years ago.
"We're just sort of [expediting] that co-evolution process," he said.

blocks.caption: Jakub Krupa

blocks.text: Jakub Krupa

Europe wakes up this morning to final results of the Saxony-Anhalt state election in Germany, with the far-right Alternative für Deutschland confirmed as the winners – but without a majority in the state parliament.

blocks.caption: AfD leaders Ulrich Siegmund, Tino Chrupalla, and Alice Weidel, on stage at AfD election party for the 2026 state election under a slogan “It begins here.” Photograph: dts News Agency Germany/Shutterstock

blocks.text: Cue chaotic discussions about what’s next, including theoretical scenarios with defections, a minority government backed on issue-by-issue basis by the far-left Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance, or even… a snap election to resolve the deadlock.

We are expecting to hear from the embattled German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, around lunchtime. With German media running grainy pictures of Merz looking glumly on the backseat of his car, it is probably fair to say that the pressure on him will only increase.
There are also lots of political reactions from across Europe, with no doubt more to come.
I will bring you all the latest here.
Separately, I will keep an eye on Ursula von der Leyen’s trip to Greenland amid renewed US interest in the territory, and on the funeral of Bosnian Serb war criminal Ratko Mladić.
It’s Friday, 4 September 2026, it’s Jakub Krupa here, and this is Europe Live.
Good morning.
Key events

items: 3m agoEuropean leaders concerned about AfD win
10m agoRussian presidential aide praises 'historic' win for 'pragmatic' pro-Russian AfD
16m agoAfD state leader thanks Elon Musk for support after Saxony-Anhalt win
22m agoMorning opening: What now after AfD's election triumph?

blocks.text: European leaders concerned about AfD win
We are also getting first reactions from European ministers.
Donald Tusk, the prime minister of Poland, said:
“In Poland, only idiots or traitors can rejoice at the triumph of the AfD in Germany.”
Poland’s foreign minister Radosław Sikorski called the AfD’s win “a very worrying” signal for Europe.
France’s Europe minister, Benjamin Haddad, described the win as “a serious moment in Europe”, warning that “nationalism and xenophobia will never be a solution”.
“We must listen with humility to the anger, the concerns, the fears, and respond to them,” he added. “We cannot forget our history. That is the meaning behind the choices made by France and Germany.”
French finance minister Roland Lescure joined in his warnings, saying Europe faced “a major challenge in the face of a populist wave” across the continent.
But former Hungarian prime minister Viktor Orbán celebrated AfD’s win, saying it was “a huge night for Germany and Europe!”
“Buckle up. This is just the beginning!”
Russian presidential aide praises 'historic' win for 'pragmatic' pro-Russian AfD
Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev took a screen grab of US president Donald Trump’s post on Saxony-Anhalt and praised a “historic win for the pragmatic AfD”.
AfD is pro-Kremlin, urging a stop to support for Ukraine and pushing for Ukrainians to no longer receive refugee status.
AfD state leader thanks Elon Musk for support after Saxony-Anhalt win

On Sunday night, Ulrich Siegmund, the AfD’s lead candidate, thanked Musk on X “for your support and for your clear and highly important perspective on the political developments of our time”, adding: “I would very much welcome the opportunity for strong and constructive cooperation”.

blocks.caption: Alice Weidel, co-leader of the Alternative for Germany party (AfD), speaks as SpaceX CEO Elon Musk appears on screen during a central election campaign event of the AfD in Halle (Saale), Germany in January last year. Photograph: Karina Hessland/Reuters

blocks.text: Siegmund wrote his comments after Musk said “Well done!” in German to AfD co-founder Alice Weidel, when she posted about the projected win.

articles.summary: The building was located in New Delhi's Satya Niketan, popular among students from nearby colleges and universities. At least 12 people have been rescued from the rubble. DW has more.

image.caption: The incident took place close to Delhi University's South Campus, in an area popular with studentsImage: Francis Mascarenhas/REUTERS

blocks.text: Below is a roundup of the top headlines from India on Monday, September 7.
Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.
September 7, 2026
At least 7 people killed as rescue efforts continue

blocks.caption: Officials said water accumulated at the base of the buildingImage: Francis Mascarenhas/REUTERS

blocks.text: The death toll has risen to seven after rescue personnel recovered another body amid the rubble of a five-story building in India's capital city Monday, a day after the nearly 50-year-old structure came crashing down.

The building was located in Satya Niketan, a popular student hub that houses hundreds of university students often living in crowded conditions. It is situated in close proximity to Delhi University's South Campus, making it a popular destination for students.
Local media reported that the building housed a private hostel.
In its latest update, Delhi Police said a total of 12 people had been rescued during the operation. Emergency crews say more people may be trapped in the rubble.
Rescue teams, including personnel from disaster agencies as well as fire and police teams, were using heavy machinery and sniffer dogs to locate those trapped.

blocks.caption: The exact moment that the building collapsed was caught on CCTVImage: Vipin/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Earlier, the All India Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS), which is treating victims of the collapse, said its trauma center received 10 people: "Out of the 10 patients, five were brought dead, while one patient who was in critical condition later succumbed to his injuries."

Delhi Chief Minister Rekha Gupta addressed the potential cause of the collapse, saying: "It is certain that there was ‌water in the building's basement, and due ‌to ​accumulation of water, due to ongoing repair work, the old building collapsed."

The police have registered a First Information Report (FIR) under Sections 105, 290 and 125(a) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (the official criminal code of India) against the building owners, local media reported. The specific sections relate to culpable homicide, negligence in the construction or repair of buildings as well as acts that endanger human life.

articles.title: Crowds gather for war criminal Ratko Mladic’s funeral in Belgrade
articles.summary: BELGRADE — Crowds began gathering in Belgrade on Monday morning for the funeral of convicted war criminal Ratko Mladic, as Brussels accused some in the country of “glorification” of…

blocks.text: BELGRADE — Crowds began gathering in Belgrade on Monday morning for the funeral of convicted war criminal Ratko Mladic, as Brussels accused some in the country of “glorification” of a man convicted of genocide during the 1990s war in Bosnia.
Mladic died in late August, aged 84, while serving a life sentence in The Hague for genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity committed during the war in Bosnia.
Mourners streamed into St Luka church in Belgrade from 7am (0500 GMT) to pay respects, with many kissing Mladic’s closed coffin, as Serbian Orthodox priests read prayers.
Police had closed off streets in the surrounding part of the city as crowds began arriving.
AFP reporters saw large crowds outside the church, many wearing shirts praising Mladic, as doors opened with aerial images showing hundreds already queuing to enter.
Serbian flags had been hung nearby, and a huge banner unfurled across the street read: “Welcome, General, thanks be to your mother for bearing a hero, so that Serbdom’s glory may return.”
“I am here to see off the general, a national hero,” pensioner Radojka Visic, who had travelled from Bosnia’s Serb entity, Republika Srpska, told AFP.
“They couldn’t defeat us on the battlefield, so they sent him to prison and tortured him there instead,” Visic said, referring to the “international community”.
Backlash
Mladic’s casket arrived in the country last week aboard a government plane, where it had been carried by six soldiers and draped in flags.
As it was driven from the airport in a motorcade, groups of young men held banners praising the former general, and some police were seen saluting as it passed.

Last week’s scenes drew condemnation from the European Union’s enlargement commissioner, Marta Kos, who cancelled a forthcoming visit to Serbia on Friday, saying the “glorification surrounding his death is incompatible with the values on which the EU path is built”.
Denis Becirovic, chairman of Bosnia’s tripartite presidency, called it “an act of identification by Serbia’s leadership with one of the worst killers in European history”.
“This has unforeseeable consequences for the future of the entire region,” he wrote on Facebook on Friday.
Mladic’s wartime atrocities during the break-up of the former Yugoslavia earned him the nickname “Butcher of Bosnia” in international media.
The 1992-1995 war left around 100,000 people dead and displaced 2.2 million.
Mladic was the military figurehead of the Bosnian Serb leadership alongside former Yugoslav president Slobodan Milosevic and Bosnian Serb leader Radovan Karadzic.
The United Nations war crimes court convicted him of genocide over the 1995 Srebrenica massacre, where Bosnian Serb forces killed around 8,000 Bosnian Muslim men and boys in a UN-protected safe zone.
The atrocity was Europe’s worst act of bloodshed since World War II.
Fadila Efendic, whose son and husband were killed in Srebrenica, told AFP earlier that it pained her “to know that his ideas are not dead”.

Mladic was also convicted of persecuting and forcibly expelling Bosnian Muslims and Croats, terrorising civilians during the siege of Sarajevo and taking UN peacekeepers hostage during NATO air strikes in 1995.
‘Hero’
Mladic was arrested in 2011, 16 years after he was first indicted, and sentenced to life in prison in 2021 after a nine-year trial.
Despite the verdicts, he is still hailed as a hero by some Serbs, particularly in Republika Srpska, where his death was marked with vigils and gatherings.
Many from the entity have applied to travel to Belgrade for the funeral.
Mladic’s son Darko, who is officially organising the funeral, said he was “proud of the role” his father played.
On Saturday, around 300 people gathered at a commemoration for Mladic at a military facility in Belgrade, organised by an association of retired and active Serbian army generals.
Darko and other family members also attended, as well as Serbian Justice Minister Nenad Vujic and officials from Republika Srpska, including President Sinisa Karan.
Speakers at the ceremony praised Mladic’s wartime role, describing him as a “towering figure both as a man and a soldier”.
Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic said that tens of thousands of people were expected to attend the funeral and that the state would ensure the event passed “safely”.
He would not attend in person due to a prior engagement, he explained. /dl

articles.title: Man given 6 months to live; spends it finding home for autistic son
articles.summary: SINGAPORE — Jeon Gyeong-cheol, the author widely known as the “Peter Pan Dad” for documenting his search for a home where his disabled son could live after his death, died Saturday.…

blocks.text: SINGAPORE — Jeon Gyeong-cheol, the author widely known as the “Peter Pan Dad” for documenting his search for a home where his disabled son could live after his death, died Saturday. He was 64 and had been fighting late-stage liver cancer.

Jeong Yu-jin, head of the Developmental Disabilities Support Expert Forum, announced Jeon’s death on social media Sunday, saying the funeral would be held without a formal wake, in accordance with his wishes.
“He is currently at the hospital, and no separate memorial hall will be set up. We extend our deepest condolences,” she wrote.
Jeon spent more than two decades as the sole caregiver for his son, who is now 27 and has autism, with his developmental level assessed as that of a 2- or 3-year-old.

After receiving a terminal diagnosis of late-stage liver cancer in April last year, Jeon traveled across the country, reaching out to nearly 1,000 care facilities in hopes of finding a place that could look after his son once he was gone. Few, however, were able to take him in.

Jeon later began writing about his search on the content publishing platform Brunch, and his accounts struck a chord with many readers. His story soon reached a wider audience through television programs including MBC’s “True Story Expedition” and tvN’s “You Quiz on the Block.”
Jeon later compiled his writings on Brunch into the essay collection “Annyeong, Peter Pan,” published in June.

Readers moved by his story raised some 80 million won ($59,000) in donations, and with growing nationwide support, Je-won was able to move into a community village for people with profound developmental disabilities.

“I want to tell him to forget about his dad and live happily. But I don’t want him to forget me completely. I hope he remembers me with a faint sense of longing, as an old man who once looked at him with warmth,” Jeon said on “You Quiz on the Block” last month.
Jeon also sought to help families facing struggles similar to his own, working to establish a welfare foundation for adults with severe autism-related disabilities, like his son.

On Aug. 26, shortly before his death, he announced the launch of a preparatory committee for the foundation. With the committee now in place, its members are expected to carry on Jeon’s efforts and continue discussions on launching the foundation, according to news reports. /dl

articles.summary: Lebanon says renewed attacks jeopardise a US-brokered ceasefire meant to end the conflict between Israel and armed group Hezbollah.

blocks.text: Israeli air strikes on a village in southern Lebanon have killed at least 11 people, including two children, Lebanese state media say.

Nine people were killed in one strike that destroyed a three-storey residential building in Kfar Rumman shortly after midnight, while two paramedics were killed in a second strike on a car, according to the National News Agency.
The Israeli military said it was looking into the reports.

On Sunday, Israeli strikes killed seven people in southern Lebanon, as the Israeli military retaliated for what it said were drone attacks by the armed group Hezbollah on its troops in occupied areas of the country.

Lebanese President Joseph Aoun warned that the attacks were a "dangerous escalation" that jeopardised the US-brokered ceasefire agreed in June, which was meant to end the conflict between Israel and Hezbollah.

articles.title: Kyiv air raid alerts at record high as Russia launches round-the-clock strikes
articles.summary: Schools, businesses and public transport are all struggling with the surge in Russian air attacks.

blocks.text: Kyiv is suffering more daily air raid alerts than at any time since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022, according to BBC Verify analysis of government figures.
Most air attacks used to come at night but Russia's new tactic of striking Ukraine's capital during the day is causing huge disruption to schools and businesses.
The round the clock attacks have forced people to head for shelter as many as 13 times a day, with air raid alerts lasting from a few minutes to nearly four and a half hours.

Residents in Kyiv are struggling to adapt to this new reality, adding to existing stress and anxiety. The alerts force pupils to leave their classrooms and workers their offices and leave commuters struggling to get home as overland trains stop.
This has forced the government to plan a new, two-tier warning system that allows people to carry on working, travelling and studying depending on the scale of the threat.
There was a brief pause in attacks on Kyiv over the weekend while US envoys were in town for talks about trying to end the war.

But analysis of figures from the state-owned app Kyiv digital shows that since the round-the-clock Russian attacks began at the end of August, air raid sirens have sounded across Kyiv's skies on average 10 times a day.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has held an emergency meeting with ministers and commanders to work out how to produce new high-speed missiles that can intercept the faster Russian drones.

"You can all see that the Russians have changed the tactics of their strikes against Ukraine and, since August, have been terrorising our people, our cities and our villages far more intensely," the president said.

Diplomats say the risk is that Russia will manufacture its fast attack drones more quickly than Ukraine can develop a new generation of interceptors. Some military sources say this threat could become far greater than Russia's ballistic missiles which have largely overcome Ukraine's depleted Patriot defences.
Ukraine uses warplanes, anti-aircraft guns and shoulder-launched missiles to try to bring down the jet-powered drones.
But Yurii Ihnat, spokesman for the Ukrainian Air Force, said only about 60 percent of the drones were being shot down and they needed new interceptors to tackle the threat.
"The task now is to make them faster and equip them with specialised guidance systems so that they can shoot down jet-powered UAVs, the jet-powered Shaheds," he said.

"The key issue really is having guidance systems, because that is one of the crucial elements. It is not enough for the interceptor simply to fly fast — it has to hit the target. That is very important."
Analysts say Russia's aim is not only to weaken Kyiv's morale but also damage Ukraine's economy by targeting businesses and warehouses.
The alerts are also disrupting the start of the new academic year and forcing school children to leave their classrooms throughout the day.

When another air raid began, some students at the Drahomanov Ukrainian State University in central Kyiv headed underground; others stayed chatting on the street, such is the normality of these alerts.

Diana, a student teacher, said she did not sleep well at night and her schedule was disrupted during the day. "Sometimes it is hard because most of the day I need to go to safe places, like the metro or somewhere underground," she said. "It's a terrible time, but thank God we are alive. We go day by day."

Ihor, studying to become a chemistry teacher, said he was used to the alerts after many years of war but life was still hard. "We are annoyed by the sirens because they are constant," he said. "It destroys the quality of our education… We cannot study normally."
After a drone attack in a residential part of central Kyiv, students from a nearby school were evacuated for fear of explosions or a secondary, so-called "double-tap" attack.

Sophia, 17, told us it was very sad but this is what life was like now. "It's a little bit scary to live here in Kyiv," she said. "It's very difficult." The interview was then interrupted by another siren. "We need to go," she said. "It is very dangerous for you to stand in the streets. Maybe we can have a second detonation."
