articles.title: China prepares £40bn stimulus for financial sector amid fears over sluggish growth
articles.summary:
Beijing wants banks and insurers to bolster investment in stock market as it helps to replenish cash reserves

China will inject $54bn (£40bn) into its financial sector as Beijing attempts to…

blocks.text: China will inject $54bn (£40bn) into its financial sector as Beijing attempts to shore up banks and insurers in the face of faltering economic growth.

A host of financial institutions said they were due to receive billions of yuan in capital from state institutions including the ministry of finance and even the company that runs the country’s tobacco monopoly.

The stimulus is designed to help China bolster the ability of its financial sector to invest in the stock market and lend to businesses, amid signs that the world’s second largest economy is struggling to escape weak growth.
The country’s largest life insurer, China Life Insurance, will get 35bn yuan, while the China Taiping Insurance Group said it would receive 7bn.

The People’s Insurance ⁠Company of China said it planned to raise up to 15bn yuan through a private placement of A-shares – stock that specifically allows investors to trade in China-based companies – to the ministry ​of finance, with the proceeds used to replenish ‌its capital.

The initiative could help bolster ‌state insurers that have been directed by Beijing to support the stock market with medium- and long-term funds, while positioning them to help regulators ‌manage smaller, higher-risk insurance companies.

The insurance sector has been struggling with eroding profitability owing to persistently low interest rates, with numerous small and mid-sized insurers reporting deteriorating solvency ratios, a measure of financial health.

“The injection is an important step by the country to enhance the financial sector’s ability to serve the real economy and promote the high-quality ‌development of the financial and insurance industries,” China Life said, adding that it would strengthen the group’s ability to withstand risk.
Separately, three state lenders on Sunday also announced they will receive a combined 290bn yuan in capital injections.
after newsletter promotion
The plan was first announced at an annual parliamentary meeting in March this year, extending a financing tool that had helped bolster some other big state banks last year.

The Agricultural Bank of China and the Industrial and Commercial Bank of China, two of the country’s largest state banks, said ⁠they planned to raise up to 160bn yuan and 100bn yuan respectively through private A-share ​placements to the finance ministry, China National Tobacco ​Corp and its subsidiaries.

The two lenders said the ​proceeds would be used entirely to replenish cash reserves, helping them ​sustain credit expansion, as Beijing leans ‌on state banks ​to support growth despite weak demand for loans.

articles.title: Volcanic eruption halts flights at Jakarta and seven other Indonesian airports
articles.summary:
Ash cloud from Anak Krakatau affects hundreds of flights and some school and fishing activities

Indonesia halted operations at eight airports on Sunday, including from its main international…

blocks.text: Indonesia halted operations at eight airports on Sunday, including from its main international hub, affecting hundreds of flights as a result of an ash cloud from the Anak Krakatau volcano.
Saturday’s eruption, which produced lava and booming sounds that were heard up to 435 miles (700km) away, according to Indonesia’s geology agency, also interrupted some school activities and fishing.
Two more eruptions were recorded on Sunday.

Ash was detected in the airspace around Soekarno-Hatta international airport near Jakarta, prompting authorities to suspend operations. They announced several extensions of the shutdown, keeping the airport closed to flights until 9.30pm local time on Sunday.

The suspension affected hundreds of flights, including international ones, the airport operator, Angkasa Pura, announced. Singapore Airlines said it had cancelled flights to and from Jakarta for the rest of Sunday.
The Australian flag carrier said there were “disruptions to a number of Qantas services, including cancellations to and from Jakarta today”.
“Our meteorologists and operations teams are closely monitoring conditions in and around Jakarta and any impact on our operations,” it said in a statement.
“Safety remains our highest priority. We have contacted affected customers and are providing assistance. Services will resume when conditions allow.”
Volcanic ash can damage jet engines – baking on to hot internal parts and quickly wearing out turbine blades, as well as clogging fuel and air systems. It can also damage pilots’ windscreens.

blocks.caption: Passengers wait in the check-in lounge at Soekarno-Hatta international airport.  Photograph: Faisal Ramadhan/EPA

blocks.text: Ash ‌reached as high as 6,000 metres (20,000 feet) ‌on the Java side of the volcano and 15,000 metres on the Sumatra side and some parts of Banten province in Java, the meteorological agency BMKG said.
Several ​schools cancelled activities on Saturday after students and residents ​suffered eye irritationand fishers cancelled fishing trips, the local media outlet Kompas reported.
The disaster mitigation agency BNPB said it would conduct a weather modification operation, which could ​include cloud-seeding to promote rain.

“If it rains heavily enough, the volcanic ash that has been disrupting our daily lives since yesterday and continuing today will be washed away quickly,” the BNPB chief, Lt Gen Suharyanto, told a press conference.
More than 22,000 passengers and 209 flights were affected, the transport ministry said, particularly those bound to and from Singapore.
Other affected international routes included Doha, Sydney and Kuala Lumpur.
At least 16 domestic flights to Bali were cancelled, local airport authorities said.

Anak Krakatau, which means “child of Krakatau”, sits in a strait that separates the islands of Java and Sumatra. The volcano has been sporadically active since it emerged from the sea in the caldera formed after the 1883 eruption of Mount Krakatau. That was one of the deadliest and most destructive volcanic eruptions in human history. About 35,000 people were killed.
Port authorities said ships passing through the strait were prohibited to go within a two-mile radius of the volcano and should be vigilant.
With Agence France-Presse

articles.title: Dozens feared trapped in collapsed building in Delhi
articles.summary: As many as 50 people are thought to have been inside the five-storey hostel when it came down.

blocks.text: Many of the students staying there were thought to be in their rooms at the time of the collapse as there were no lessons on Sunday.
A legislative assembly member said at the scene that some of the trapped students had been making calls from under the rubble.
Eyewitnesses told local media that another building beside the hostel had also collapsed.
Chief Minister of Delhi Rekha Gupta said an adjacent building had been evacuated "as a precautionary measure".
"Every possible effort is being made to safely rescue those trapped," she added.
Delhi Police said the building had only been 40 or 50 years old.
The owner of a nearby shop told news agency ANI that it was under a 100-year lease and that the leaseholder had undertaken excavation work in the basement to increase their income.
"They strengthened the upper building, but the pillars below were weak," he said, noting that the construction workers had also been buried.
The National Students' Union of India called on the government to investigate the cause of the collapse and hold anyone found responsible to account.
"Negligence with the safety of students and common people will not be tolerated at any cost," it said.
Police are searching for the owner of the building, Times of India reports.

articles.title: Iran threatens greater force if US launches more attacks
articles.summary: TEHRAN, Iran — Iran’s top negotiator on Sunday threatened a more forceful response to any further US attacks after Tehran targeted American warships in their latest round of clashes. The…

blocks.text: TEHRAN, Iran — Iran’s top negotiator on Sunday threatened a more forceful response to any further US attacks after Tehran targeted American warships in their latest round of clashes.
The exchanges of fire, which began with US raids last week, come amid a deadlock in the six-month war between the two sides.
Iran has maintained its stranglehold on the strategic Strait of Hormuz while Washington continues a counter-blockade of Iranian ports.
Washington is also seeking to choke Iran’s economy, rolling out sanctions on entities with financial links to the Islamic Republic in a bid to force it into submission.

“The Americans must have understood that the era of proportionate responses has come to an end,” said Iran’s parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, who has acted as chief negotiator in talks to end the war.
“Any aggression against Iran’s interests and security will receive a faster, more intense and more painful response,” he added, in a speech carried by state media.

On Saturday, US Central Command (CENTCOM), which oversees American military operations in the region, said Iran had unsuccessfully fired at two American warships — an aircraft carrier and a destroyer.

The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, the ideological arm of Iran’s military, said the warships had been “forced to retreat” after “suffering damage”, but CENTCOM said they successfully evaded the attacks.
In response, the US military said it struck three oil tankers linked to the Iranian Guards.
“Following Iran’s failed attacks, CENTCOM permanently disabled the IRGC crude oil carriers M/T Downy off the coast of Kharg Island and M/T Stark 1 near Jask,” CENTCOM said.

“American forces also completely destroyed the unladen crude oil carrier M/T Kylo… in the Gulf of Oman, striking the vessel in multiple critical locations to render it inoperable after the crew was directed to abandon ship.”
Video posted by CENTCOM showed large fireballs and billowing flames after projectiles slammed into the ships.
The three vessels were “part of a multibillion-dollar shadow network that funds the IRGC and its regional proxies,” CENTCOM said.

Iran quickly retaliated, with the Guards saying their naval forces “targeted three oil tankers on the unauthorized route of the Strait of Hormuz and three vessels affiliated with the child-killing America in other areas.”
It warned ships not to attempt to transit the key trade waterway via routes unapproved by Tehran.
Early on Sunday, Iran’s Guards also said they attacked a US naval drone trying to enter the strait, according to a statement carried by state television.
‘Higher economic cost’
CENTCOM commander Admiral Brad Cooper said after the exchange of strikes: “If you shoot at two of our ships, we will impose an even higher economic cost — taking out three of yours.”
The Iranian Foreign Ministry hit out at Washington over the attacks on its oil tankers, calling them “illegal and aggressive actions.”

A correspondent for Iranian state TV in Jask in the southern province of Hormozgan said one of the tankers was empty and the second was carrying oil. The crews were transported to shore on lifeboats, they said.
Another state TV correspondent on Kharg Island said the attack there caused no casualties.
The administration of US President Donald Trump has tried to downplay the significance of the six-month conflict, which has proven increasingly unpopular at home as midterm elections near.
US Vice President JD Vance has gone so far as to say that he “wouldn’t call it a war.”
Trump reiterated that view on Friday, calling the war “small potatoes” for Washington.
Iran’s security chief Mohsen Rezaei warned this week that the Islamic Republic had adopted a “new strategy” against Washington that “will shatter your foundations.”
The US has been trying to step up pressure on Tehran in a bid to wrestle control of the Strait of Hormuz, through which one-fifth of world oil supplies previously flowed.
A fragile ceasefire between the two sides collapsed in July after attacks on commercial ships in the waterway.
Trump has in recent weeks repeatedly threatened to claim sovereignty over the strait, even posting a map showing it as “new US territory.”
Vance has insisted the US will not reopen talks with Iran until it ends attacks on commercial shipping in the strait.

articles.title: PCSO GM Robles elected APLA vice chair, another 1st for PH
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Melquiades A. Robles, general manager of the Philippine Charity Sweepstakes Office (PCSO), has been elected vice chairman of the Asia Pacific Lottery Association (APLA),…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Melquiades A. Robles, general manager of the Philippine Charity Sweepstakes Office (PCSO), has been elected vice chairman of the Asia Pacific Lottery Association (APLA), becoming the first Filipino to hold the prestigious leadership position in the regional lottery organization.
Robles was elected during the 2026 APLA General Assembly held from Sept. 1 to 4 in Seoul, South Korea.
The 2026 APLA General Assembly gathered lottery leaders and industry experts from across the region under the theme “Sustainable Gaming and Innovation, New Trends.”
Discussions covered responsible gaming policies, emerging technologies, sustainable lottery operations, and evolving global industry trends.
“This is not only a personal honor but, more importantly, a recognition of the Philippines and the meaningful work being undertaken by PCSO,” Robles said.
“Through this position, we hope to contribute more actively to regional cooperation, responsible gaming, innovation, and the use of lottery revenues to uplift communities.”
His election marks another historic milestone for the Philippines in the international lottery sector, according to a PCSO statement issued on Sunday.
In September 2024, Robles became the first Filipino elected to the APLA Executive Committee during the association’s Regional Conference in Hanoi, Vietnam.
Responsible lottery operations

His election as vice chairman, for which he will serve a two-year term until 2028, reflected the growing recognition of the transparency and integrity of the Philippines and the PCSO among lottery organizations in the Asia-Pacific region, as well as the country’s commitment to transparent, ethical, and responsible lottery operations.
Under Robles’ leadership, PCSO advanced from Level 1 to Level 3 accreditation under the World Lottery Association’s Responsible Gaming Framework in a record three years.

This feat demonstrates how PCSO translated its commitment to responsible gaming into structured programs, dedicated resources, player-protection measures, and internationally aligned practices focused on integrity and ethical operations.

Founded in 2000, APLA is one of the five regional associations of the World Lottery Association. It represents lottery operators and industry partners from the Asia-Pacific region and provides a platform through which members exchange knowledge, share international best practices, and work together on issues affecting the global lottery industry.
The association has 21 full members from 12 countries and 26 associate members from 13 countries across Asia, Europe, and North America.
Stronger voice

Robles’ election gives PCSO and the Philippines a stronger voice in discussions on responsible gaming, technological innovation, lottery security, industry integrity, and the use of lottery-generated funds for public benefit.
It also creates further opportunities for PCSO to learn from international best practices and share its experience as a government lottery institution with a distinct charitable and social mandate.

The APLA and the World Lottery Association promote responsible gaming, which seeks to ensure that lottery games are conducted fairly, safely, and transparently while protecting players, particularly minors and vulnerable individuals, from the potential risks associated with excessive gambling.
Responsible gaming measures include the following:

items: age restrictions,
clear information for players
spending and play controls
self-exclusion mechanisms
access to appropriate support services=

blocks.text: “Lotteries must always be operated with responsibility and a clear public purpose. Our role is not simply to generate revenues but to ensure that these resources are translated into healthcare assistance, social services, and other programs that improve people’s lives,” Robles said.

APLA also recognizes the important contribution of lotteries to society and good causes. Across the region, member organizations use lottery proceeds to support healthcare, education, community development, sports, culture, disaster response, charitable initiatives, and other social programs.

This closely aligns with PCSO’s mandate as the Philippine government’s principal charity arm. Revenues generated from its lottery and sweepstakes operations help finance medical assistance, health-related programs, mandatory contributions to national government initiatives, support for local government units, and assistance to communities affected by calamities and other emergencies.

“PCSO’s participation in APLA allows us to bring home valuable lessons from other jurisdictions while also showing the international community how lottery revenues can become a meaningful instrument for charity and nation-building,” Robles added.

articles.title: Jamaican delegates arrive in UK to hand slavery reparations petition to King Charles
articles.summary:
Slavery’s legacy continues ‘to deprive our country and our people’, says minister, as group prepares to appeal to Jamaica’s head of state

A landmark petition is to be handed to King Charles…

blocks.text: A landmark petition is to be handed to King Charles by Jamaican over slavery reparations, aiming to confront historical crimes that still disadvantage former British colonies, the Caribbean nation’s culture minister has said.
The petition will be lodged with Charles, Jamaica’s head of state, on Monday.

“We’re a resilient people. We were able to bounce back from [Hurricane] Melissa, for example,” said Olivia Grange, who arrived in London at the weekend with members of Jamaica’s National Council on Reparations.
“But we still have a lot of work to do, and you can imagine if we did not have those inherited problems, the legacy that came out of slavery, how much better we would have been able to do so.”

First announced in June last year, the petition asks the monarch to use his authority to request legal advice from the judicial committee of the London-based privy council, the final court of appeal for UK overseas territories and some Commonwealth countries.

It wants Charles to ask whether the forced transport of Africans to Jamaica was lawful, if it constituted a crime against humanity, and whether Britain is under obligation to provide restitution to Jamaica for slavery and its enduring consequences.
Grange said that these questions and a privy council response were critical to progressing the country’s reparations claims.
Between the 15th and 19th centuries, more than 12.5 million Africans were kidnapped, forcibly transported to the Americas and sold into slavery.

Grange said that Jamaica had been the first Caribbean nation to create a national reparations mechanism, establishing it in 2009. She said the aim was to address the enduring impacts of slavery, that put countries such as Jamaica at a grave economic disadvantage and affected its ability to respond to modern-day challenges in the Caribbean, such as the climate crisis.

“We have inherited systems that continue to deprive our country and our people. The legacy in education, even in health, the way we eat, our diet because of what we were fed, our ancestors were fed,” she said.
Ralph Gonsalves, a former prime minister of St Vincent and the Grenadines who was instrumental in setting up the Caribbean Community Reparations Commission, echoed Grange’s sentiments.

“The present is very much the past, because what we are dealing with is the legacies of underdevelopment which you can source, and we do source, to native genocide and enslavement of African bodies,” he said on Sunday.

“People must remember this: that European nations were enriched because of the enslavement of African bodies.” Gonsalves is an elder and adviser for the Repair Campaign, a social movement for reparatory justice.

He said Jamaica’s visit was a critical milestone among a number of upcoming events, including a Caribbean reparations conference in Barbados later this month, and planned advocacy at the upcoming UN general assembly in late September and the Commonwealth heads of government meeting in Antigua in November, which King Charles is scheduled to attend.
after newsletter promotion

There are growing global calls for Britain and other former colonial powers to recognise hundreds of years of transatlantic slavery that treated African people as chattel as a crime, and to engage in a process of reparatory justice.

In March this year, 123 nations voted for a landmark UN resolution that described chattel slavery as the gravest crime against humanity. In June, the Caribbean launched a manifesto outlining the “moral, ethical and legal case for reparations”. And last month, a UN committee on the elimination of racial discrimination said countries were legally obliged to consider reparations for the transatlantic slave trade and take other ⁠measures to address the enduring ⁠legacy of racial ​discrimination.

The UK was one of several European countries that abstained from voting in the March UN resolution, and in October 2024, the former British prime minister Keir Starmer resisted pressure from member states to include reparations in the Commonwealth heads of government meeting agenda.
Grange said she hoped the visit would facilitate a unifying response to the complicated history.

On Sunday, the delegation will host a remembrance church service in Brixton, and later in the week they are due to meet UK members of parliament. Grange said there would also be a visit to the British Museum, to discuss repatriation of Jamaican artefacts.

She said: “We may have different history, different heritage, different skin colour, but it’s about humanity. It’s about, as a people, being able to live together, to work together, and to respect each other.

“And in our efforts to seek reparatory justice, we will use the opportunity to also promote and encourage what Jamaica is known for, One Love, because we have the song of the century through Bob Marley.”

articles.title: U.S. envoys Witkoff and Kushner arrive in Kyiv after talks with Putin in Moscow
articles.summary: U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner arrived in Kyiv on Sunday in their first official visit to Ukraine as part of a renewed push for peace more than four and a half years after Russia's…

image.caption: Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, left, greets U.S. President Donald Trump's envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff prior to talks in Kyiv on Sunday, Sept. 6, 2026. (Efrem Lukatsky/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New

U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner arrived in Kyiv on Sunday in their first official visit to Ukraine as part of a renewed push for peace more than four and a half years after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Saturday's meeting in Moscow ended without any major developments being announced
The trip by the Americans follows a meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow on Saturday, as both sides have engaged in escalating aerial attacks recently.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Sunday that his government is ready for a "constructive" discussion with the U.S. emissaries.

"We are interested in bringing the end of the war closer. Peace is needed. Security guarantees are needed. A just and sustainable postwar peace is needed. Our proposals are prepared," Zelenskyy said in a post on Telegram.
The envoys arrived by train and were welcomed at the station in Ukraine's capital by high-ranking Ukrainian officials, before being met by Zelenskyy at a ceremony in St. Sophia Square.

Washington's push to end the fighting has lost momentum, with the Trump administration focused for the past six months on the Iran war. The last known visit to Moscow by Witkoff and Kushner, U.S. President Donald Trump's son-in-law, was in January when they also held talks with Putin at the Kremlin.

items: Putin meets with U.S. envoys at the Kremlin in renewed talks over war in Ukraine

blocks.text: No breakthroughs in Moscow talks

Saturday's meeting in Moscow lasted more than three hours behind closed doors and ended without any major developments being announced. Putin's foreign policy adviser, Yuri Ushakov, described the talks as constructive, frank and useful, but he didn't discuss specific outcomes.
U.S. officials in Moscow with new proposal to end Russia-Ukraine war
While Moscow offered its "comprehensive assessment" of the battlefield situation in Ukraine, Ushakov said, the talks weren't purely focused on the war in Ukraine.
"Economic issues and potentially large, mutually beneficial joint projects for Russia and America were discussed in considerable detail," he said.
Russia and Ukraine continue to exchange fire

The air war between Russia and Ukraine has intensified as troops have struggled to make progress along the 1,250-kilometre front line. Russia has recently been using fast-flying, jet-powered drones, and the recurring wail of air-raid sirens has become part of daily life in Kyiv.
Putin and Zelenskyy had agreed to pause strikes on each other's capitals while the talks take place. Still, the two traded fire overnight into Sunday, officials said.
Russian attacks across multiple Ukrainian regions killed one person and wounded at least 10 others overnight into Sunday, Ukraine's State Emergency Service said.

items: Russian attack hits Ukraine's security service headquarters

blocks.text: In Zaporizhzhia, drone strikes killed a 74-year-old man and wounded three people, while a drone damaged an apartment building, wounding seven people, in the Khmelnytskyi region.
Ukraine's air force said Sunday that it intercepted 82 drones out of the 108 launched by Russia overnight, along with six missiles.
In Russia, a man was killed and a woman was seriously wounded when a Ukrainian drone struck a vehicle, according to local authorities in the Belgorod border region.

The Russian Defense Ministry said Sunday that its air defenses overnight shot down 258 Ukrainian drones over 14 Russian regions, the Russia-occupied Crimean Peninsula and the waters of the Black and Azov Seas.
Mixed hopes on the ground
In Kyiv on Sunday, dozens gathered for a nationwide 9 a.m. moment of silence honouring Ukraine's fallen soldiers, a daily ritual held in cities across the country.

Nataliia Lipei, 67, whose son Viktor was killed in December 2022, was among those who attended. Despite a health condition, she has travelled from city to city to take part, and said she hopes the talks in Moscow and Kyiv will finally bring an end to the war.

"I hope these steps and these meetings will definitely produce results, because there has been so much bloodshed and so many deaths here that we have to stop all of this," Lipei told The Associated Press.
Not everyone shared her hope for the talks. Oleksandr Pastukhov, a 27-year-old video editor who joined the commemoration, was skeptical that the envoys' visit would change anything.

"We've already seen delegations like this come here before," he said. "We've seen this so-called ceasefire for three days, which ended after just a couple of hours, and now we're supposed to naively think that two people will come and change something."

articles.title: Trump envoys arrive in Kyiv for first Ukraine visit
articles.summary: KYIV, Ukraine — US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff arrived in Kyiv Sunday for their first visit to the Ukrainian capital, a day after holding talks with Russia’s Vladimir Putin at the Kremlin…

blocks.text: KYIV, Ukraine — US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff arrived in Kyiv Sunday for their first visit to the Ukrainian capital, a day after holding talks with Russia’s Vladimir Putin at the Kremlin on ending more than four years of war between the neighbors.
US President Donald Trump’s business partner Witkoff and son-in-law Kushner had visited Moscow several times but had not held talks in Kyiv, which has been hit by deadly Russian strikes since 2022.
They are due to meet with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky. An AFP reporter in Kyiv saw the American envoys arrive by train.
They are hoping to revive negotiations to end Europe’s worst conflict since World War II, after a summer of escalation.
Moscow’s invasion of Ukraine has killed hundreds of thousands of people and displaced millions.
Witkoff and Kushner met with Putin on Saturday to “advance President Trump’s agenda of peace in the Russia-Ukraine War,” a White House official said in a statement to AFP.
“The two sides discussed substantive plans for next steps, which will be announced in the coming weeks, and look forward to equally productive meetings tomorrow in Ukraine.”
Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov called the talks “extremely frank,” saying the Americans “put forward a number of ideas on possible routes to a settlement,” but did not elaborate.
The Russian side told the Americans that Moscow was “confident” it could achieve its military goals of seizing the rest of eastern Ukraine, Ushakov added.
Both Russia and Ukraine have vowed not to strike each other’s capitals for three days to allow the negotiations to take place.
It was Kushner and Witkoff’s eighth visit to Moscow during the war, but it is their first in the Ukrainian capital, which has been hit by deadly Russian strikes throughout the war.
Russia’s TASS news agency reported early Sunday that Witkoff and Kushner had arrived in Rzeszow, Poland, on their way to Kyiv.
Zelensky on Sunday said Ukraine was “ready for the conversation.”
“Ukraine has always been and will remain constructive,” the wartime leader said on social media ahead of their visit.
The country’s airspace has been closed since Moscow launched the war in February 2022, and visiting leaders have been arriving by train.
For many Ukrainians, hopes of a breakthrough remain slim.
“At this point it doesn’t give me any hope. There have already been too many negotiations,” Yaroslav, a 29-year-old Kyiv resident, told AFP.
Putin thanks Trump
In televised comments before the talks, Putin said Russia would ensure the safety of the envoys in Kyiv, a city Moscow has pounded with deadly strikes throughout the war.
“We will do everything that depends on us to ensure the safety of the negotiation process and mediators such as yourselves,” Putin told Witkoff and Kushner.
Earlier Saturday, Putin had thanked Trump for persisting in his efforts to end the war despite it being “not simple.”
Of the envoys’ trip to Kyiv, he said: “No matter what happens next, contacts of this kind are undoubtedly always beneficial.”
Trump said on Friday his envoys were bringing a “proposal” to end the fighting.
“We have an idea for peace,” he said, without elaborating.
US efforts have so far not led to a breakthrough in the war, and peace efforts have stalled in part because of Washington’s war with Iran.
Russia occupied large swaths of eastern and southern Ukraine, and Putin has insisted Moscow is intent on seizing the rest of eastern Ukraine.
Limited truce
Both Moscow and Kyiv committed to suspending strikes as the negotiations took place.
“The Russian president, the commander in chief, has given the order from midnight not to strike Kyiv for three days,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said.
Zelensky said he had spoken to the US envoys and also promised Kyiv would not strike Moscow.
“From now through the end of Saturday, as well as on Sunday and Monday, Ukraine is ready to refrain from strikes on Moscow,” Zelensky said.
But fighting continued elsewhere. Ukraine’s air force said Russia attacked overnight with 108 drones and missiles, while Moscow said it had shot down 258 drones.
On Saturday, Putin said he had “noted that the Ukrainian side significantly reduced” its strikes on Russia and Moscow.
However, Kyiv said that Russian strikes had killed 10 people across the country on Saturday, including a child and his family members in the Kharkiv region and two people outside Kyiv. /mcm

articles.title: Indonesia’s main airport suspends operations after volcanic eruption
articles.summary: JAKARTA, Indonesia — Indonesia halted operations at its main international airport outside Jakarta on Sunday after ash spewed from the Anak Krakatoa volcano more than 150 kilometers away, impacting…

blocks.text: JAKARTA, Indonesia — Indonesia halted operations at its main international airport outside Jakarta on Sunday after ash spewed from the Anak Krakatoa volcano more than 150 kilometers away, impacting thousands of passengers.
Mount Anak Krakatoa erupted on Saturday, producing a fountain of lava and booming sounds that could be heard up to a few hundred kilometers away, the geology agency said in a statement.
Two new eruptions were recorded on Sunday, the volcanology agency warned.

Ash from the volcano was detected in the airspace surrounding Soekarno-Hatta International Airport, prompting authorities to initially suspend operations from 1:30 a.m. Sunday (Saturday 1830 GMT) to 5:30 a.m.
The suspension was extended three times, with the latest ending at 5:30 p.m. Sunday “due to increased eruptive activity,” the airport said in a social media post.

Operations have been suspended at six airports, including Husein Sastranegara Airport in Bandung and Radin Inten II Airport near Bandar Lampung on Sumatra, the country’s Transportation Minister Dudy Purwagandhi said.
Several airports in cities, including Semarang and Surabaya, have been prepared as “alternatives for landing,” Dudy added.
Passengers scrambling
The disruption left some passengers scrambling to find alternative flights.
Henny Yensan, 44, who had hoped to go back to her hometown with her mother, said “everybody was disappointed.”
“No one flew into a rage, because after all, this is due to a natural disaster,” the businesswoman, who had to reschedule her flight to Tuesday, told AFP.
Samuel Guiberteau, a Danone executive on a business trip to Lombok since Friday, said “nothing is certain for the moment,” as he searched for alternative flights back to the capital.
“I had found another flight on Citilink, but it was also canceled,” the 47-year-old told AFP by phone, adding that he had no alternative but to stay in Lombok for the time being.
More than 22,000 passengers have been impacted by the suspension, the Transportation Ministry said, adding that 209 flights were affected, in particular those to and from Singapore.
Other affected international routes included Doha, Sydney and Kuala Lumpur.
At least 16 domestic flights to and from Bali were also canceled, local airport authorities said.
Hazard warning
Anak Krakatoa, which means Child of Krakatoa, sits in a strait that separates the islands of Java and Sumatra.
Ships passing through the strait were asked to increase vigilance for possible disruption to navigation safety due to volcanic activity.
Vessels are prohibited from approaching the exclusion zone within a three-kilometer radius of the volcano, local port authorities said in a statement.
The volcano has been sporadically active since it emerged from the sea at the beginning of the last century in the caldera that formed after the 1883 eruption of Mount Krakatoa.
That disaster was one of the deadliest and most destructive in history, with an estimated 35,000 people killed.
Geology agency head Lana Saria said “seismic activity indicates the movement or release of volcanic fluids within the volcanic system.”
“However, the timing, magnitude and nature of the next eruption cannot be precisely predicted,” Lana added.
Lana warned against approaching Anak Krakatoa, saying materials ejected from the volcano could endanger those within the exclusion zone.
She said the most recent series of eruptions does not have the potential to trigger a tsunami at this time.
A 2018 tsunami, triggered by a collapse of parts of Anak Krakatoa, killed 429 people and left thousands displaced.
Indonesia, a Southeast Asian archipelago nation, sits on the Pacific Ring of Fire, where the meeting of continental plates causes high volcanic and seismic activity.

articles.title: Counter-tariffs won't just affect the cost of goods for Canadians. They'll hit the trailers moving them too
articles.summary: Canadians bracing for billions of dollars in counter-tariffs won't just see prices rise on American items like produce, toilet paper and furniture, but on the very semi-trailers used to haul those…

image.caption: Semi-trailers built in the U.S. are on a long list of items included in Canada's counter-tariff measures, set to come into effect Tuesday. (Vitpho/Shutterstock)

blocks.text: Manitoba

Canadians bracing for billions of dollars in counter-tariffs won't just see prices rise on American items like produce, toilet paper and furniture, but on the very semi-trailers used to haul those goods.
Semi-trailers, largely built in U.S., expected to see 25% counter-tariff take effect Sept. 8

Canadians bracing for billions of dollars in counter-tariffs won't just see prices rise on American aluminum, toilet paper, furniture and more — but on the very semi-trailers hauling those goods into and around the country.
Ocean Trailer, the largest retailer of semi-trailers in Western Canada, is waiting on a $45-million order of 600 trailers from U.S. manufacturers.
The company is rushing to get as many over the border before a 25 per cent Canadian counter-tariff on trailers, and scores of other items, takes effect on Tuesday.

"The extra cost, the 25 per cent, is well above our profit margin on a trailer, so we would have no choice but to pass that along to the customer," said Mack Keay, Ocean Trailer's chief operating officer, told CBC News from Vancouver.

The federal government announced dollar-for-dollar countermeasures will take effect at 12:01 a.m. on Tuesday on $27.6 billion worth of U.S. goods, in response to the latest round of tariffs imposed by President Donald Trump's administration.

Keay said it's possible Ocean Trailer may be able to cancel some of its order, which was expected to flow in trailer by trailer until the end of the year, but it's on the hook for the trailers that are already in the process of being fabricated in the U.S.
The ones the company can't get into Canada by Sept. 8 will have to be parked somewhere in the U.S. or sold to American-based retailers, and Keay said he wouldn't get back what he paid for them.
Industry 'very much concerned'
Ocean Trailer isn't alone.
The head of the Manitoba Trucking Association said the vast majority of semi-trailers in Canada come from the U.S.

"I know a number of members that currently have trailers on order and are very much concerned about the cost of those trailers, because they ordered them before the counter-tariffs," said executive director Aaron Dolyniuk.
"I don't know that they'll be able to afford to pay 25 per cent more for them when they get here."
Dolyniuk said many businesses that rely on those trucking companies to ship product are also "rushing to get things north of the border before the [counter-]tariffs come on."
"I was talking to one member late last week … [who] said normally, they hauled two loads for this one customer northbound, and they wanted 15 this week," he said.

items: Stand together, buy Canadian and 'diversify away from the United States of America': Manitoba trade minister

blocks.text: A variety of types of semi-trailers are towed along Canadian roadways, but the two most common are called dry vans and refrigerated vans.
The latter, also known as "reefer" vans, haul groceries, pharmaceuticals and other items that need temperature-controlled conditions during transport to avoid spoilage.
Dry van trailers are used to haul everything from kitchen appliances to car and machine parts, paper products, furniture, televisions, canned goods and other non-perishable items.
'This is not going to be OK'

There are just two semi-trailer manufacturers in Canada — one based in Ontario that doesn't manufacture reefer van trailers and another in Quebec which does, along with making dry vans, flat fright vans and other specialty trailer types.
Neither would have the capacity overnight to absorb the increased demand for trailer orders or rentals from Canadian trucking companies following counter-tariffs.
Ocean Trailer's Keay said Canada's domestic manufacturing capabilities are less than half of what the trucking industry would need to meet demand.

items: Winnipeg business that dropped U.S. shipping, suppliers 'cold turkey' last year relieved to dodge tariffs

blocks.text: At the industry level, the potential added costs from counter-tariffs are eye-watering.
The average cost across trailer varieties is about $75,000, said Keay. A 25 per cent tariff would drive that closer to $95,000.

Each of the seven Ocean Trailer branches from Manitoba to B.C. is bringing in one or two trailers per day, either associated with orders from trucking companies or to be added to the company's rental fleet, said Dallas Senebald, the branch manager for the Winnipeg office.
"This is not going to be OK. Not just us not being OK, the industry is not going to be OK," said Senebald, whose Winnipeg office employs 40 people.
"There will be a shortage of trailers, which then increases demand, increases the cost of the trailers, and that gets filtered down right to consumer goods that are needed to be shipped."
If this lasts many weeks ... there could be companies going bankrupt.- Aaron Dolyniuk, Manitoba Trucking Association
Senebald said trends in semi-trailer sales can be unpredictable year to year, depending on supply and demand of goods that need shipping.

One year, a larger corporate customer might order 100 trailers for purchase, and then none the next year, said Senebald. The Winnipeg branch might bringing in 300 to 400 trailers one year, and 80 the next, he said.
The variability is one reason the industry relies on a mixed model. Ocean Trailer has about eight suppliers — seven in the U.S. and one in Mexico, said Senebald.
On top of being the largest retailer of semi-trailers west of Ontario, it's also the largest business for rentals.

In the short term, Canadian trucking companies may turn to rentals as they hold off on buying U.S. trailers that cost them 25 per cent more due to counter-tariffs, said Senebald — and that's a concern.
"Demand for rentals is going to skyrocket so much so that we probably won't have enough to fulfil customer needs," he said.
"Saying no to customers repeatedly is never a good thing. Eventually, they stop calling."
The trucking association's Dolyniuk said the depth of pain felt will ultimately depend on how long the tariff war goes on.
"If this lasts many weeks ... there could be companies going bankrupt within the trucking sector and outside of it," he said.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Bryce Hoye is a multi-platform journalist with a background in wildlife biology. He has worked for CBC Manitoba for over a decade with stints producing at CBC's Quirks & Quarks and Front Burner. He was a 2024-25 Knight Science Journalism Fellow at MIT. He is also Prairie rep for outCBC. He has won a national Radio Television Digital News Association award for a 2017 feature on the history of the fur trade, and a 2023 Prairie region award for an audio documentary about a Chinese-Canadian father passing down his love for hockey to the next generation of Asian Canadians.

articles.title: Germany, Kosovo unite against ticks carrying deadly virus
articles.summary: Germany has high-security labs while Kosovo has Hyalomma ticks and experience with the deadly Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever. Working together, German and Kosovar scientists are fighting the disease…

image.caption: The Hyalomma tick prefers warm, dry conditions and, thanks to climate change, it is increasingly finding these further northImage: Fabian Sommer/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: It can spot its prey from up to 200 meters (about 650 feet) away — but unlike many of its fellow species, it doesn't lurk in the grass waiting for its victim to come closer. Instead it runs after it, chasing animals and humans alike.

The Hyalomma tick, often called "the great hunting tick," was previously found mostly in Africa, Asia, and southern Europe. But climate change means it can now survive further north and it has already been spotted in Germany and various Eastern European countries. Kosovo, in southeastern Europe, has been a hot spot for the tick for some time now.

The Hyalomma tick is also a vector of the highly pathogenic virus for Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever, a potentially deadly disease with a high fatality rate. Symptoms of the disease are comparable to those of Ebola fever or the Marburg virus. These are capable of destroying blood and lymphatic vessels, which can lead to internal bleeding and death.
Ticks are spreading

Kurtesh Sherifi first read about Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever in the newspaper in 2005, when he was completing his studies as a veterinarian in Berlin. The article said that 11 people in his homeland, Kosovo, had contracted the disease and five had died. He was already interested in pathogens that can be transmitted between animals and humans, known as zoonoses, and Crimean-Congo fever intrigued him.

Back home, Sherifi started work with the faculty of agriculture and veterinary medicine at the University of Pristina. But the budget for research was tight. Kosovo, a small country with only about 1.6 million citizens, didn't have a high-security laboratory or the equipment necessary for investigating the Crimean-Congo fever virus.
Seeking German cooperation
Sherifi got in touch with Germany's largest institution for study in this area, the Bernhard Nocht Institute for Tropical Medicine in Hamburg.

One of the researchers was Petra Emmerich, a virologist and expert on what are known as Risk Group 4 viruses — viruses that cause severe, often fatal, diseases and usually have no widely available treatment. The Crimean-Congo virus is in that risk group.

Emmerich also acts as a reservist in the German military, which is especially interested in viruses that could be used as biological weapons. She was sent to Kosovo in 2009, which is when she met Sherifi.

blocks.caption: While the much smaller common longhorn beetle (left) waits for a suitable victim to pass by, the Hyalomma tick prefers to go huntingImage: Fabian Sommer/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: A lively exchange began between the researchers. In Kosovo, a structure was established to monitor the spread of the Hyalomma tick and the virus. In 2013, the researchers' joint work began to receive funding through the German Biosecurity Program, run by the country's Foreign Ministry and "intended to help partner countries tackle biological threats."

"It's give and take," said Emmerich of the scientific partnership. "We have the diagnostic expertise and the necessary resources but we don't have the patients." Doctors from Germany regularly come to Kosovo with Emmerich where they can exchange information with their counterparts there.
Raising public awareness is another important pillar of the Germany-Kosovo cooperation.

Farmers in Kosovo are particularly susceptible to infection — and not solely due to ticks biting them, but because they often use their bare hands to remove ticks from animals. If infected blood from the animals gets into a small wound on the human hand, the virus can be transmitted to the human.
"This is quite likely how a large proportion of the [infected] population in Kosovo got infected," Sherifi explained.
Patients require intensive care, isolation
He and Emmerich have visited schools to educate students about the dangers of the virus and how to protect against it. For example, certain tick repellents help, as do long pants and sturdy shoes.

Not all Hyalomma ticks carry the virus, and most people who are bitten by a Hyalomma tick do not become ill. However, the larger problem is that there is neither a vaccine nor any specific course of treatment for those who do end up suffering from Crimean-Congo fever.

blocks.caption: Farmers in Kosovo are at particular risk from the Hyalomma ticksImage: Idro Seferi

blocks.text: "If you do get sick, it's particularly severe," Emmerich explained. The disease begins with nonspecific, flu-like symptoms including fever, chills, aches and headaches. In severe cases, a patient will begin bleeding from the skin, nose and gums and may also experience gastrointestinal bleeding. The worst causes can result in organ failure.
Patients require intensive care and isolation because they are highly contagious.

Much of the treatment in intensive care focuses on maintaining a patient's vital functions, but they are also given the antiviral drug, ribavirin. But, as Emmerich said, "ribavirin is not all that effective in acutely ill patients." That is something the scientists have seen firsthand with cases in Kosovo.

The best answer is prevention, which is why it's also very important for the researchers to monitor the spread of the Hyalomma ticks and for them to recommend avoiding certain areas where the ticks are prevalent, if possible.
Successful tick tactics

Over the years, the researchers have not only collected thousands of the ticks but they have also conducted so-called seroprevalence studies. These use blood tests to find antibodies from past infections. This allows the scientists to determine whether humans or animals have come in contact with the virus.

Farm animals are particularly suitable for this type of study, Sherifi said, as the virus doesn't affect them. And unlike wild animals and humans, they usually remain in a clearly defined area. That means that if antibodies are detected in the blood of these animals, it's clear the virus is circulating in that area.

In Kosovo, the number of serious infections has dropped drastically in the past decade, amounting to just five cases in total. In the previous decade, there were about 100 cases. Sherifi and Emmerich believe this indicates how successful their work has been.
Of course, that doesn't mean the ticks and the virus won't spread further in Europe, and the researchers both expect this to happen.
Hyalomma ticks with the Crimean-Congo virus have just been detected in France although, so far, no humans have been infected there.
"Over the past 13 years, Hyalomma ticks have spread geographically," said Emmerich. "As a virologist, that's something to think about, and it needs to be closely monitored."

This is why it's important for the German and Kosovar scientists to pass on what they've learned to countries that haven't yet had as much experience monitoring the Hyalomma ticks, such as Macedonia and Albania.
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: Germany plans anti-drone shield over Leipzig attack — report
articles.summary: Several German cities will receive rapidly deployable units capable of defending against drone strikes on critical infrastructure, according to Bild am Sonntag newspaper.

image.caption: Germany reportedly plans a new shield against sabotage at critical sitesImage: Ardan Fuessmann/IMAGO

blocks.text: Germany is planning a comprehensive protective shield to prevent attacks like the failed assault on Leipzig airport, Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said Sunday.
On August 4, several small drones targeted Leipzig-Halle Airport in eastern Germany, with one hitting a parked plane, while another is thought to have struck an inbound cargo jet.
German intelligence agencies blamed Russia for the incident, which Moscow has denied.

blocks.caption: Leipzig-Halle Airport is a major cargo hub used to fly weapons and supplies toward UkraineImage: Daniel Kessler/imageBROKER/picture alliance

blocks.text: What did Dobrindt say about the shield?
Dobrindt told Bild am Sonntag newspaper that Russia's hybrid attacks are now a "daily" reality, adding: "These attacks will increase, but we can defend ourselves and protect ourselves."
The newspaper cited information from the Interior Ministry showing the government plans to expand the federal police's mobile drone-defense units.
The measures include vehicles and helicopters that can be quickly deployed to protect airspace over key cities like Frankfurt, Munich and Berlin to counter drone attacks.
Bild said the shield would not only intercept drones, but could also defuse drone bombs and other explosive devices.
The newspaper described how a change in the law would allow critical infrastructure operators — including water, power and defense companies — to detect and defend against drone sabotage.

blocks.caption: Jammers flood drones with radio noise, so its pilot can no longer steer itImage: Michael Bihlmayer/Bihlmayerfotografie/IMAGO

blocks.text: Russia's Lavrov accuses Merz of wanting war
On Sunday, Russia's Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov claimed the German accusations levelled against Russia were "by ​and ​large, the ​start of ‌a real war."

He reiterated Russia's denial of any involvement with the Leipzig drone attack and criticized German Chancellor Friedrich Merz for wanting to boost the country's military capability in response to hybrid threats.

"All ‌these statements by Merz about making Germany the leading military power in ‌Europe once again — they are ‌being ​put into practice. He is, in effect, declaring war on us," Lavrov told Russian state-run TV channel Vesti.
He also criticized Germany's closure of Russian House cultural center in berlin and the Russian consulate in Bonn.
Putin denies Russian involvement in Leipzig drone attack
New tech planned to boost cyber security
Bild also described how a national protective cyber shield would be set up to detect and intercept hacking attacks.
The measure comes amid hundreds of cyberattacks on government departments, infrastructure and companies each day, many of them blamed on Russia, other states and criminal gangs.

The newspaper said the government ⁠also wants to increase the use of AI, biometric facial recognition ⁠and video surveillance, especially at transport hubs, to identify suspected attackers before they carry out attacks.
Over 1,000 drone sightings in 2025
The head of Germany's Federal Criminal Police Office (BKA), Holger Münch, told Bild in December that more than a thousand suspicious drone flights were recorded over Germany last year.
These incidents mostly targeted military sites, airports, ports and defense firms and were treated as surveillance or harassment, rather than attacks.
Leipzig airport has been targeted by sabotage before. In July 2024, a suspected Russian incendiary parcel caught fire at the airport's DHL hub.
The cargo hub is also utilized by the Ukrainian military and NATO to airlift arms for use in the Ukrainian defense against Russia's invasion.

articles.title: How Prince Harry and Meghan's return to Britain is setting off 'shockwaves'

image.caption: U.K. newspapers were full of headlines after word broke last month that Prince Harry and Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, would be returning to Britain for an extended period. (William J Connolly/Getty Images)

blocks.text: After Prince Harry and Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, stepped back as working members of the Royal Family and settled in California in 2020, there was little to suggest they would want to return to the United Kingdom any time soon.
So it came as a considerable surprise when word broke that Harry, Meghan and their two children were on their way back and would settle outside London for an extended period.
"It seems so counterintuitive and so contradictory to everything that they have said since the moment they left," royal historian Justin Vovk said in an interview.

But now they're back, and even though there has been much telegraphing of the idea that Harry and Meghan are not going to be working royals again, the move carries broader implications for both the institution of the monarchy and other members of the Royal Family.
"Regardless of whatever their reasons are, their return creates massive shockwaves," Vovk said.
Harry and Meghan moving back to the U.K.
"What does this mean for Harry and Meghan as a couple? What does this mean for Harry and Meghan and their children as a family unit? How will this impact relations with the rest of the Royals?

"How will the monarchy respond to this? How will the British public respond to this? How will in particular the tabloid and the predatory media respond to this? How will Harry engage with the media in light of his wins and losses in court over the past year regarding media intrusions?"
Harry and Meghan have their supporters and detractors, and as much as they have stepped back from official royal duties, what they do and say continues to draw attention.

"They may not be working royals, but they're still members of the Royal Family," Craig Prescott, a constitutional expert and lecturer in law at Royal Holloway, University of London, said in an interview.
"Harry is the son of the King at the end of the day, and he will never not be the son of the King."
For the monarchy, Harry and Meghan's return could divert attention from day-to-day activities of the House of Windsor.
Londoners react to Prince Harry and Meghan’s move back to U.K.

"Officially, nothing changes," Prescott said. "But clearly, Harry will get attention wherever he goes, whatever he does, and so there is a sort of risk of that being a distraction from the work of the monarchy."
To avert that, Prescott sees a need for "some element" of communication between Buckingham Palace and Harry and Meghan.
Vovk sees their return as potentially a new "crisis point" for the monarchy.

"It all depends on how things are handled on both sides. We know the palace is going to — and they've already taken the position — that [Harry and Meghan are] not working royals, 'we won't be commenting on their lives now that they're back.'
"So a lot will depend on how Harry and Meghan proceed."

How they proceeded over the past few years — in what became a visible estrangement from the wider Royal Family — included several instances of pointed criticism of the monarchy and the family itself, whether through their interview with Oprah Winfrey, a Netflix docuseries or publication of Harry's memoir Spare.
More recently, there has been no public criticism, and with King Charles, there appears to have been some rapprochement.

Harry, Meghan and their children, Prince Archie, 7, and Princess Lilibet, 5, visited with the King and Queen Camilla privately when they were in the U.K. last month, prior to word breaking of their return.
"You can imagine at the personal level [King Charles] would want to see his son and the children, as I assume Camilla would at one level," Prescott said.
"But … Harry did single Camilla out for criticism in [Spare] and … that dynamic would be interesting to know more about, how Camilla views all this."

There is, however, no sense that Harry's estrangement from his elder brother, Prince William, has thawed in any way. Much media speculation since the return has focused on how William and his wife, Catherine, Princess of Wales, will be feeling about it.
"We're probably not going to hear a word about anything from them because anything that is said, people will jump on, people will try to read into it," Vovk said.

For William, Prescott suggested, there could be a risk that there would come a point when — particularly if Charles is seen to be a bit more forgiving — that the lack of contact with his brother could start to look "quite surly and sulky."
"At some point, you may have to just let bygones be bygones and just move on and not hold a grudge for forever and a day."

The return also spawns numerous questions around issues that have been at the heart of some of Harry's most vocal grievances, whether over actions of the media — particularly the tabloids — or security for him and his family.
Still, it seems likely that whatever Harry and Meghan do will draw headlines, fuel much conversation on social media and continue to divide opinion.
"Anything that they do creates a public response because whether people like them or people hate them … there is clearly something about them that still activates public opinion," said Vovk.

items: Prince Harry and wife Meghan arrive in U.K.
How will the British press cover Harry and Meghan this time around?

blocks.text: He sees multiple reasons for that, one of the biggest being Harry is the younger son of the late Diana, Princess of Wales.

People who have felt like they connected with Harry after his mother's death in 1997 have continued to feel that connection, said Vovk. He likens Harry to "a reflecting mirror that has a billion different reflecting facets on it, because there are so many millions and millions of people who take an interest in him."
"It says more about us … consuming celebrity culture than it does necessarily about Harry personally."
A new royal face on Canada's $20 bill
Canadians just got their first glimpse of King Charles on the $20 bill. Our CBC friend Natalie Stechyson had this report:
It's official — Canada has a new $20 bill.

Bank of Canada governor Tiff Macklem unveiled the new, vertical bill featuring a portrait of King Charles on Thursday in Ottawa. It's the first Canadian bank note to feature Charles, whose image replaces that of the late Queen Elizabeth II.

In a news conference, Macklem called the unveiling "historic." It's been more than 70 years since a new monarch appeared on a Canadian bank note. The late Queen Elizabeth first appeared on the bank's inaugural $20 note in 1935 as a young princess, Macklem added.
Two years later, in 1937, the bank's bilingual series featured King George on most of its bills. By 1954, with its landscape series, every note carried the portrait of Queen Elizabeth, until now.
The new bill is also historic because it "features security technologies never before used on a Canadian bank note," Macklem said.
"Our new $20 note is both visually stunning and more secure than ever."
The new note is polymer, predominantly green and vertical in orientation.
The Canadian National Vimy Memorial remains on the back. Charles is centred on the front.
The new note will gradually enter circulation in late February 2027.
In a news release, the bank explained that the portrait of Charles is surrounded by a floral and leafy tapestry "inspired by the King's lifetime dedication to the environment."

Also on the front are provincial and territorial floral emblems representing the 13 provinces and territories. A circular window, which the bank explains is visible from both sides of the note, "features plants that are culturally significant to Indigenous Peoples in Canada."

As for security features, the note has a purple security stripe that includes elements that "spin, transform and pulse" when the note is moved, the bank said. This makes the bill "easy to check and hard to counterfeit."
Bank of Canada governor unveils new $20 bill

"The new $20 note reflects important parts of who we are as Canadians, honouring our Commonwealth roots and our ties with international allies," Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne said in the news release.

"It honours our constitutional traditions through the portrait of His Majesty King Charles III and recognizes the service and sacrifice of Canadians through the Vimy Memorial, a symbol that continues to resonate across generations."
The Bank of Canada has previously noted that the $20 bill is its most-circulated currency.

The government announced that King Charles would replace his mother on Canada's currency during his coronation celebration in 2023. The first Canadian coins bearing the image of the King began circulating that December.
Back to royal work
This time of year has a back-to-school, back-to-work, holidays-are-over feel to it, and that seemed to be the case for some senior royals this week, too.
After a traditional summer break at Balmoral in Scotland, King Charles and Queen Camilla had a noticeably busier roster of engagements over the past few days.
They were at the British Museum in London on Wednesday evening to view the historic Bayeux Tapestry.

Other engagements included Charles meeting the Pakistani national cricket team at Clarence House. Camilla was at the Royal Academy of Dance, and had engagements that focused on her literary interests in Liverpool on Friday.
On Thursday evening, Camilla also made a surprise appearance at an event that celebrates "the enduring power of literary correspondence," Buckingham Palace said.
Camilla read out loud a letter that was written by Queen Elizabeth the Queen Mother after the death of her husband King George VI in 1952.
The notable uptick in royal engagements early in September is a change from the reign of Queen Elizabeth, who stayed much longer at Balmoral each summer.
"It's a slight modernization of … the royal calendar," said Prescott, who noted that there was a time when it was more based on the ecclesiastical calendar.
"The Queen just followed that rhythm of decades gone past, whereas [now] it's just more typical that September is a fully working month."
There is also, Prescott said, a sense that Charles likes his royal work, "so is perhaps, in a sense, itching to get back."
William to represent Charles at royal funeral in Norway

After the death last week of King Harald V of Norway, King Charles offered condolences and praised the late Scandinavian monarch for his "unwavering dedication," guiding his country "through times of great change with warmth and humility."

Charles also noted "close historical and family ties" between the U.K. and Norway, "with Britain one of the first countries to recognize Norwegian independence and establish diplomatic relations in 1905."

At Harald's funeral on Wednesday in Oslo, Charles will be represented by his son and heir, Prince William, Buckingham Palace announced Saturday. Princess Anne will also attend in a private capacity as godmother to the new Norwegian king, Haakon VII.
Who would represent the Royal Family in Oslo had been a matter of some curiosity.
"Everyone's asking me: 'Who will the Windsors send to the funeral?' because that is quite … significant," Vovk said.
"Over the last … 20 years, the Windsors have not done a great job in terms of participating in the royal community at things like funerals, investitures, those sorts of ceremonials."
One possibility for attending Wednesday's funeral was Prince William. Prescott noted that tradition has held that the British heir to the throne attends such occasions.
Still, there has been some inconsistency around all of this.
"When Elizabeth the Second died, we … sort of just assumed that the kings and queens of everywhere else would come, and so there's a bit of unevenness there in that relationship," Prescott said.

Harald's funeral will be held in Oslo Cathedral. Other royals expected to attend include King Willem-Alexander and Queen Maxima of the Netherlands, King Frederik and Queen Mary of Denmark, King Philippe and Queen Mathilde of Belgium and Crown Prince Akishino and Crown Princess Kiko of Japan.

items: Norway's new king takes oath before parliament after his father's death
King Harald V, Norway's reform-minded head of state, dead at 89

blocks.text: Headlines have also focused on the Norwegian royal family since Harald's death, given the presence at a related event earlier this week of his disgraced step-grandson, Marius Borg Hoiby, and the expectation that he will be at the funeral.

Hoiby, who was convicted of rape in June, is the son of Harald's daughter-in-law, now Queen Mette-Marit, from a relationship prior to her marriage to now King Haakon. Hoiby is appealing his conviction and has received permission to attend the funeral.
Royally quotable

"The Bayeux Tapestry — or the Canterbury Embroidery, as it might just have been called — recounts a conflict. Yet here it is today, nearly a thousand years later, as a precious symbol of trust, at a time when trust seems sadly to be in short supply between nations."

— King Charles, during a speech on Wednesday at a viewing of the Bayeux Tapestry Exhibition at the British Museum. The fragile tapestry that depicts the 1066 Norman conquest of England is on loan from France for the 10-month exhibition.
Royal reads
A senior equerry to King Charles and Queen Camilla who captured widespread attention online is to step down from his role supporting the Royal Family. [The Independent]

Sarah Ferguson will return to the U.K. after relocating to a Swiss chalet amid the fallout over the friendship between her and her ex-husband, Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor, and the late convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, according to reports. [The Guardian]

Amid family feuds, damaging headlines and questions about its future role, the Royal Family has spent much of the past decade managing its public image. But the importance of good royal PR dates back centuries. [The Conversation]

Princess Ingrid Alexandra has stepped into a historic new role as heir to the Norwegian throne — and appeared to pay a touching tribute to her grandmother as she stood alongside her father at his swearing-in ceremony. [Daily Mail]

articles.title: Nepal flood disaster puts climate justice under spotlight
articles.summary: Days after devastating floods swept through Nepal’s Bhotekoshi-Trisuli river basin, the true scale of the disaster is still emerging. More than 1,250 people have been confirmed dead and almost…

blocks.text: Days after devastating floods swept through Nepal’s Bhotekoshi-Trisuli river basin, the true scale of the disaster is still emerging.
More than 1,250 people have been confirmed dead and almost 4,000 are still missing.

Buildings, bridges, roads and more than a dozen hydropower facilities have been destroyed, causing an estimated $2.6 billion (€2.24 billion) in damage to public and private infrastructure, according to the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA).
Search and rescue operations for missing people remain underway, with families still hoping for their safe return.
The exact cause of the glacial collapse remains unclear, but experts say climate change is causing glaciers to melt worldwide, increasing the risk of such disasters.
A global responsibility?
For Nepal, the disaster has raised a question that goes beyond rescue and reconstruction.

It’s about climate justice and who should bear the costs and responsibility for such environmental disasters when the Himalayan nation contributes only a tiny fraction of global greenhouse gas emissions yet faces increasingly severe climate-related risks.
Nepal’s Prime Minister Balendra Shah said responding to the catastrophe is a “global responsibility.”

“As we work tirelessly to address the damage caused by this sudden and massive disaster, a deeper question has also emerged: How did this destruction happen to us?” Shah asked while addressing Parliament this week.
“Mitigating and managing its impacts is regarded as a shared responsibility of the international community,” he stressed.
Kathmandu is planning to raise climate justice issues in the upcoming United Nations General Assembly session in New York, where Prime Minister Shah himself is likely to lead the Nepali delegation.

“We will make our case about the impact of climate change and seek global support and moral obligation to tackle it,” Nepal’s Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal told DW. “We will also take the initiative of building a coalition of climate-vulnerable countries to raise our collective concerns.”
Highly vulnerable to climate impacts
Nepal, a largely rural nation of 30 million people, has contributed little to the greenhouse gas emissions driving global warming.

The country accounts for just 0.1% of global greenhouse gas emissions and emits about 0.5 tons of CO₂ per person each year, making it a “negligible contributor to climate change,” according to the World Bank.

But the landlocked Himalayan nation is highly vulnerable to the effects of climate change, with flooding, landslides, glacier-related hazards and other environmental risks threatening lives and livelihoods.
Nepal’s leaders say the country needs long-term international support to adapt to a rapidly changing mountain environment.

The country’s government estimates that implementing adaptation priorities between 2025 and 2035 could require as much as $18 billion to $20 billion. And Kathmandu wants international climate finance to provide most of these funds.
Nepal has spent years arguing in global climate forums that vulnerable mountain countries need greater support for adaptation and resilience.

In December 2009, Nepal held a historic Cabinet meeting at Kala Patthar, near Mount Everest base camp, at an altitude of 17,192 feet, to highlight the threats that climate change and glacial melting pose to Nepal and other mountainous nations.

Bimala Rai Paudyal, a former Nepali foreign minister, said the latest disaster meant “this is an opportune time for us to highlight glacier melting and climate justice issues in international climate forums.”
“Earlier, we were only advocating about climate impacts. Now, we are heavily suffering from it,” she told DW.
Paudyal believes Nepal is well positioned to lead an alliance of vulnerable countries, given its exposure to climate risk as well as its expertise and contribution to the climate justice effort.
An opportunity for global climate action?
Kathmandu has formally approached the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC)-backed “Loss and Damage Fund” for assistance over the latest floods.
But the fund, set up by the UN in 2025 to aid the impacts of climate change, has not yet begun distributing its limited cash.

The fund also relies on voluntary contributions and lacks legally binding commitments under current international climate agreements, leaving major emitters such as China, India and the US under no direct obligation to compensate for climate change impacts.
Still, some observers and climate advocates believe Nepal can present a strong case for urgent global climate action.

“Nepal can turn this tragedy into an opportunity for global climate action,” Dinesh Paudel, professor of sustainable development at Appalachian State University in North Carolina, told DW. “For which, Nepal needs to build a consensus among national stakeholders and maneuver cautiously, considering geopolitical factors.”

According to him, Kathmandu can create an ethical movement for climate justice by highlighting the recent flood. This could then lead to creating an effective and legally binding mechanism to deal with climate impacts in the future.
Ashok Swain, professor of peace and conflict research at Uppsala University and also UNESCO Chair on International Water Cooperation, shares a similar view.

“Nepal should not be left to pay for a climate crisis it did little to create or for regional non-cooperation over which it has limited influence,” he said. “This is not a question of charity. It is fundamentally a question of climate justice and a fair distribution of responsibility.” /dl

articles.title: Outrage as Maltese tycoon acquitted in journalist’s murder
articles.summary: “Murderer!” — “Scum!” — “Mafia!” As Yorgen Fenech left the courthouse in Valletta on Wednesday evening, he was confronted by the furious crowd outside. The…

blocks.text: “Murderer!” — “Scum!” — “Mafia!”

As Yorgen Fenech left the courthouse in Valletta on Wednesday evening, he was confronted by the furious crowd outside. The 44-year-old Maltese businessman pushed through, flanked by his security guards. Just minutes earlier, a jury had acquitted him of ordering the murder of the 53-year-old investigative journalist Daphne Caruana Galizia.

The verdict came as a shock to her family. Her son, Matthew Caruana Galizia, said it was a “terrible decision by the jurors that our country may never recover from.” He later doubled down on his criticism, describing the verdict in a post on Facebook as “obscene” and saying: “Their decision flies in the face of all evidence, of all logic, of the truth.”

Almost nine years after Caruana Galizia’s murder, Malta is again confronted with the crucial question: Who was responsible for her death on October 16, 2017? The men who procured the bomb, placed it under the driver’s seat and detonated it remotely have already been convicted. But the person who contracted them to do it has still not been legally identified.
A difficult trial

For years, Fenech was considered to be the central figure in the investigations. His arrest on the morning of November 20, 2019, was like something out of a movie. His luxury yacht, Gio, had just left harbor when it was stopped by a Maltese military patrol boat. Fenech was arrested on board and subsequently interrogated by the police.

Fenech’s arrest, and suspicion that people in government circles were involved in the crime, sparked protests all across the country. Joseph Muscat, prime minister at the time, was accused of protecting political allies and stepped down in January 2020. Fenech spent more than five years in detention before being released on bail, under strict conditions, in early 2025.
His trial only began this summer, and the final verdict was decisive. Eight of the nine jurors rejected the prosecution’s argument that it was Fenech who had ordered the journalist’s murder.
Who was responsible?

The prosecution case relied above all on the testimony of Melvin Theuma, who confessed to being the middleman and testified that Fenech had contracted him to organize the murder. Theuma received a pardon in exchange for his cooperation.
But Fenech’s defense called Theuma’s credibility into question, highlighting contradictions in his testimony and false statements he had made previously.

Fenech’s lawyers also sought to prove that evidence pointing to Keith Schembri, chief of staff to Muscat at the time, was not properly followed up. Schembri has denied any involvement in the murder, and the investigators did not charge him as a suspect in this case.

blocks.caption: Investigative journalist Daphne Caruana Galizia was killed by a car bomb on October 16, 2017 Image: Rene Rossignaud/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: The public prosecutors’ argument was that Caruana Galizia had been investigating Fenech, specifically his company 17 Black and the energy consortium ElectroGas, on suspicion of corruption. This, they said, meant Fenech had a motive for silencing her. She had not, however, been on the point of publishing anything that could have threatened him.
Open questions

Many in Malta are outraged by the not-guilty verdict. But there is no indication to date that Fenech did not receive a fair trial, or that the process was manipulated. For him to be convicted, Fenech’s guilt had to be proved beyond reasonable doubt.

Caruana Galizia’s family are therefore also focusing on institutional failures that they believe facilitated the murder. They complain that these have not been addressed, and necessary reforms not implemented. An official investigation already established, in 2021, that an “atmosphere of impunity” in Malta created conditions that made the murder possible.
