articles.title: Nepal-Tibet floods: two workers pulled alive from tunnel nine days after disaster
articles.summary:
Officials say pair were rescued from Trishuli 3A hydropower tunnel in Nepal after being trapped in depth of 170 metres

Two people have been pulled out alive from a hydropower tunnel in Nepal…
articles.byline: Hannah Ellis-Petersen and Gaurav Pokharel in Kathmandu

blocks.text: Two people have been pulled out alive from a hydropower tunnel in Nepal nine days after deadly flash floods buried the projects in deep mud and left them trapped.

The workers were rescued during an ongoing operation at the Trishuli 3A tunnel, a hydropower project in one of the areas worst-affected by last week’s deadly Nepal floods, according to army spokesperson Brig Gen Raja Ram Basnet.

Sanjay Shah was the first to be rescued and was taken to the Nepal army barracks in Trishuli. Another person, identified as Kabir Maharjan, was also rescued from the tunnel. They were rescued from a depth of 170 metres inside the tunnel, confirmed Basnet.
Sanjay Shah was foreman at Upper Trishuli 3A and Kabir Maharjan was a superviser.
Nepal’s army released images of Shah being pulled from the small dark entrance of a tunnel. He emerged covered in mud but conscious and was carried from the site on a rescuer’s shoulder.
Speaking to army officials after he was rescued, Shah’s first question was: “What day is it?”
Describing his ordeal, Shah said he had been in the tunnel’s control room at the time of the flood.

“Usually there would be only five or six people there but at this time there must have been around 40 to 45 people inside,” he said. “Since I was in the control room, my responsibility was to save everyone’s lives. After such an accident, I couldn’t just run away by myself. I had to save everyone.
“While trying to get everyone out, I told them that there had been a major accident at the dam and urged everyone to run. In doing so, I lost time. In the end, I couldn’t get out myself.”
To keep himself calm in the darkness of the tunnel, Shah said he spent his time chanting mantras. He said that while trapped, he had been communicating with only three or four others.
“They were communicating by shouting to each other from nearby. There could also be people inside the powerhouse. Some of them may not have been able to escape,” he said.
Officials said the two men were in stable condition and flown to a hospital in Kathmandu.
Nepal’s communication minister, Bikram Timilsina, said officials remain hopeful that more workers will be rescued. “We are waiting for the rescue of more and more people,”he wrote on social media.

Most of the hydropower projects along the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers were destroyed when a surge of water, debris and mud came coursing down the valley last week, triggered by ‌the collapse of a melting glacier on the border between Nepal and China-controlled Tibet.

blocks.caption: A survivor is carried out after being rescued from inside the tunnel. Photograph: Nepal Army/Reuters

blocks.text: At least 1,287 people were killed in the floods and more than 5,000 remain missing, according to the Nepal’s disaster management agency.

Rescue efforts have increasingly centred on the hydropower tunnels, where authorities believe workers may ⁠have survived for more than a week due to air pockets. So far, more than 270 people have been rescued across several projects.

Large boulders and flood waters had deluged the hydropower tunnels, blocking off the entrances, and some were buried deep in mud. At the Upper Trishuli 3A facility, it took rescue workers almost six days to find the tunnels.

Army and specialist teams have been working round the clock to try and clear debris from the tunnel entrance. It was confirmed that voices of many people had been heard inside after a breakthrough was made on early Friday morning.
After the rescue team called out, “Don’t panic, we are rescuing you,” they received a response from inside: “OK.”

At least 557 workers are missing from the hydropower project along the Trishuli River, with about 115 believed to be trapped in the main tunnel, according to the Independent Power Producers Association of Nepal.

Families of those missing in the tunnels have been gathering at hospitals in Kathmandu and at the Nepal electricity office for nine days, desperate for answers about their relatives. Posters of workers missing in Trishuli 3A and other projects line the wall of Tribhuvan University teaching hospital in Nepal’s capital.
In total, local authorities estimate about 900 workers are missing from 12 hydropower projects high up in the Himalayas, with about 500 believed to be trapped in tunnels.
Rescue efforts have also been focused on Rasuwagadhi hydropower plant where Nepal authorities said they are confident that 46 workers trapped in an underground chamber in the plant are still alive.

articles.title: UN to vote on adopting new world map that shows Africa’s true scale
articles.summary:
Togo-sponsored resolution calls to phase out traditional map that depicts continent as similar size to Greenland

The UN general assembly will vote on Friday on a resolution for the world to…

blocks.text: The UN general assembly will vote on Friday on a resolution for the world to formally phase out the traditional Mercator map of the globe in favour of one that more accurately displays Africa’s size.

Robert Dussey, Togo’s foreign affairs minister, said the resolution was sponsored by Togo and backed by countries including the African Union’s 54 other member states. He did not specify the total number.

blocks.caption: The 1569 map by Gerardus Mercator (1512-1594) has remained the global standard. Photograph: Stock Montage/Getty Images

blocks.text: “This discussion is not a political discussion [but] a scientific discussion, because there is scientific proof so we all have to accept the reality,” he said.

UN resolutions are non-enforceable but if the vote passes, it could lead to an update of classroom curriculums and everyday technology, given the wide usage of the Mercator projection in education, technology and governance.
The layout was introduced by the Flemish cartographer Gerardus Mercator in 1569 to help sailors navigate the seas. Almost five centuries later it remains the global standard.

Because of its projection style, however, regions near the equator appear significantly smaller than they are, whereas high-latitude areas look much larger. For example, the map shows Africa as being similar in size to Greenland, but the continent is 14 times larger than the Danish territory.

“You could fit the United States, China, India, Japan, Mexico and much of Europe into Africa and still have land to spare,” says a petition on Change.org for the #CorrectTheMap campaign, which has more than 11,000 signatures. The African Union endorsed the campaign in August 2025 and then asked Togo to spearhead its adoption.
Historians and geographers have said for years that the Mercator projection is rooted in western stereotypes. Activists have echoed this, with some coining the term “cartographic colonialism”.

Some argue that the map has subtly shaped international power dynamics by minimising the physical presence of the global south and visually inflating northern hemisphere nations while shrinking equatorial regions. This, they say, has reinforced systemic biases in international trade, development priorities and educational frameworks.

One of the Mercator projection’s most prominent critics was Arno Peters, a German historian, who launched the Peters world map based on the Gall–Peters projection in 1973. It has often been used as an alternative to the Mercator map.

blocks.caption: The 2018 Equal Earth Map. Photograph: equal-earth.com

blocks.text: Togo’s #CorrectTheMap campaign is promoting the use of the more accurate 2018 Equal Earth design, which was developed by an international team of cartographers. Supporters say it will help to reverse perceptions of Africa and decolonise global curriculums.

Some analysts agree too. JJ Enoch, a London-based senior associate at JS Held, a geopolitical risk advisory firm, said the Mercator projection visually diminished Africa’s true scale. He linked the campaign to a quest by African nations for “greater influence in global institutions and greater control over how the continent is represented”.

He added: “Adopting an equal-area map … would provide a more accurate basis for education and public understanding, while signalling that Africa’s demographic, economic and geopolitical importance should no longer be viewed through inherited and distorted conventions.”

blocks.caption: A map of Africa from Mercator's atlas dating between 1595-1602. Photograph: Royal Geographical Society/Getty Images

blocks.text: Togolese authorities hope the vote will go the same way as another African Union-backed decision at the UN this year. In March a Ghana-sponsored resolution to describe the slave trade as “gravest crime against humanity” passed, with 123 states voting in favour. Three states voted no and 52 abstained.

Ghana’s success has given supporters of the map cause to believe in a favourable outcome. Togo’s government is planning an event in Lomé, the Togolese capital, with Unesco, the African Union and tech brands such as Google Maps during the first quarter of next year to map out the implementation of the resolution.
Dussey said: “To those who say why now, I say, why not? When we look at the world map … it is time for us to change the narrative.”
He added: “It’s time for us in Africa to take responsibility to change what we can change ourselves.”

articles.title: Spain’s PM says no evidence ‘whatsoever’ Morocco behind Ceuta border breach
articles.summary: Pedro Sánchez continues to defend Rabat after police report claiming border forces helped 70,000 cross border

blocks.text: Spain has seen no evidence “whatsoever” that Morocco planned or facilitated a mass border breach into its north African territory of Ceuta, the Spanish prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, has told parliament.

The address on Thursday followed the emergence of a police report, commissioned by a judge and widely quoted in the media, claiming Moroccan border forces had actively aided about 70,000 people to cross the border in late July.

“I ‌can assure you ‌that no institution – not the diplomatic service, nor the European Commission, ‌nor any international body – has provided the Spanish government with any solid evidence that Morocco planned or carried out the incident. None whatsoever,” Sánchez told parliament.

Speaking the morning after about 50,000 people marched in Madrid to protest his handling of the Ceuta crisis, the socialist prime minister also denied the government had received any warning of the mass breach, saying no reports to authorities had anticipated “the scale or probability of what eventually happened”.

blocks.caption: A protest against the Spanish government’s handling of the recent border breach at Ceuta. Photograph: Francesco Militello Mirto/NurPhoto/Shutterstock

blocks.text: Sánchez has repeatedly defended Morocco during the crisis, highlighting Rabat’s cooperation in returning most of the migrants in the days after the surge.

But he said on Thursday that Spain had summoned Morocco’s ambassador on 21 August because of “unacceptable statements” made by two ministers over Ceuta and Melilla, another Spanish north African territory. Last month, Morocco’s justice minister, Abdellatif Ouahbi, publicly reiterated Rabat’s sovereignty claims over the cities.
Sánchez said he had “for now” ruled out Moroccan government involvement but conceded that Moroccan forces had allowed crossings to occur during a key 10-hour period on 30 July.
Many of those who crossed said in interviews they had been actively encouraged to do so. Moroccan officials have denied enabling the crossing.
Alberto Núñez Feijóo, the leader of the conservative People’s party, called on Sánchez to resign for his “incompetence and complicity”.

In response to Sánchez summoning the Moroccan ambassador to discuss the crisis, Santiago Abascal, the leader of the far-right Vox party, said: “Morocco doesn’t need an ambassador in Spain – you are its ambassador.”

blocks.caption: People who entered Ceuta from Morocco in late July on hunger strike last month to demand asylum.  Photograph: Laura Rincon/EPA

blocks.text: As many as 141 people are thought to have died trying to enter Ceuta at the end of July. The influx unleashed a political crisis, a humanitarian emergency and reignited tensions within the EU over immigration.

On Thursday, Sánchez appealed for European solidarity over the crisis. He did not single out any countries by name but, in a pointed passage apparently aimed at Italy and Denmark, the two countries that had led public criticism of Spain, said the principle of solidarity should apply to Ceuta as much as it applies to Greenland and Lampedusa.
Although 90% of the people had returned to Morocco within 24 hours, several thousand, including at least 500 minors, are thought to remain, either living on the street or in makeshift shelters.

Amid calls from Vox to return them to Morocco, Sánchez reminded parliament that under Spanish, European and international law, migrants had a right to be treated as individuals. “You can’t just grab someone by the arm and drag them across the frontier as though they were a sack of dirt,” he told MPs.

In reference to the hundreds of destitute minors, Aina Vidal of the leftwing group Sumar, said: “They’re children, not invaders, not soldiers. They didn’t come carrying bombs, they arrived wearing water wings, in tears.”

It seems likely the government will invest in facilities in Ceuta to accommodate the remaining migrants rather than risk the political backlash both in Spain and across Europe were they to bring them to the mainland.
There is also evidence that, faced with hunger as well as hostility from many local people, some migrants have already begun going back to Morocco.

However, as Sánchez told parliament, the per capita income of Ceuta is eight times that of Morocco and “even if we build a wall 100 metres high there will still be people prepared to throw themselves into the sea to get across”.
“We will not stop working until Ceuta emerges from this difficult situation: stronger, more prosperous, and more integrated with the rest of Spain and the EU,” he added.
Additional reporting by Jakub Krupa

articles.title: Dozens of trapped hydropower tunnel workers in Nepal could still be alive, official says
articles.summary: About 46 people believed to be trapped in ‘room-like’ structure inside hydro plant tunnel on Nepal-Tibet border
articles.byline: Hannah Ellis-Petersen and Gaurav Pokharel in Kathmandu

blocks.text: Nepal authorities have said they are “confident” that dozens of workers in Nepal’s Rasuwagadhi hydropower plant are still alive, more than a week after deadly flash floods left them trapped in an underground chamber.
Authorities said that at least 639 workers were still missing from hydropower plants built along Nepal’s Bhote Koshi and Triushuli rivers.

Most of the projects were destroyed when a surge of water, debris and mud came coursing down the river valley last week, triggered by ‌the collapse of a melting glacier on the border between Nepal and China-controlled Tibet.
The deadly flash floods reached up to 100mph (160km/h), according to scientists, and travelled more than 60 miles down the river valley, wiping away whole villages, bridges, and hydropower dams.
At least 1,252 people have been confirmed dead from the floods. More than 4,200 remain missing.

According to a preliminary estimate by the UN Development Programme, the disaster created at least 2.2m tonnes of debris, including parts of buildings, rocks and sediment. Large boulders and flood waters deluged the hydropower tunnels, blocking off the entrances, and some were buried deep in mud.

Rescue efforts have increasingly centred on these tunnels, where authorities believe workers may ⁠have survived for more than a week due to air pockets. So far, more than 270 people have been rescued from the hydropower projects.

blocks.caption: A turquoise-green house stands tall amid sludge near Trishuli River in the aftermath of flash floods.  Photograph: Arun Sankar/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Speaking on Wednesday, officials said they believed 46 people were still alive in an underground room in Rasuwagadhi hydropower plant, and efforts were ongoing to locate them using excavators and other heavy equipment.

“We are very confident that they must be alive after one week because … they have food and water over there in the building,” Amhsu Kiran Shahi, a board member of the Nepal ⁠electricity authority, told Reuters.

Durga Gurung, 60, said his brother Jhappad Bhujel was among those trapped in a hydropower tunnel. “Right now, we are just relying on God,” he told the Guardian. “We have not been given any information about whether the people inside are alive or not.

“Neither the army nor the people from the electricity authority are telling us anything. So many days have passed that we have reached a point where it feels like all we can do is hope for a miracle.”
“Our relatives are sitting inside a dark tunnel,” he added. “How long can they possibly survive?”

blocks.caption: The area around Rasuwagadhi hydropower plant before the flash flood.  Photograph: Maxar/DigitalGlobe/Getty Images

blocks.text: Major rescue operations were under way or planned at four hydropower projects. Two sites – the Rasuwagadhi hydroelectric project and the Upper Trishuli 3A facility – where about 90 people are missing, offered the strongest prospect of finding survivors because of the presence of air inside the tunnels, Shahi said.

The Rasuwagadhi hydroelectric project is located in Rasuwa district, about three miles away from the border with Tibet, which was one of the areas of Nepal hardest hit by the floods, and remains almost inaccessible except by helicopter. “This is the only project where it’s possible to walk through ‌the tunnel,” Shahi said. “The army tried doing that three days ago, but they didn’t find the room. We are going in again.”

At the Upper Trishuli 3A facility, another project hit by the floods, it took rescue workers almost six days to find the tunnels ⁠because of the thick mud. The authorities believe about 30 to 40 people may still be alive in the tunnel. “We are expecting [survivors] in there because we ​are told there is a ​dry space inside. We are ​trying to break into the tunnel now,” said the Nepali army spokesperson Raja Ram Basnet on Wednesday.

The army said the search and rescue operation would go on for as long as there was hope for survivors, but that efforts would also continue to recover the dead bodies. “We are using every technology ​available in Nepal ‌right now, and we ​are taking help ​from the Indians, Chinese, Koreans. We have experts from Australia too,” added Basnet.

Families of those still trapped in the projects have returned to the Nepal electricity office for the past eight days, in the hope for information. Laxmi Adhikari’s brother Jeevanlal Adhikari had gone to the Trishuli 3A Hydropower Project to test the machines, when the floods hit.

She accused the authorities of withholding information from the families, and of not acting fast enough to save their relatives. “We have been running from one ministry to another and from disaster management authority to another government office, trying to find my brother,” she said. “We keep going from place to place, but the rescue operation has not been accelerated.”

She said the lack of answers made the wait even more painful: “When the water came rushing in, where did he go? Did he manage to get to safety? They haven’t even given us definite information about whether our people are alive or not.”

Nepal has invested more than $9bn (£6.7bn) in building hydropower dams across the mountains, huge sums given the country’s small economy. According to preliminary surveys, the floods debilitated or destroyed 11 hydropower plants and knocked out about 10% of Nepal’s total electricity-generation capacity.
According to the authorities, more than 20,000 houses will have to be rebuilt in the aftermath of the flood. Nepal has put the cost of recovery at more than $5bn (£3.7bn).

articles.title: Victims sue South African government over 1961 Sharpeville massacre that left 91 dead
articles.summary:
Claim relating to infamous apartheid-era shooting of protesters part of wave of litigation for apartheid-era crimes

The day dawned brightly on 21 March 1960, as residents of the South…

blocks.text: The day dawned brightly on 21 March 1960, as residents of the South African township of Sharpeville gathered to protest against pass laws, which forced “Black, Indian and Coloured” South Africans to carry documents at all times specifying where they were allowed to be.

Abraham Mofokeng joined the march, one of dozens organised nationwide by the Pan Africanist Congress (PAC), a breakaway group from the African National Congress. “The weather was very nice, the sun was out. You could not have suspected that the day would go so horribly,” said Mofokeng, who was then a 20-year-old factory worker.

blocks.caption: Abraham Mofokeng, who was shot in the foot and back while protesting against South Africa’s apartheid pass laws during the Sharpeville massacre on 21 March 1960.  Photograph: Rachel Savage/The Guardian

blocks.text: Mofokeng, now 86, was among the thousands gathered peacefully outside the police station in Sharpeville, which is about 40 miles south of Johannesburg in a heavily industrialised region known as the Vaal Triangle.
The crowd was singing, he said, when officers opened fire without warning. At least 91 people were killed and 238 injured, in what became known as the Sharpeville massacre.

As Mofokeng fled, a bullet grazed the inside of his right foot, ripping his shoe off. A woman fell to the ground before him; he jumped over her and kept running. Only later, when he noticed blood running down his legs, did he realise he had been shot in the back, where a bullet remains lodged in his spine.
Mofokeng is among three claimants suing the South Africa government, in a case filed on Thursday, for compensation for the massacre. If the case is successful, dozens more could file claims.

The case is part of a wave of litigation demanding justice for apartheid-era crimes, amid widespread disillusionment with ANC-led governments that have failed to rectify South Africa’s huge racial inequality and poverty since the end of apartheid over three decades ago.

blocks.caption: Dead and wounded South Africans lie outside the Sharpeville police station. Photograph: PN2

blocks.text: In January 2025, 25 survivors and relatives of victims of apartheid state violence sued South Africa’s government for failing to prosecute cases referred to it by the post-apartheid Truth and Reconciliation Commission. That May, the president, Cyril Ramaphosa, announced a judicial inquiry into potential political interference, which is still ongoing.
Spokespeople for South Africa’s justice department did not respond to a request for comment on the Sharpeville compensation case.

In the immediate aftermath of the Sharpeville massacre, police claimed that protesters had been throwing rocks at them. “I don’t know how many we shot,” said Colonel J Pienaar, the local police commander, according to a story published by the Guardian the following day. “It all started when hordes of natives surrounded the police station. My car was struck with a stone. If they do these things they must learn their lesson the hard way.”

In July 1961, in response to victims filing compensation claims, the white minority regime passed a law indemnifying the government and anyone acting under its authority for any actions taken “in good faith for the prevention or suppression of internal disorder, the maintenance or restoration of good order, public safety or essential services, or the preservation of life or property”.

blocks.caption: Members of a choir perform during the commemorations of the massacre, at the Phelindaba cemetery in Sharpeville, on 21 March 2026.  Photograph: Marco Longari/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: The law, which was made effective retrospectively from the date of the massacre, is still in force today. The claimants’ legal team is arguing that the law is unconstitutional.

The claimants are hoping to get compensation of about 500,000 rand (£23,000), said Daniel Leader, a partner with UK law firm Leigh Day, which is advising the South African legal team, led by Lawyers For Human Rights, an NGO.
Mafokeng was awarded 30,000 rand as a one-off payment, after the TRC concluded in 2003. The TRC had recommended annual reparations payments of around 20,000 rand for six years.
“We continued to suffer,” said Mofokeng, who still lives in Sharpeville. “Especially now … I am struggling and my health is not up to standard.”

blocks.caption: Paulina Mathinye, whose father Samson was killed by police in the Sharpeville massacre Photograph: Rachel Savage/The Guardian

blocks.text: The other two test claimants were children when their fathers were killed in the massacre. Paulina Mathinye was five when her father Samson was shot. “Every time he came back from work, I would be so happy to see him that I would run to him, and then he would pick me up,” she said.
Mathinye didn’t initially understand what had happened that day in 1960. “I kept on asking my mum: ‘Mummy, why are you crying?’”

Mathinye’s mother struggled to raise her five children on a domestic worker’s wages and Mathinye, who had wanted to train as a teacher but couldn’t afford the bursary, had to leave education at 17 to find work.

Mathinye, who is now 71, said she hoped for compensation that would make up for some of what she lost when her father died. “Some of my friends are teachers, some of them are nurses, and I’m staying in the same house that my father did,” she said.

Sharpeville’s problems didn’t begin with the massacre in 1960, but with the dispossession of Black South Africans from productive land, their forced removals to townships and their exclusion from the economy, said Vincent Thamae, a PAC member who supports the massacre victims and their families.

“When people talk about compensation now,” he said, “compensation is a concept to them that includes all the land that they lost, the economy that they were taken out of and even how they have been treated in the new democracy.”

articles.title: Barclays faces complaint over backing for power plant near world’s largest mangrove forest
articles.summary:
Bangladeshi complainants allege Rampal power station’s pollution and climate risks threaten the Sunderbans, a world heritage site

Barclays Bank is facing a formal complaint over its…

blocks.text: Barclays Bank is facing a formal complaint over its financial links to a coal-fired power station near the Sundarbans, the world’s largest mangrove forest and home to millions of people in Bangladesh and India.

Three complainants from the region have submitted a case to the UK government’s Office for Responsible Business Conduct, alleging that the British bank breached international guidelines by underwriting companies involved in the emission-heavy Maitree super thermal power project, also known as the Rampal power plant.

The coal-fired power station is situated near the Sundarbans, a Unesco world heritage site made up of more than 100 tiny islands across a river delta that supports hundreds of plant and animal species, including the Bengal tiger.

Sharif Jamil, an environmental campaigner based in the Bangladeshi capital, Dhaka, who is one of the complainants, said heavy-metal pollution from the plant and the industrial development surrounding it was entering the Sundarbans through its interconnected rivers and canals.
“The Rampal power plant is right on the bank of the Pasur River, which is the lifeline of the Sundarbans,” he said. “The health of the forest is in trouble.”
Last November, a study found elevated levels of mercury and arsenic in water samples taken from the Sundarbans, with the highest concentrations recorded in the Pasur River.

Researchers identified industrial discharge and port-related activities among the sources of heavy-metal contamination and said the Rampal power station posed “a significant environmental threat due to emissions from coal combustion and increased navigation traffic”.

blocks.caption: The Sundarbans, the world’s largest mangrove forest and one of the last habitats of Bengal tigers, supports the livelihoods of millions of people.  Photograph: Bengal Picture Library/Alamy

blocks.text: Millions of people live in the Sundarbans, and many depend on the river and forests for food and other resources.

The claimants allege that Barclays failed to conduct sufficient due diligence on the environmental and human rights risks before providing financial services to organisations connected to the project.

Barclays underwrote debt of India’s state-owned NTPC Ltd (formerly the National Thermal Power Corporation), one of the joint-venture partners behind the plant, according to King’s Legal Clinic, which is assisting the complainants. It also says Barclays underwrote bond issues for the Export-Import Bank of India between 2016 and 2019, which provided a loan for the Rampal project.

The complainants argue that emissions from the plant will contribute to global heating, rising sea levels and extreme weather in a region already highly vulnerable to the climate crisis. Mangroves act as a natural barrier against cyclones and other extreme weather.

The power station faced sustained opposition during its planning and construction, including concerns raised by Unesco in a report in 2016, which concluded that “air and water pollution have a high likelihood to irreversibly damage the … World Heritage property”. Some financial institutions, including banks in France, refused to support the project because of its potential environmental and social effects, the complaint says.

Jamil said Barclays’ international standing obliged it to consider the consequences of financing. “The greater your reputation, the greater your responsibility to behave responsibly towards the planet and its people,” he said. “Barclays is a reputed global organisation, and that is why it also has a responsibility.

“Other banks and financial institutions were divesting from, or declining to finance, this project,” he added. “Barclays and other financial organisations should change their policies and examine how their operations can protect the planet from climate catastrophe.”

Jamil also called on banks to direct more funding towards renewable energy rather than imported fossil fuels. “Bangladesh has sunlight throughout the year,” he said. “Why should we expand fossil fuels when there is enormous potential to produce electricity from renewable energy?”
The other complainants include Animesh Mandal, a farmer and politician, and the Dakshinbanga Matsyajibi Forum, a trade union representing fish workers in West Bengal.
They are being assisted by students and lawyers at King’s Human Rights and Environment Clinic, part of King’s College London’s law school.

Sue Willman, a solicitor at the clinic, said: “Rural communities in the Sundarbans are on the frontline of the climate and nature crisis. We hope to persuade banks and financial institutions to think again before financing oil and coal developments that are contributing to that crisis.”
The Office for Responsible Business Conduct, part of the Department for Business and Trade, will assess whether to consider the complaint.
Barclays Bank and BIFPCL (Bangladesh India Friendship Power Company Ltd), the holding company for the Maitree super thermal power project, declined to comment.

articles.title: Relief as five Australians missing in Nepal-Tibet flood disaster found alive
articles.summary: Several missing Australians have been found since Tuesday morning, bringing the total citizens unaccounted for to 38

blocks.text: A total of five Australians missing after devastating floods ravaged the Nepal-Tibet border last week have been found.
Of the five Australians confirmed safe, one was found in Nepal, one in Tibet, and three outside the crisis-hit area. The total number still missing is 38.
These Australians had not spoken to families and next of kin since the disaster struck seven days ago.
There were “grave concerns” for the dozens of citizens still missing in the disaster, the minister for multicultural affairs, Anne Aly, told the ABC on Wednesday morning.
“There are real logistic issues, including communications to find out where people are,” she said.

“For those families that are still waiting, those 38 individuals unaccounted for, we understand that it’s a really concerning time, and we’ll continue to do what we can to try and locate those people.”
Earlier, the minister for the Pacific, Pat Conroy, told Radio National the government was “focused on establishing their whereabouts and supporting their families”.
The Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade (Dfat) has received nearly 800 calls in relation to the floods, with 18 Australian personnel having travelled to Nepal to join staff on the ground.
More humanitarian and disaster relief from Australia was due to arrive in Nepal on Wednesday afternoon.
Another Australian, 25-year-old Cara Severino, was safely located last week.
After an Australian in Tibet made contact with family and Dfat yesterday, the foreign affairs minister, Penny Wong, said the government was “incredibly thankful”.
“It’s hard to imagine the sense of relief their loved ones must be feeling after what will have been an incredibly harrowing few days.”
The death toll from the ⁠unprecedented deluge of ice, rock, mud ​and debris on Wednesday last week has risen to 939 people, with 16 more dead reported in Tibet.
More than 4,400 people are missing.
Wong said the government needed to “remain realistic” about the days ahead.
“Communications remain difficult, infrastructure has been destroyed and many areas are still difficult to reach,” she said.
“As each day passes, our grave concerns for those still unaccounted for inevitably grow.
“Our thoughts remain firmly with all those waiting for news of family and friends, and with the search and rescue teams working in extraordinarily difficult circumstances.”
Australia has sent a $8m assistance package for affected communities on the border between Nepal and the Chinese region of Tibet.
Nepal has deployed nearly 20,000 security personnel to support search and rescue, and Chinese state media has reported that 2,141 emergency personnel have been deployed.

articles.title: British aid worker mistakenly identified as a survivor of Nepal-Tibet disaster
articles.summary:
More than 1,000 people confirmed dead and more than 4,000, including 36 British nationals, remain missing

A British aid worker was mistakenly identified by Nepalese authorities as a rescued…

blocks.text: A British aid worker was mistakenly identified by Nepalese authorities as a rescued survivor after returning to Kathmandu on a humanitarian aid flight.
Alastair Chambers, a 45-year-old former Gloucester councillor, said he flew to Nepal last week to distribute sleeping bags, food and essentials to communities cut off by collapsed bridges.
After spending several days in a village near the Trishuli river in central Nepal, Chambers returned by helicopter to the capital, where he was greeted by police officers asking for his details.
“I gave them my details, just abiding by the rules, and they obviously thought that I’d been rescued,” Chambers told the Press Association.
Chambers appeared on a list of 119 names released by local authorities on Tuesday. An army spokesperson then told reporters at a press conference that a British national was among those rescued.

“I was contacted by about 15 different journalists in the last few hours, just asking how I was and how I’m feeling after being rescued, and I had to say: ‘Well sorry, I haven’t been rescued,’” Chambers told PA.
Those rescued included 118 Nepali nationals – 44 women and 74 men.
Thirty-six British nationals are missing, the Foreign Office minister, Stewart Wood, told the House of Lords on Tuesday. The figure had previously been put at 33.

Chambers was fined £49,000 after pleading guilty in June 2022 to breeding and selling dogs without a licence. The 45-year-old, who was the leader of a group of community independents on Gloucester city council until 2024, is due to face trial in November after denying he used homophobic slurs against a bar owner and former council worker.
At least 1,050 people have been confirmed dead in Nepal since Wednesday’s flash floods, while Chinese state media said 66 people had been killed in Tibet. More than 4,000 people are still missing.
Nepal’s prime minister, Balendra Shah, said 11,000 people had been rescued across the affected region. This included 330 foreign nationals, the Nepalese tourist board said in an update on Tuesday.
Preliminary analysis of satellite imagery suggests the collapse of a glacier high in the Himalayas was the primary cause of the disaster.

The collapse – so large it was initially recorded as a magnitude-4.4 earthquake – triggered a deadly torrent of water, mud and ice that tore along the Lhende Khola, Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers on Wednesday.
Crews have faced dangerous and difficult conditions while searching unstable terrain and flood debris.
Search efforts are now focused on attempts to reach about 600 workers believed to be trapped inside tunnels at several hydropower stations in the region.
“Massive work has been going on in the tunnel, all the tunnels,” the army spokesperson said on Tuesday.

A rapid deployment rescue team from the UK arrived in Nepal on Saturday to provide support for Britons and their families as part of the government’s £5m commitment to support relief and recovery efforts.
The Red Cross estimates that 93,000 people have been directly affected by the disaster.

articles.title: Stephen Fuhr was mocked for opposing purchase of F-35s. Now he's in charge of Canada's defence procurement

image.caption: Stephen Fuhr during his time as a pilot with the Royal Canadian Air Force. He is now secretary of state for defence procurement. (Stephen Fuhr/Facebook)

blocks.text: Stephen Fuhr got his "Picasso" nickname back in his days as a fighter pilot in the Royal Canadian Air Force (RCAF).
He'd been ordered to produce detailed attack maps, but his abstract scribbles earned him a call sign inspired by the cubist master, according to former military officials.
Today, the 57-year-old holds a more serious title: Canada's secretary of state for defence procurement.

In this role, he leads the Defence Investment Agency, an organization created last year by Prime Minister Mark Carney's government to speed up the procurement of tens of billions of dollars worth of military acquisitions.

items: Canada announces Defence Investment Agency to manage purchase, delivery of military equipment
Canada joining international program to build next generation of fighter jets

blocks.text: It's been a quick rise for the former CF-18 pilot who, after retiring from the Armed Forces in 2009, drew mockery from members of the military community by vigorously opposing the purchase of American F-35 aircraft.
Multiple sources indicate that relations remain strained to this day between Fuhr and the RCAF, whether over fighter jets, radar planes or helicopter replacements.
In an interview with CBC News, Fuhr said he is always ready to fight for his convictions.
"I'm not afraid to stand out on the hill by myself," he said. "It's just a principled place to be. And sometimes it's lonely, but that's just the way it is."

CBC News spoke with a dozen people who have interacted closely with Fuhr over the years. Some requested confidentiality to avoid harming commercial relations with the government, or were not authorized to speak publicly.

Fuhr — who is from Edmonton but now lives in B.C.'s Okanagan Valley and is MP for Kelowna — first became interested in aviation when his grandfather took him to model airplane competitions. He never lost his taste for speed and flight.
In addition to his pickup truck, he enjoys getting behind the wheel of his sporty Porsche 911 or flying his own aircraft, a two-seater Van's RV-8 featuring a shark mouth on the nose.
Sitting in the cockpit in a hangar at the Kelowna airport, he tells CBC News this plane is his "happy place."

But he rarely gets time to fly over the nearby mountains. After travelling the world in recent months, his summer schedule was once again disrupted by wildfires in the area. Fuhr's house in West Kelowna was burned to the ground by a wildfire in 2023 and was only recently rebuilt.

Now, his political career is set to become even more demanding. Under the Liberal government's Bill C-31, he could soon inherit new powers as head of the Defence Investment Agency to award sole-sourced contracts in order to protect Canada's "economic security."
The measures proposed in Bill C-31 would create a "super minister" in charge of military procurement, said Justin Massie, a defence expert at Université du Québec à Montréal.

"He would have more power than Mélanie Joly at industry or [David] McGuinty at national defence, because he would combine many of the powers that were usually or historically delegated across several departments," Massie said.
Fuhr is in line to oversee a dramatic increase in Canada's defence budget, amid a promise to reshape the military relationship between Canada and the U.S.

items: Canadian military goes to U.S. for F-35 ceremony despite renewed trade tensions

blocks.text: He says he's aiming for a sweeping transformation of the military procurement system, either by producing more equipment in Canada or by finding new global partners.
"We are going to become less reliant and more resilient," he said.
"The good news is we have friends in every time zone. And everybody wants to work with Canada."
Fuhr gets an obvious political boost from being a former CF-18 pilot. Being a member of Canada's select "top gun" club is an enviable calling card.
Still, sources said Fuhr is seen as an outsider by many prominent members of Canada's fighter pilot community.

During his four years in a CF-18 squadron at CFB Cold Lake in Alberta, from 1999 to 2003, he was known for standing up to his commanding officer and his career had its share of ups and downs, according to several sources.
Fuhr did not wish to comment on personal issues during the interview.
Some former pilots argue Fuhr lacks "operational credibility" within their community, having never been part of deployments in conflict zones.

He counters by pointing to a defining moment of his piloting career after the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks, in which airliners were turned into missiles. He said he had trained for war, but not the scenario in which he took to the skies to protect North American airspace as commercial planes were redirected to Canada.
"When you've got hundreds of civilian airliners full of people coming your way, and that is now a threat you have to work through, that's a different mind space," he said.
After leaving CFB Cold Lake, he worked in Winnipeg managing Canada's fighter fleet and then training pilots and instructors. He retired from the RCAF after 20 years with the rank of major.
Fuhr made more of a name for himself after returning to civilian life in the early 2010s.
What Canada’s fighter jet decision could mean for NORAD
While many in the fighter pilot community were tireless supporters of the F-35, he became a fierce critic.
"It may be a great airplane, it's not the right plane for Canada," he said on CBC's Power & Politics in 2011.
Friends and former colleagues speak of his fixation against the Lockheed Martin aircraft, which had been chosen by the Stephen Harper government to replace the CF-18s.
F-35 proponents say the aircraft is superior to any other Western fighter jet due to its stealth capabilities and the extraordinary amount of data it can process.

Still, Fuhr objected to the purchase for Canada, citing the project's staggering costs, numerous delays and some of the technical difficulties faced by some air forces. His opinion was based on a thorough review of every major study on the aircraft, including various public reports from the U.S. and Canadian governments on the program's failures.

items: Canada not angling to get out of F-35 contract with U.S., says head of defence procurement

blocks.text: He knew by publicly attacking the F-35, he was taking on many of his former air force colleagues.
"From the fighter pilot community, the F-35 has basically been considered the be-all and end-all," said Mike Reyno, a military magazine publisher and friend of Fuhr.
"What Stephen has done, and this is all with publicly available documentation, is [point out] the F-35 has actually failed to meet almost every critical point along its development."

A former supporter of the Conservative Party of Canada, Fuhr ran as a Liberal Party candidate in the 2015 federal election alongside Justin Trudeau, drawn in part by the Liberal promise to cancel the F-35 purchase.

He won the Kelowna-Lake Country seat but lost it to the Conservatives in 2019. He then became a consultant for Boeing, among other roles, and continued to criticize the F-35, describing the aircraft as "unaffordable" in 2021.
Two years later the Trudeau government announced the purchase of 88 F-35s, signing a firm contract for 16 aircraft.
Fuhr returned to politics last year, this time alongside Carney, who responded to growing tensions with the U.S. by subjecting the F-35 purchase to a review.

items: Saab offering 10,000 jobs, Joly says, as Canada's F-35 review drags on

blocks.text: There is no doubt Canada will integrate F-35s into its air force, but the real question is how many aircraft the government will ultimately buy, and whether it will decide to add Swedish Gripen fighters to its military arsenal.
Canada quietly makes payments related to 14 more F-35 jets
Easygoing and approachable, Fuhr is a fixture at defence trade shows, announcements, business trips and media interviews.
He is a prime target for lobbyists and executives hoping for a share of the new defence investments.
"He talks to everyone," said a lobbyist whose clients find it easier to get meetings with Fuhr than the defence minister.

Numerous procurement files are moving ahead much faster than expected under his leadership, including Swedish GlobalEye radar planes, German-Norwegian submarines and the purchase of over 60,000 assault rifles from Colt Canada.

items: Carney chooses German submarines for Canadian navy fleet
Canada fast-tracks army rifle upgrade with $307M initial order

blocks.text: But Fuhr has ongoing tensions with the RCAF regarding the diversification of equipment supply sources.

"The Canadian Army and the Royal Canadian Navy have welcomed the change," said Reyno. "I would say that the air force hasn't been as welcoming to that because the Royal Canadian Air Force basically wants to operate everything the Americans operate."
Fuhr is not closing the door to new mixed fleets of aircraft or helicopters, while the RCAF has stated its objections to the purchase of Gripens.

"Many of our allies … run a mixed fleet with fighters," says Fuhr. "I don't necessarily subscribe to the fact that we can't do it. We certainly can and we've done it and our allies do it now. So it's a function of 'do we want to do this or not?'"
Despite disagreements on the matter, a former pilot says he wishes Fuhr the greatest success in his bid to modernize Canada's sclerotic military acquisition process.
"Stephen Fuhr has to succeed. Whether anyone likes him personally or not, it is crucial for Canada to procure the right equipment to do the right job in a timely manner," they said.

Fuhr is aware he carries the reputation of an unyielding politician who holds firm views on various procurement projects. He says he is always ready to change his mind — but only if he is given compelling evidence.
"That evidence better actually bring something to the table and be credible. And if it doesn't do those two things, then I don't see a reason anyone should change their position," he said.
Throughout the interview, Fuhr made an effort not to speak directly about the F-35, a particularly sensitive topic given the trade and diplomatic tensions with the U.S.

items: Canada ready to further distance itself from U.S. on military procurement

blocks.text: Still, he smiled as he was asked about recent comments by U.S. Gen. Gregory Guillot, the commander of NORAD, who said F-35s weren't necessarily the best aircraft to protect the Canadian and American borders.
"He is the commander of NORAD. So I think what he says, I take him at his word," Fuhr said, breaking into a laugh.
